More than 800,000 new trees have been planted across Surrey over the past five years, exceeding the council's own target, according to a report.
Surrey County Council's report found 116,359 trees had been planted in the 2025/26 financial year alone.
It said the total planted between 2021 and 2026 was around 885,000, surpassing its initial target of 600,000.
However, Elmbridge Borough Council recently passed a motion calling for the future East Surrey council to update its tree strategy to consider survival rates.
It said many trees planted in the borough were dying within a year as a result of not receiving the right aftercare.
"There is little point celebrating the number of trees we plant if a significant number of them are dead a year later," said councillor Katerina Lusk.
'Economic pressures'
Surrey County Council has committed to 1.2 million trees being planted by 2030, representing one for every resident.
The authority's report looked at the progress of its climate change delivery programme over the past five years.
It said the council was "broadly on track" to meet its 2030 net zero targets, stating that its carbon emissions have been reduced by around 60%.
The report said: "A major success of the programme has been supporting residents to reduce energy bills and improve their homes.
"More than 1,438 low-income households received energy efficiency improvements, including insulation, solar and low-carbon heating measures."
It also acknowledged challenges ahead in continuing to pursue decarbonisation policies.
The programme was "significantly affected by external market conditions, supply chain constraints and wider economic pressures", it added.

This story is part of an investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project. Read the other stories here.
For two thousand years, the Ambracian Gulf in western Greece provided life to its Mediterranean neighbors. Today, it’s an industrial graveyard.
Trace the Gulf’s northern coast, and you’ll uncover beaches of Styrofoam, not sand. Descend into its murky depths, and you’ll find waters depleted of the oxygen essential for marine life. Scour the nets of local boats, and you’ll encounter few fish.
A national park, protected wetland and marine protected area, the Gulf is supposed to be a sanctuary for sea life. Yet critically endangered bottlenose dolphins, loggerhead turtles and Dalmatian pelicans share this home with 19 active and 11 abandoned fish farms. Despite the damage that’s already been done, the Greek government wants to allow more.
As the home of the most valuable farmed finfish industry in the European Union, Greece produces over 120,000 tons of fish annually, exporting most overseas. But here, in the Ambracian Gulf, the continent’s gamble on the blue economy has hit a biological wall. This is the epicenter of an intensifying debate over industrial aquaculture.
“It’s like having a vulnerable cancer patient and letting him keep smoking,” said Roxani Naasan Aga-Spyridopoulou, a marine scientist from Thessaloniki who opposes plans to double the Gulf’s fish farming output. “Something needs to be done for Amvrakikos because it’s dying,” she said, referring to the Gulf by its Greek name.
While Greek waters have hosted industrial aquaculture since the 1980s, the blueprints for its recent wide-scale expansion—into designated aquaculture regions known in Greece as POAYs—were never debated in public nor decided by the communities they’d displace. Instead, they were fast-tracked by eight government ministers in the dead of night during a Prime Ministerial confidence vote at the height of the 2011 Eurozone crisis.
In November 2011, amid mass protests over Greece’s austerity measures and the deepening economic crisis, 3,000 protestors packed the streets outside the Greek parliament, chanting “Thieves! Thieves!” Inside, cabinet members—including one whose family owned the oldest industrial fish farm in Greece—signed a decree to expand aquaculture areas 24-fold.
By dawn, 60,000 acres of coast had been earmarked for multinational companies in a desperate bid for foreign investment. By dusk the following day, Prime Minister George Papandreou had resigned, and the government had collapsed. The POAYs, however, remained, and have been slowly rolled out across Greece’s once-pristine waters over the last 15 years.
Greece is not alone in its ambition to farm more fish. Globally, aquaculture is a $313 billion industry, the fastest-growing sector of the food business, whose growth is driven by the planet’s explosive appetite for seafood; we now consume twice the amount of seafood that we did decades ago. More than half of all seafood consumed by the world’s population now comes from aquaculture rather than fish caught in the wild.
But the rapid expansion of fish farming has come with a variety of social and environmental impacts, according to a five-year investigation of the global fishmeal industry by The Outlaw Ocean Project. These “externalities” are costs most often borne by poorer countries where feed is harvested and processed, far from the places where the seafood is eaten.
Many of these costs are especially hidden because they are buried within the feed that goes into producing farmed fish. The most popular types of farmed seafood around the world—salmon, shrimp, trout, seabass, sea bream—are fed what is known as fishmeal, protein-rich powder made from the very kinds of wild fish that aquaculture claims to be saving, thereby accelerating ocean depletion.
Greece’s Ambracian Gulf offers an example of the highly visible impacts suffered by the communities engaged in farming seafood. A semi-enclosed fjord-like ecosystem, the Gulf is only connected to the Ionian Sea by a narrow bottleneck less than half a mile wide. Unable to breathe like open seas, it takes years for the Gulf’s water to fully replenish. It’s a slow-moving, almost stagnant basin, where nearly every drop of aquaculture waste—uneaten nutrient-rich feed, fish excrement or carcinogenic chemicals—sinks to the seabed.
Exacerbating existing factory pollution and agricultural waste runoff from two feeder rivers, fish farms here are accelerating eutrophication—a process that triggers deadly algal blooms and strips water of oxygen.
The result is an underwater desert. Once home to critical carbon-capturing seagrass meadows, the areas surrounding the Gulf’s cages are a biological “no man’s land,” according to divers. Arms-length visibility. Murky brown water. And a ghostly white, bacterial blanket.
Trapped between the anoxic seafloor and surface temperatures warmed by climate change, wildlife find themselves squeezed in the middle of a shrinking habitable zone.
For the fishermen who have spent their lives hauling nets, anoxia simply means the end. Fifty years ago there were over 5,000 fishermen in the Gulf. Now, in the wake of aquaculture’s expansion, there are just a few hundred, according to Pavlos Charalambous, a fourth-generation fisherman who now leads the local fishing association.
“There is no fish in the bay, no fish in the lagoon, no fish at all,” Charalambous said. Since he caught his first fish at age 6, Charalambous has watched the Gulf slowly wane in health while fish farms creep in at the edges. “The sea is about 70 to 80 percent dead,” he said over the hum of his boat’s engine—a vessel dwarfed by the farms measuring up to a thousand feet in length.
A Growing Wealth Gap

This investigation was reported in a collaboration between Inside Climate News and Columbia Journalism Investigations.
CALIPATRIA, Calif.—On a border-town road surrounded by alfalfa and grain fields, William Cooper stopped before a dusty, vacant lot. Its owner, he said, is one of many investors drawn to the arid Imperial Valley by a critical mineral propelling the green energy transition.
“They buy it up and leave it, just waiting for the opportunity,” Cooper said of the land investors.
Now, with each gust of desert wind, dust drifts from the lot into the yards of two adjacent schools. Often, the buildings disappear behind a haze and the schoolchildren gasp for air, said Cooper, who moved here from San Diego years ago.
The pollution adds to a litany of burdens plaguing one of the nation’s poorest areas. And it hints at a new pressure reshaping the area’s future: a lithium deposit buried beneath a nearby lake called the Salton Sea—the mother lode for prospectors rushing to extract this key ingredient for the batteries that power electric vehicles.
Companies are racing to draw out lithium from brine bubbling below the Salton Sea. With hefty government support, developers say they will create “the most sustainable lithium and power project in the world,” bringing hundreds of jobs and billions of dollars here.
In Calipatria’s county, Imperial, local officials greenlit two mines and launched an ambitious proposal to use direct lithium extraction, a fledgling technology touted as a cleaner alternative than traditional lithium mining. Company executives and government officials alike promise to transform Imperial Valley into a renewable-energy hub—what they call “the next Silicon Valley.”
These lithium ventures are among 100 proposed mining projects advancing through the permitting pipeline in the country today, as the U.S. ramps up critical-mineral production. By 2030, at least half dozen new mines are expected to extract lithium, with another 13 soon to follow, an investigation by Columbia Journalism Investigations and Inside Climate News has found. Most are concentrated in the dry Southwest.
Using corporate filings and other records collected by the financial firm S&P Global, the news organizations identified roughly 540 proposed lithium mines worldwide, as well as the companies and investors behind them. The first-of-its-kind dataset offers a window into just who controls America’s lithium rush—from global mining conglomerates and smaller explorations firms, many based in Australia and Canada, to powerful American financial institutions that dominate the sector’s funding network.
Nearly two-thirds of the proposed and developing mines in the U.S. bump up against some of the nation’s most socially and economically vulnerable communities, according to an analysis by Columbia Journalism Investigations and Inside Climate News of demographic measures like income, age and race. Topping that list is Imperial County, an area of mostly Hispanic residents that has severe unemployment rates, low schooling levels and crowded housing conditions.
Interviews with dozens of residents, advocates, government officials and company executives and visits to four states reveal the stark tension in the energy transition: Who gets to define “clean”? And who has to live with the impacts of mining needed to build cars that don’t foul the air?
In Imperial County, where lush farms dominate an otherwise parched landscape, rising heat and drought are colliding with the lithium industry’s water demands. Control over increasingly scarce water supplies determines who will benefit from lithium extraction and who will bear its costs. A small number of landowners whose water rights date back a century are set to profit, while many nearby residents struggle to pay the basic utility rate for clean drinking water.
Lax and inconsistent regulations leave these same residents with few enforceable economic, environmental and community protections.
James J.A. Blair, an associate professor of anthropology at California State Polytechnic University, Pomona, has studied lithium mining’s social impacts. Places like Calipatria already face significant inequities, he said, and lithium development that doesn’t attempt to mitigate them is likely to deepen those rifts. The mineral’s importance to the clean energy transition means its impacts on communities and the environment often receive little scrutiny, he added.
“They’re using lithium as a kind of loophole to make everything seem green,” Blair said.
Across the West, the lithium boom is on a collision course with climate-driven declines in rivers and aquifers. Federal data shows that almost all proposed or developing lithium projects are in counties where risk of drought is expected to rise sharply—much more so than in most of the nation. Nearly six in 10 are in places where drought is projected to cause some of the most severe impacts.
A recent study concludes that most lithium mining areas won’t have enough water by mid-century to meet the industry’s demands.
“Those regions are already water-stressed,” said co-author Jennifer Dunn, director of the Center for Engineering Sustainability and Resilience at Northwestern University. Adding lithium mining onto them without reducing water consumption across the board will make it extremely challenging for those mines to operate in the near future, not to mention meeting everyone’s water needs, she said. “As engineers, we can think of some technology solutions to cut water consumption, but the engineering is not going to get you over the hump in this case. It really has to be a local discussion about how we want to use water.”
In Amargosa Valley, Nevada, where wells are already running dry, residents feared that a lithium mining company’s proposed drilling would threaten their sole water supply. Queen conch larvae drift for two to three weeks before settling into seagrass, where their first food grows on the thin green blades. This is where they spend most of their first year, buried in the sand.
In the Exumas region of the Bahamas, just south of East Sampson Cay, Shedd Aquarium researchers recorded the third-highest mean density of juvenile conch among the sites in a 2019 survey.
But a developer, Miami-based Yntegra Group, plans to dredge about half a hectare (1.26 acres) of the cay’s North Bay for a service dock at Rosewood Exuma, a resort that Rosewood Hotels & Resorts would operate. Two neighboring developers, of Turtlegrass Resort & Island Club and the private island Over Yonder Cay, have asked the Bahamas Supreme Court to overturn the project’s environmental approvals. The judge has not yet ruled; a spokesperson for the Save Exuma Alliance, a coalition of Exuma businesses that includes Turtlegrass, said a decision is expected within weeks.
The case puts the queen conch, a species the U.S. lists as threatened, between these developers. The court won’t decide whether the dock harms conch, only whether the government lawfully approved the project.
Representatives for Turtlegrass argue that the public was consulted before key documents, including the environmental management plan, were released, and that the project was split into separate permits so its combined effects were never assessed together.
“They don’t need to dredge at all,” said Eric Carey, a paid consultant to Turtlegrass and former head of the Bahamas National Trust. He argued that the service dock could go in one of the resort’s southern marinas “without any additional dredge footprint.” He hopes the judge will rule that the consultation and assessment were too deficient to justify a commercial dock in the bay, pushing it to the south.
Yntegra says the southern end of the cay cannot support a service area, and the Bahamas’ Department of Environmental Planning and Protection director called the North Bay site “the most feasible option.”
An engineering analysis Turtlegrass commissioned estimated that, at the developer’s own design depth, a navigable channel and turning area would roughly double the volume of seabed dredged at sea compared with the developer’s assessment.
More dredging would result in disturbed seagrass, and scientists who study conch in the Exumas say it is the channels’ tidal flow, not just the acreage, that keeps nurseries like this one alive.
In April, Justice Leif Farquharson barred dredging and other works in North Bay until the case is decided. He wrote that he did not regard Turtlegrass’ case “at present to be particularly strong,” and he ordered Turtlegrass to post $3 million in security to cover Yntegra’s losses if the challenge fails.
Records filed in the case show the DEPP has twice stepped in at the site. After a March 2025 monitoring report, it issued a cease-and-desist order, finding that land clearing for soil testing had gone beyond what was needed. According to a sworn affidavit from DEPP Director Rhianna Neely-Murphy, the developer was told “not to widen the paths as if clearing for road construction.” The order was later lifted. Yntegra’s own environmental consultant reported to the department that “a large area was cleared” for a plant nursery that was “not within the plans,” before its environmental monitor reached the island.
In July, videos on social media showed a sediment plume spreading from barge deliveries to the cay. They “appeared to indicate” that a silt curtain meant to contain the sediment “had not been effective,” Neely-Murphy said in a sworn affidavit, and the developer’s consultants were told to halt that delivery method. A floating dock was installed so barges no longer touch the beach and seafloor.
Defending the approvals in court, Neely-Murphy said the project “did not initially meet with the standards for sustainable development” and that the review reduced its footprint. However, the review failed to factor in the conch.

The developer’s 2025 environmental impact assessment includes a photo of a juvenile conch in seagrass near the site but it does not estimate how many conch live there or how densely; queen conch does not appear in its list of marine species observed. Responding to public comments, the developer said conch “were not observed in abundance” during its surveys and that the project “does not intend to impact conch nurseries.”
Andy Kough, a Shedd Aquarium research biologist who studies queen conch in the Exumas, said nurseries like Sampson Cay’s persist because flood tides flush them with larvae and clean offshore water.
“Disrupting the flow patterns into these channels may irreversibly change their suitability as a place for young conch to settle and grow to maturity,” he said. Scientists still know little about how conch respond to development, he added, but in the Exumas most young conch settle in seagrass, and destroying it “would have detrimental effects on young conch.”
The stakes reach beyond one bay. NOAA Fisheries listed queen conch as threatened in 2024 and identified overfishing as the main threat. Florida closed its commercial conch fishery in 1975 and recreational harvest in 1985, and the population there has been slow to recover.
“You can’t expect the conch to recover if you’re harming their habitat,” said Megan Davis, a research professor who directs the Queen Conch Lab at Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute.

9f3b0dc2e954.text: America's youth sports boom is quietly rewriting Sunday mornings, turning the family calendar into a competition between the pews and the playing fields. Why it matters: For generations, churches helped organize American family life around a shared weekly ritual. Youth sports are increasingly filling that role on Sundays — reshaping what families treat as sacred time. The U.S. has undergone one of its fastest religious shifts in modern history, marked by a rapid increase in the religiously unaffiliated and in church closures . Youth sports are one of the less visible forces driving that broader cultural change. As it's boomed into a multi-billion-dollar industry , more games are moving to Sundays, something less common a generation ago. "The idea of missing church for sports is just assumed," Linda Flanagan, author of " Take Back the Game : How Money and Mania Are Ruining Kids' Sports — and Why It Matters," tells Axios. "It's just not even a consideration anymore." By the numbers: Among parents of children ages 5-17, Sunday religious participation fell from 26.8% in 2003-07 to 16.7% in 2021-24, an Axios analysis of American Time Use Survey data found. Meanwhile, youth sports participation climbed to 58% in 2024, up from 53.8% in 2022 and marking a third consecutive annual increase, according to the Aspen Institute's Project Play . Another measure found 65% tried a sport at least once — the highest share in Sports & Fitness Industry Association data dating to at least 2012, the Aspen Institute's Project Play found. State of play: The youth-sports industrial complex is rapidly commercializing, fueled by private equity , massive tournament complexes and the normalization of out-of-state travel teams. Parents are increasingly treating sports not just as recreation, but as a primary identity and community anchor. How it works: Youth sports often start in local rec leagues, then move into club and travel teams that play weekend tournaments across a wider region. Across basketball, baseball, softball, volleyball and soccer, many weekend tournaments use Saturday for pool or preliminary play and Sunday for elimination rounds and championships. That fuels cities' and towns' investments in sports complexes built to draw traveling families and their hotel and restaurant spending. Zoom in: The average sports parent spends 3 hours, 23 minutes every day their child has a practice or game, including driving, attending activities, washing uniforms, preparing meals and communicating with coaches. Families are spending heavily, too: The average sports family spent an average of $1,016 on a child's primary sport in 2024, up 46% from 2019, Aspen found. What they're saying: Tim Morey, lead pastor at Life Covenant Church in Torrance, Calif., tells Axios that sports don't necessarily sever families from church, but they make attendance "more spotty" at times. "If we inadvertently teach our kids that sports (are) more important than weekly worship, then everything is more important than weekly worship." Yes, but: Religious institutions are attempting to adapt rather than surrender. Morey said some families "divide and conquer," sending one parent to church and the other to the field. Others have kids attend the first 10 minutes of service in their sports uniforms or stream services live from team hotels. Between the lines: Youth sports can create the same sense of community that mirrors what church did — to a point, Flanagan said. Parents form tight bonds because they spend so much time together, but competition for positions and playing time can also strain those relationships, Flanagan said. The bottom line: For generations, Sunday was about getting the family closer to heaven. For many families today, Sunday can also be about getting a daughter closer to UCLA's softball team.

Pope Leo XIV has announced he will be operated "in the coming days" after a nodule was found on his lung during a medical check up.
"The doctors found an early, well-localised nodule on my lung," he told the public during his weekly Sunday prayers in St Peter's Square in Rome.
The 71-year-old pontiff said his medical team "believe it would be right to intervene" and he had agreed to the operation.
Pope Leo reassured pilgrims that the mass was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage".
He concluded his Angelus prayer by thanking everyone for their "spiritual closeness" and said he entrusted himself to their prayers.
Holy See Press Office spokesperson Matteo Bruni told the media that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of next week".
Bruni added that the Pope is expected to take about a week to recover.
Vatican News, the Holy See's news portal, said the operation will take place at Gemelli Hospital in Rome.
The hospital set up a special Papal suite following the failed assassination attempt on Pope John Paul II's life in May 1981, which is still in use today.
Pope Leo, born Robert Francis Provost, succeeded Pope Francis in 2025. He is the 267th occupant of the throne of St Peter â and is the first American.
He was ordained in 1982 and spent years as a missionary in Peru, where he is remembered as a figure who worked with marginalised communities and helped build bridges.

84929eaa6ea8.text: Pope Leo said Sunday tests had discovered a nodule in his lung , which he will have removed surgically this week. The big picture: The first American pontiff, aged 71, is less than 18 months into a papacy that has been defined by public stances at odds with the White House , including clashes over immigration and deep skepticism about AI. What he's saying: "Dear friends, during some recent medical examinations, doctors found a localized nodule in my lung. It was detected at a very early stage and is well localized. The doctors believe surgery is appropriate," the pope said during public remarks, per a translation from the Vatican. "Following their advice, I have therefore decided to undergo an operation to remove it. The operation is already scheduled for the coming days. I thank you for your spiritual closeness and entrust myself to your prayers." The pope did not explicitly say the nodule was malignant. Vatican officials later said the operation would be in the next few days and the recovery would take about a week. This is breaking news.

At least 109 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) has said.
The boat was travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 350 people on board, when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Around 80 people were rescued, the IOM said.
IOM's Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the tragedy a "stark reminder" of the dangers migrants face while seeking a new life elsewhere.
Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa make the perilous journey each year hoping to reach Gulf countries for safety and work, according to the UN agency.
In a statement on Friday, the organisation said 52 men, 42 women, nine girls and six boys were among the bodies recovered.
"This is a devastating loss of life," Coissac said.
"Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives," he added.
Local authorities are also arranging burials for those who have died, while the survivors - all Ethiopian nationals - have medical care readily available to them.
Yemen remains engulfed in a devastating civil war which has lasted more than a decade. Despite this conflict - and growing instability across the wider region - migrants still cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen driven by poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change.
Since 10 September, the IOM said its Displacement Tracking Matrix has observed more than 20,000 "movements" from Ethiopia to Djibouti.
IOM said it is providing assistance to 64 of the survivors at its response centre in Obock, including healthcare and support to "restore contact with their families".
The UN agency is working in "close collaboration" with local authorities to help migrants and "prevent deaths at sea and on land", it added.
According to IOM figures, more than 900 migrants died or went missing taking the same route in 2025, with an 18% increase in the number of people attempting the journey.
In March 2026, nine people were killed and 45 were missing after a similar incident.

- Published
A major river in Nepal has flooded, sweeping away houses, bridges and damaging a part of hydropower station, authorities have said.
Around 50 people have been rescued from along the bank of the Budhi Gandaki River in the central Gorkha district, the army confirmed. No casualties have been reported yet, however five people are missing.
A video of the flood shows the moment raging waters sweep down a valley and wash away an entire building complex.
Nepal is on high alert and still trying to recover from catastrophic floods that hit its border towns with Tibet two months ago, leaving more than 1,400 people dead and thousands missing.
Sunday's flood tore through the Gorkha district as children and communities prepared to mark the first day of the Dashain festival, a major moment in the Nepali calendar.
Families have been forced to flee their homes, with many facing uncertainty over where they will find safe shelter and access to essential supplies.
The flood swept away about a dozen houses and several suspension bridges, while a hydroelectric project was damaged, carrying some of the construction equipment away, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said.
Within a couple of hours, the river's water levels at one location had risen from two metres (6ft 5in) to nearly 8.5m (27ft 9in), officials said.
Binod Parajuli, a meteorologist who works with the Nepalese government, said: "Our hydrological station was swept away and we are not getting any data from that location."
However, experts say the debris-flow is much smaller and travelled more slowly than the devastating flash floods in August.
What caused the latest flood is still unclear. Some say a landslide may have blocked the river or its tributary for some time, causing the dammed water to burst out, while others say locals upstream saw an ice-avalanche.
Save the Children is mobilising an emergency team to respond to Sunday's flood.
"Children's lives have been ripped apart in an instant yet again", the charity's director in Nepal, Tara Chettry, said.
"We are yet to see the full scale of the damage, but they may have lost their homes, schools and communities. Many children in Gorkha will still be in shock and distress after the mega floods in August, barely having a chance to get back on their feet."
The Budhi Gandaki is a tributary of the Trishuli river, downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse caused the previous disaster.

172b94f6322e.text:
- Published
Saturday's attack on King Khalid Airport in Riyadh is another dangerous moment in a region that is already fraught with tension and conflict.
Saudi Arabia wasn't ready for this.
In recent weeks the Houthis have stepped up their attacks on Saudi Arabian soil, but their attacks over the past few days have hit the country's critical infrastructure in the form of the capital's main airport, apparently penetrating Saudi air defences with ease.
The physical damage can be quickly repaired, but the country's reputation as a safe haven of stability is taking a battering.
As well as all the airport attacks, the Houthis have sought to take control of strategically significant positions along the Red Sea coast and around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. This further increases the risk to safe navigation along the vital maritime corridor - although the Yemeni government says it has "secured" the strait.
The civil war in Yemen between the country's government - which is internationally recognised and supported by Saudi Arabia - and the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, has been going on for more than a decade. It has left many thousands of people dead and plunged Yemen into one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
It is a complex and often confusing geopolitical conflict, and this latest escalation needs to be seen in the broader context of the tension between Iran, the United States and Israel.
Not since the al-Qaeda insurgency of the mid-2000s has the Kingdom faced such a serious threat.
The Saudi government overcame that challenge through an effective hearts and minds campaign. Then it weathered the Arab Spring uprisings around the region which saw off leaders in Tunisia, Libya, Egypt and Yemen.
It even shrugged off â with some annoyance â an Iranian ballistic missile attack on Riyadh in March.
But this is different. Saudi Arabia may have one of the most powerful air forces in the Middle East, and it has been carrying out devastating air strikes on Houthi positions. Despite this, the opposing forces have managed to seize large portions of the country, particularly in the north and west.
But the Houthis know exactly where to hit back: at the soft underbelly of the Saudi economy.
As part of the "axis of resistance", the Houthis are a vital strategic partner for Iran. From Jizan on the Red Sea to the petrochemical complex at Khurais, the Houthis are delivering explosive drones and missiles with deadly accuracy.
The Red Sea shipping route has become increasingly important, because the Strait of Hormuz, on the other side of the Gulf, has still not fully reopened since the US and Iran have failed to reach a deal to end their war.
Targeting ships in the Red Sea is another way that the Houthis are trying to exert leverage - the attacks cause global economic damage, which is a key bargaining chip for Tehran.
In early September, the White House stated it would not directly intervene in the Yemen conflict, but could provide intelligence support to the Saudis. It later confirmed that it was supplying intelligence and had deployed military experts to Saudi Arabia.
However the situation may have taken a new turn following the latest attack on Riyadh, which killed a US citizen.
Speaking to reporters, US President Donald Trump called Saturday's attack "terrible" and indicated he may intervene militarily with the Saudis.
"We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," Trump said.
But that now seems unlikely, at least before crucial US midterm elections next month.
When he was re-elected in 2024, Trump promised to end America's role in wars around the world. Despite this, the US is currently involved in three unresolved conflicts in the Middle East - in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
Should Trump get embroiled in another one, this time in Yemen, it is unlikely to go down well with voters.
This war now looks like it will intensify before it ends in another shaky truce - with or without US involvement.
Additional analysis from Abdelbassir Hassan, BBC Arabic

- Published
Russian tech giant Yandex has been forced to pause its operations at a data centre near Moscow after the facility was damaged in a Ukrainian drone strike - the third attack on Yandex sites this week.
The company - dubbed "Russia's Google" - said no one was injured at the centre in Vladimir, east of the capital, but some of its services were unavailable to users.
Earlier this week, Yandex said it was struggling to maintain its services after two of its five data centres were hit in Ukrainian strikes.
Sunday's attack came hours after US President Donald Trump warned that Ukraine should "damn well stop" attacking Russia's oil refineries.
Later on Sunday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that "any de-escalation steps must be reciprocal and backed by real guarantees."
"Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure," Zelensky wrote on X.
He has reacted furiously to a new deal between the US and Russia, which will see millions of tonnes of Russian diesel released into the US.
In response to the criticism, Trump said he thinks "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president".
Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between them continues into its fifth year following Russia's full-scale invasion.
Kyiv said it is targeting places that help the revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the latest attacks could force Russia to divert its resources to repair the damage at Yandex.
Writing on Telegram, the company confirmed that its data centre in Vladimir was damaged and that operations had been "completely suspended," although they were working to restore connectivity.
The other strikes against Yandex facilities were on Thursday in Sasovo and Friday in in Kaluga, south-west of Moscow, causing operations to be suspended.
The tech company - which also runs a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people - said its data centres were critical for the normal operation of its services, and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.
Meanwhile, Russian strikes on Ukraine have also continued through the weekend.
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said six people were injured in Russian attacks overnight on four districts in its south-eastern Dnipropetrovsk region.
On Saturday, at least 20 people including four children were killed in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia, local officials confirmed.

d67a8a94296f.text:
Buildings swept away as flash floods hit central Nepal
A flash flood has washed away houses, bridges and damaged a hydropower project along a river in central Nepal.
The army said on Sunday that it had rescued 49 people from flood affected areas, but five are still missing, the district's top official confirmed.
It is believed that the flood was caused by a landslide upstream of the Budhi Gandaki River in the Gorkha district.
Four bridges and nearly two dozen houses have been swept away, as well as a camp at a hydropower project along the river.
Nepal is still trying to recover from catastrophic floods and landslides that swept through its border towns with Tibet two months ago, wiping out thousands of houses, destroying critical energy infrastructure and leaving thousands dead and missing.

Three violent attacks at Polish schools this week were driven by the "glorification of violence" online, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.
The attacks have left one woman dead and others injured, including children.
"These are very often spontaneous actions inspired by online activity," Tusk said on Sunday, during a crisis meeting with security services.
Police have arrested 117 people across the country for possession knives or other weapons, or for threatening to attack schools or fellow students, after searching tens of thousands of schools.
A woman was arrested on Saturday after injuring three people while attacking a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital, Warsaw.
It came a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland, following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which led to the killing of a female caretaker.
"We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said on Sunday.
"In the past years and months, we have noted - globally and in Poland - a rise in the fascination with violence," he added.
The prime minister said the attacks were acts "nihilistic violence" associated with the extreme right.
"Some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment," he said, adding that police had noticed a rise in online searches of Nazi content as well as of "mass killers who have become idols online".
On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian.
A day later, the 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in LeszczydÃ³Å-Nowiny, north of Warsaw.
Interior Minister Marcin KierwiÅski also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone".
Thousands of Polish âpolice officers visited schools nationwide to try to reassure pupils after the stabbings sparked rumours of a "Bloody Friday" of more attacks stemming from a supposed online challenge.
Meanwhile, Polish security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about a potential attack on Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, a spokesperson said.
A special services spokesman said officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious".

c67cb56e463c.text: President Trump claimed Sunday that Russia and Ukraine agreed to an "energy ceasefire" and will halt attacks on each other's energy facilities. Ukrainian President Zelensky tells Axios the announcement "was news for me. But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire, Ukraine will agree." Why it matters: An "energy ceasefire" would be a dramatic diplomatic breakthrough ahead of the winter. It remains unclear if Russia indeed agreed to stop the strikes. Trump made a similar announcement last month, but neither party confirmed that there was a deal. Both Russia and Ukraine continued attacking energy infrastructure. What they're saying: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote on Truth Social. In a short interview after Trump's announcement, Zelensky told Axios, "If President Trump negotiated it with Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready, and we will accept it." Catch up quick: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday on ABC's "This Week" that Ukraine was prepared to stop attacking Russian refineries if Moscow halted strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

A couple say their dog may have died after being exposed to an orange substance on contaminated land during a walk.
Donna and Pete O'Brien noticed Misty's health deteriorating rapidly after wading through a swampy pool close to the Cefn Viaduct near Wrexham.
She stated to cough up blood and then, around the time of her death, an ultrasound revealed that she had a heart tumour, which affects just 0.19% of dogs.
Donna and Pete said they believe it was linked to the historical chemical dumping that was recently explored in the BBC's Buried documentary, and they are calling for the examination of pet records to see if there are any clusters of rare illnesses.
Donna said they did not think much of it at the time after going for a walk near Ty Mawr in December 2019.
Misty loved to run in the mud and swamps, but on this occasion, she came back "covered in a sort of greasy orange film".
"At the time you think it might be copper or iron washing down through the landscape but it stank and it was sort of oily all over her coat," Donna added.
They vowed not to go back after the orange substance stained Misty for weeks, but the four-year-old dog, who had always been an "really healthy dog", soon became sick.
Vets records show that she started to have periodic diarrhoea and vomiting and by 2024, then aged nine, Misty was struggling.
"She would get to the end of a walk and just stop for a while," said Pete.
"It was unusual but I put it down to her wanting to stay out a bit longer."
Misty started to cough up blood and expel it from her nose, with an ultrasound scan showing a growth â believed to be a tumour â on her heart and potentially others on her stomach and lungs.
Pete said they were watching the Buried documentary, which premiered in August 2026, when they saw something that made them "sit up and take notice".
"People were describing substances similar to what we washed off Misty â greasy, oily orange deposits.
"Then we went to the meeting of the Monsanto Contamination Action Group and heard more stories that resonated."
He said it was worrying for the many visitors that go to Ty Mawr who might be unaware of the risk, and it has left them with "so many questions" about Misty's health.
"That's why we feel that as well as human medical records, pet medical records need to be examined for clusters of rare illnesses," Pete added.
Pete and Donna believe that due to many suspected or undocumented dump sites and water run-offs being in public rural areas, pet health data may provide more evidence of the impact of "forever chemicals" on communities.
"Illnesses that take decades to develop in humans often progress much quicker in animals," said Pete.
"There are so many sites. Who knows what we and they are being exposed to.
"That's why we need clear answers."
Their concerns were raised at a Wrexham council meeting by councillor Derek Wright.
He called for significant changes to monitoring and management of the contaminated sites that were "just a stone's throw" from the Ty Mawr Country Park.
During the meeting he questioned why the areas have a fence that is "only three foot" with no sign saying that chemicals are there, or why it was fenced off.
He said one of the ponds has since become a public footpath and that dog walkers and family frequently walk across them, despite no "publicised tests of what is in those lagoons, or what used to be lagoons".
A spokesperson for Wrexham council said investigations indicated deposits came from mining activity.
"We have inspected the area with Natural Resources Wales and they have undertaken liaison with the Coal Authority â we are satisfied there is no requirement for any further action to be taken," he said.

6e153f616b6e.text:
- Published
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a man accused of plotting an assassination attack against him and his defence minister has been detained.
The interior ministry earlier reported that police had received credible information about possible attacks against Tusk and Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz.
Security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about the planned attacks, with a spokesman saying officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious".
Tusk thanked the police for "swift and decisive action" in arresting the suspect.
The suspect was arrested in the Lower Silesia region and is a Polish national, Jacek Dobrzynski, a spokesman for the Special Services Coordinator told local media.
"In this case we are talking about a strong likelihood that these threats could actually be carried out," he said.
The plan was uncovered when an email with information about the potential attack was forwarded to police by the State Protection Service, which is responsible for ministers' security, Interior Ministry spokeswoman Karolina Galecka said.
Tusk has been Polish prime minister since 2023 after previously holding the office from 2007 to 2014.
He served as president of the European Council from 2014 to 2019.

- Published
An international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh has been hit by a second strike in as many days, officials have said.
A Saudi military spokesman said a projectile had hit King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, causing a fire in one of its passenger halls. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said there had been injuries.
It comes a day after a strike on the same airport killed 13 people and injured 308 others, following similar strikes earlier this week.
The Houthis in Yemen said they were behind the attacks and warned airlines and passengers against using Saudi Arabian airports and airspace.
The group said they had targeted the airport with a mix of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones in the past 24 hours.
They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said.
He vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia", warning that all Saudi airports were potential targets apart from those in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The Houthis have said they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war, as well as an air strike on the airport in Sanaa.
On Sunday Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition, said air defences had intercepted a missile near the airport in Riyadh, while authorities were dealing with the fire caused by an "unknown projectile" that hit Passenger Hall No 4.
US President Donald Trump has said the US would "make a decision" and "move very quickly" on whether to strike the Houthis, while UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting suggested the UK could "potentially" provide more support for Saudi Arabia.
Saturday's strike was the deadliest single attack on a Gulf Arab country since the war between Israel, the US and Iran began in February. The Saudi-led coalition vowed to respond, calling it a "war crime".
Four Saudi nationals, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt were among the dead, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said on Sunday that an Indian man had succumbed to the injuries he sustained in the attack.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks and confirmed that a US citizen was killed in the strikes. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he was "appalled".
The UK Foreign Office is advising against all travel to parts of Saudi Arabia, including areas within 10km (6.2 miles) of the border with Yemen, while other western embassies have warned their nationals about travel in the region.
Houthi-run Al Masirah TV said "the Saudi enemy" had launched an air strike on Sanaa International Airport in Yemen's capital. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the attack and the BBC has been unable to verify this claim.
Abdullah Al-Alimi Bawazir, vice-president of Yemen's internationally recognised government, called for "decisive actions" from regional and international partners.
Riyadh's airport was struck on Thursday, an attack that killed three Saudi nationals. The Houthis claimed responsibility and said they had used cruise missiles to target the airport.
There were two other deadly attacks on Saudi airports in Abha and Riyadh in the two days prior to that.
The latest uptick in violence comes after a temporary ceasefire between the Houthis and Saudi-led forces, brokered in 2022, collapsed in July.
The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive, prompting Saudi strikes. Yemeni pro-government forces later said they had secured the regions.
The Houthis currently control around a quarter of Yemeni territory and as much as 80% of the country's population. The Iran-backed armed group hopes to eventually seize complete control.
Saudi Arabia fears this would lead to the establishment of an Iranian satellite state on its southern border.

7b949f612db2.text: By — Jamey Keaten, Associated Press Jamey Keaten, Associated Press By — Claudia Ciobanu, Associated Press Claudia Ciobanu, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/at-least-139-migrants-dead-dozens-missing-after-boat-capsizes-off-djibouti-coast Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter At least 139 migrants dead, dozens missing after boat capsizes off Djibouti coast World Oct 11, 2026 2:05 PM EDT GENEVA (AP) — At least 139 people, including children, have died after a boat carrying more than 300 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti in east Africa, the International Organization for Migration said Sunday. That number only includes those buried by authorities in Djibouti. Others have been buried by the migrants themselves but they won't be added to the official count until authorities can verify the bodies, Alexandre Coissac, IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti, told the AP via the phone. "What is terrible is that they were buried with no names, in a common grave, like in a war situation," Coissac said. "They all have a mother, a father, and we may never learn what happened." Coissac said the migrants boarded the ship in the evening of Oct. 8 and that it sank very soon after, close to the shore, "mainly because it was overcrowded." "The local authorities did their best," Coissac said, "but they were overwhelmed with all the bodies that kept coming at once towards the shore." A pair of shoes believed to belong to a migrant lies on the shore after a boat carrying about 305 people capsized while sailing from Djibouti to Yemen, Photob by Kennedy Omondi Okoth/International Organization for Migration/Handout via Reuters. He said authorities were bringing the surviving migrants to the IOM rescue center in Obock where they receive medical assistance after swallowing sea water, and psychological support. "They're all in a state of shock," Coissac, who visited the area of the shipwreck Saturday, said. "I tried to talk to some of them but it's very difficult." Some of the migrants in the IOM center are already aware that their family members died during the shipwreck. Others were given access to phones to call loved ones back home to notify them they are alive. At least 84 people remained missing in one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Gulf nations. The boat was traveling from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized on Thursday night or Friday morning, according to the IOM. More than 80 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals, it said. The Geneva-based U.N. migration agency said the vessel had 305 people on board and warned that the death toll could still rise. Personal items likely belonging to the migrants, including shoes, were seen on a beach in a video shared by IOM. Rescue work continued as fears grew for the missing. Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa travel every year through Djibouti and across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait towards Gulf countries in search of safety and economic opportunities, the IOM said in its statement. That movement has continued despite newly escalating fighting in Yemen, on the other side of the strait. "This is a devastating loss of life," said Coissac. "This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities." In recent weeks, at least 2,000 Yemenis have received aid in Djibouti as the fighting has escalated in Yemen between the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. That's the opposite direction from the movement of the migrants who died in the shipwreck and the typical migration patterns of recent years: The tens of thousands who cross from eastern Africa toward Yemen each year have typically been looking for work in places like Saudi Arabia. Over 900 migrants died or went missing along the route last year, according to IOM's Missing Migrants Project. "No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way," IOM Director-General Amy Pope said. "We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down." Ciobanu reported from Warsaw, Poland. 48505cbfb184.text: By — Sheikh Saaliq, Associated Press Sheikh Saaliq, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/leaders-from-indias-cockroach-movement-released-from-detention-pledge-to-hold-more-protests Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Leaders from India's 'Cockroach' movement released from detention, pledge to hold more protests World Oct 11, 2026 3:08 PM EDT NEW DELHI (AP) — Leaders of a popular Indian youth movement vowed to continue protests Sunday after being released from detention, a day after police cracked down on demonstrations against a controversial revision of voter lists. The movement is demanding the resignation of the country's election chief. The protests were triggered after authorities removed more than 130 million voters from the list since last year. Critics say the move is politically motivated. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party and the Election Commission deny manipulation allegations. The Cockroach Janata Party's three leaders — Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka — were freed on condition that they commit "no breach of peace for one year," Ratna Singh, the movement's legal director, said in a social media post. It was unclear what the condition meant or whether it would restrict their participation in protests. Police boarded the leaders' flight from Mumbai after it landed in New Delhi on Saturday and took them into custody as they prepared to lead a demonstration in New Delhi. After his release, Dipke called Modi "an embarrassment to India." "Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully," he wrote on X. Security personnel detain protesters during a protest by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) seeking the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, near the protest site in New Delhi, India, October 10, 2026. Photo by Adnan Abidi/Reuters. Das, a spokesperson for the movement, urged supporters to take to the streets. "A situation has been created where the state is at war with its own citizens," he told reporters Sunday. Following Saturday's protests, authorities launched a sweeping security crackdown in the capital, detaining more than 2,000 protesters, including several opposition lawmakers. Train services to the capital were canceled, metro stations closed and mobile internet suspended in parts of the city. Most of those detained were released late Saturday, police said. Small groups of protesters returned to the Indian capital on Sunday, staging marches across the city. The police quickly broke up most of the demonstrations, detaining some protesters again. Protesters are demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the chief election commissioner. Modi's party has said the voter revision is needed to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries. The Cockroach movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India's chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites. Many young Indians embraced the remark, adopting the cockroach as a symbol of resilience. Protests led by the group forced the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare setback for the prime minister, who has been in power for more than 12 years. Eight orangutans have been released back into the wild in Borneo after they were taken into captivity when their habitat was threatened by wildfires over the summer.
Three mothers, their three daughters and two adult males were freed in a reserve in the west of the island on Friday, International Animal Rescue Indonesia (Yiari) and the forestry ministry said.
Indonesian authorities rescued 46 orangutans from fires in August and September. Wildfires in the region are usual for the country's dry season but intensified this year.
The apes are critically endangered. Around 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago, according to conservation group WWF.
While Indonesia is among many countries to grapple with wildfires each summer, this year's were more intense due to the El NiÃ±o ocean warming phenomenon, which makes weather patterns more volatile and intense.
Yiari CEO Karmele Llano Sanchez said relocating the eight orangutans to the reserve was a "necessary step" when their habitats became unsafe.
Among them was Mama Nopi and her offspring Nopi, Naufal and Nopan, who had been surviving in a coconut and rubber plantation before their rescue in early September, Yiari said.
Fires had incinerated the surrounding forestry, restricting their access to food and bringing them closer to humans.
Mama Lifa and her child Lifa were found in a patch of acacia trees entirely surrounded by oil palm plantations.
The degradation of their habitat by wildfires as well as a lack of food sources prompted their rescue in mid-September.
Mama Man and her baby, Man, had been monitored by animal rescuers since June, when they were found living in a plantation area adjacent to a small patch of forest.
Fires that spread near to the site restricted their roaming area further, leaving them without a safe route to other forestry. The threat of exposure to the blazes led to them being evacuated in early September, Yiara said.
The reserve these orangutans were released into was chosen because it there is food and water available and it is connected to other forested areas.
Yiari's Argitoe Ranting said: "We want to ensure that rescued orangutans are not simply moved from one place to another, but actually have a chance to survive in their natural habitat."
Last month, the International Union for Conservation of Nature warned that wildfires were burning in habitats containing 52% of Borneo's orangutan population.
It says a large portion of the ape's habitat will become inhospitable to them if climate change continues at its current pace.
This year's El NiÃ±o has become the strongest on record and is expected to have a knock-on effect on the climate into next year.
Experts have also pointed to land-clearing practices used to make room for plantations as another factor facilitating the spread of wildfires in Indonesia, with naturally fire-resistant forests replaced by less dense and shaded vegetation.
That the orangutan's original habitats had been burned and fragmented to the point they could no longer sustain the primates was the main driving factor behind relocating them, Yiara said.

e42c77375593.text: By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press By — Colleen Barry, Associated Press Colleen Barry, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/pope-leo-to-undergo-surgery-to-remove-nodule-on-his-lung Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope Leo to undergo surgery to remove nodule on his lung World Oct 11, 2026 2:34 PM EDT VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday he will undergo surgery "in the coming days" to remove a nodule on his lung, in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The 71-year-old Leo said the nodule was found at an early stage and was "circumscribed" or small and well-localized. The Vatican said Leo's expected recovery time from surgery would be a week. The American pope made the announcement during his Sunday noon blessing in an unusual display of transparency about his health. He thanked the crowd for their closeness and entrusted himself to their prayers. The Vatican didn't say exactly when the surgery would take place, other than in the early days of this week. Leo has one upcoming main event: the closing Mass on Wednesday of a weeklong conference on family ministry, but Vatican officials suggested he might miss it. A nodule can be benign or malignant A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (1 inch) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening. "Lung nodules are fairly common and are often benign, but benign and cancerous nodules can have a similar appearance on imaging," said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown's Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center. "When there is sufficient concern, and when it is safe to do so based on the location of the nodule and the overall health of the patient, surgical removal can provide a definitive diagnosis," he said. A statue of the late Pope John Paul II outside the entrance to Gemelli Hospital, where Pope Leo is expected to undergo surgery this week to remove a small growth on his lung, in Rome, Italy, October 11, 2026. Photo by Matteo Minnella/Reuters. If the nodule turns out to be cancerous, the prognosis is "excellent" since it will have been removed at an early stage and surgery alone might be all Leo needs in terms of treatment, he said in an interview. "It often can be a blessing in disguise to remove that cancer before it has a chance to grow or to spread," he said. Leo has no previously known health problems and is physically active, with weekly tennis matches and swimming at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo. The pope has a major trip planned Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear how or whether the planned surgery and recovery might affect the itinerary, but Leo said earlier in his remarks Sunday that he still planned to go. In his remarks, delivered in Italian, Leo said that during a recent medical check, "doctors found a circumscribed nodule in my lung. It was detected at a very early stage and is well-localized. The doctors believe it's best to take action, so, following their advice, I have decided to have surgery to remove it." He thanked the faithful "for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers." Surgery to be at the pope's hospital Leo's predecessor, Pope Francis, died April 21, 2025, of a stroke following a long hospitalization brought on by a respiratory crisis that developed into double pneumonia. Francis suffered from chronic lung disease and had part of one lung removed as a young man. Francis' illnesses were characterized by a dizzying and sometimes problematic release of information from the Vatican, which always closely guards the privacy of a pope's health. In one infamous incident, the Vatican said Francis had gone to the hospital in March 2023 for scheduled tests, but the pontiff later revealed he had felt pain in his chest and was rushed to the hospital where bronchitis was diagnosed. He ended up being admitted for three days. This time around, Leo appeared keen to control the message and deliver it himself, using one of his most public encounters with the faithful to alert them of his condition and impending hospital stay. Leo is expected to undergo surgery at Rome's Gemelli hospital, where Francis and popes before him were treated and where there is a special apartment for pontiffs. On Sunday, there was no obvious sign that the pope had already been admitted. A nodule doesn't mean cancer but should be investigated Dr. Dionysis Papadatos-Pastos, an oncologist and lung cancer specialist at The London Clinic, stressed that an incidental finding of a lung nodule doesn't mean lung cancer. And in fact "a well-circumscribed nodule does suggest that this is less likely to be cancer." But he said cancer was possible and the main imperative is to investigate. "The worst thing you can do is ignore a lung nodule," he said in an interview. Liu, the Georgetown oncologist, said surgical removal in such a case was standard, especially for someone in otherwise good health and if the nodule is in an easily accessible location. A needle biopsy on a lung nodule can be difficult and may not provide doctors with enough information, he said. "In these cases, surgery itself, while it may seem dramatic, is often very safe, very straightforward with a rapid recovery," he said, adding that Leo should be in good shape to travel to Latin America barring any complications. Leo is not known to be a smoker. Liu noted that 1 in 5 people diagnosed with lung cancer have no history of smoking. Dr. Massimo Di Maio, president of the Italian Association of Medical Oncology, said it will be important to determine if the nodule is benign or malignant, and if it is malignant, whether it has spread. When the disease is detected at an early stage "the aim … is curative,

f2bcbb9da01f.text: By — Kevin Freking, Associated Press Kevin Freking, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/bipartisan-group-of-senators-calls-on-trump-to-reverse-course-on-russian-diesel-plan Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Bipartisan group of senators calls on Trump to 'reverse course' on Russian diesel plan Politics Oct 11, 2026 4:18 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to "immediately reverse course" on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices. Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote. Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute. "The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course," they wrote. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., speaks in Concord, New Hampshire, in 2024. Photo by Elizabeth Frantz/ Reuters The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut. Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press," said there's a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan. "We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied," Tillis said. Trump's announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine. The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war. "Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies," the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. "President Trump's decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law." Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president's action would be in violation of U.S. law. "The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions," Barrasso said on CBS's "Face the Nation." He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month. "This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world," Barrasso said. Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices.
