Donald Trump has claimed that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire" in their war, with Kyiv saying it would support such a move but no comment from Moscow.
The US president insisted that it was "effective immediately" but provided no details.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky initially told a US media outlet that it was "news" to him, before saying Kyiv would support it if Moscow did. He has also accused Russia of striking Ukraine's energy facilities after Trump posted his announcement.
Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to curtailing revenue for Moscow's war machine - so Russia can fulfil a recently-struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.
The diesel deal has been criticised by Zelensky, some European officials and some US politicians, including some from Trump's Republican party.
After Trump claimed an energy truce had taken effect, Zelensky expressed surprise to news site Axios before writing on social media that his officials "look forward to clear details of America's dialogue with Russia".
"Ukraine is ready not to strike at Russian energy and we count on Russia's similar readiness and on the agreement of the president of the United States of America on this," he said.
The BBC has asked the White House for further details.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now".
French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen have also expressed their support for an energy truce.
After speaking to von der Leyen, Zelensky said Russia had hit a power plant in Kyiv with a drone, causing power outages, followed by strikes on energy facilities in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
"All of this happened after the president of the United States made his statement about an energy ceasefire," he said.
In Ukraine, six people have been killed in Russian attacks on two cities, regional officials said.
A person has been killed in Russia's Belgorod region, according to its regional task force.
For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure.
Moscow said the installations it hits were legitimate targets because they supported Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".
The attacks have disrupted energy supplies on both sides.
The deal announced with Russia earlier this week, temporarily undoing sanctions on Russian imports, is the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, having spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
The US-Israeli war with Iran has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz - a vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's oil products usually flow - and pushed up global fuel prices, particularly those for diesel.
That conflict has soured Trump's standing with the American public, who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.
Zelensky has called the diesel deal a gift to Putin. UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has told the BBC that the UK did not support it. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has echoed Zelensky's comments.
Some US politicians - including some from Trump's Republican party - have also criticised the deal.
Seven senators, including three Democrats and four Republicans, have published a statement saying Trump's deal with Russia "runs directly counter" to a law that banned Russian energy imports.
"Congress was clear: the US should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our Nato Allies," the statement said, urging the Trump administration to "reverse course".
Republican Senator Thom Tillis, one of the seven, told NBC News that the deal "absolutely will" put American lives at risk.
Following Zelensky's criticism, Trump accused the Ukrainian leader of wanting to "make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries and said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".
Zelensky responded by pledging to hold elections - despite them being suspended by the Ukrainian constitution during wartime - if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire.
The Ukrainian president previously resisted calls from the US for fresh elections, pointing to complications with holding a vote in parts of the country that are active war zones or under Russian occupation.
Trump, however, has repeatedly accused the Ukrainian leader of using the war to stay in power.

5c6f7c534f7b.text: By — Samy Magdy, Associated Press Samy Magdy, Associated Press By — Cara Anna, Associated Press Cara Anna, Associated Press By — Julia Frankel, Associated Press Julia Frankel, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/riyadh-airport-hit-by-projectile-a-day-after-deadly-missile-strike Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Riyadh airport hit by projectile a day after deadly missile strike World Oct 11, 2026 3:49 PM EDT CAIRO (AP) — A projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, a day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 12 people, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those attacks and others. Saudi authorities said there were injuries in the latest attack on the King Khalid International Airport complex for terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights. Saturday's missile attack was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began, with another 300 people wounded, some critically. The airport was still closed Sunday. The sharp escalation in the new front in the war threatens to draw in greater U.S. military involvement, as President Donald Trump has said he is weighing joining the fight against the Houthis. There was no immediate White House comment Sunday. India's embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died Sunday of injuries sustained in Saturday's attack, which would bring the toll to 13. Saudi authorities later said King Fahd International Airport in Dammam also had been attacked, with few details. The city is on the Persian Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar. Smoke and flames rise from King Khalid Airport, after Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said they attacked the airport, in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, October 8, 2026, in this screengrab obtained from a social media video. Social Media/via Reuters. The latest strike in Riyadh came shortly after the Houthis said the airport in the rebel-held Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again, and blamed the Saudis. At stake, again, in this escalation are global supplies and prices of oil as well as commercial shipping through a crucial alternative waterway to the Iran-threatened Strait of Hormuz — along with civilians and aviation throughout the region. Trump said he planned to speak to Saudi crown prince Trump on Saturday also said he planned to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who has been seeking assistance. A U.S. intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen and further restrict the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month and the Saudi-led coalition has been trying to seize them back. Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran. Sunday's attack occurred as the Saudis hosted a major international energy conference in Riyadh, with other high-profile events including an investment gathering on the horizon. Saudi Arabia under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has sought to open more to the world as a business and tourism destination, but the Houthi attacks threaten those efforts. "There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix, we come out of the ashes all the time," the Saudi energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, told the conference. He added that the kingdom is also working on pipelines in addition to the East-West one that was attacked and closed for days last month, with no details. Houthis have targeted Saudi air, military and oil facilities Earlier Sunday, the Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa. The ministry also said 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks, 60% of them women and children. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims. On Sunday, the Houthis claimed the attack on the airport in Dammam as well as attacks on oil and gas facilities in the kingdom's east. They have targeted the Riyadh airport, which has no military facilities, every day since Wednesday. The rebels again warned "all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our forces." Several international airlines have suspended flights for varying periods. The dead in the airport attack included several nationalities Saudi authorities said the dead in Saturday's attack included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. The Egyptian woman was a flight attendant for Saudi airline Flynas identified as Azza Ramzy, according to Egyptian state-run TV. The Syrian woman was a widowed mother who had been living in Saudi Arabia, relative Nisreen Oweida told The Associated Press. The Syrian Embassy identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida. Iran can use the Houthis to pressure a key US ally Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the Iran war's sidelines, but they have developed their military capabilities in recent years to become one of Tehran's most powerful allies. Now, they are helping Iran to pressure a key U.S. ally. The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government. Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. The attack revived anger over the Saudi-led bl

80d8c147cbf3.text: President Trump's announcement Sunday about an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine referred to a potential deal that includes each side stopping attacks on oil refineries — and he expects Volodymyr Zelensky to abide by it, a White House official said. The official said if attacks on oil refineries cease, a deal to stop hitting power plants and energy grids could come next. Why it matters: Trump appears to be singlehandedly trying to will a partial ceasefire into existence. But for now Russia hasn't accepted any kind of ceasefire — and Ukraine wants one that forbids attacks on power plants. Reality check: The "refinery for refinery" proposal, as the official dubbed it, is lopsided. A Ukrainian official told Axios that the country has a single oil refinery which the Russians have attacked multiple times and isn't fully functional. Russia, by contrast, has a vast network of refineries. "We import diesel and gas. What we need is for the Russians to stop attacking our electricity grid," the Ukrainian official said. "The Russians are thinking about" it, the White House official said. "We will know soon if they are ready." Case in point: Hours after Trump's announcement, Russia conducted strikes on power plants in Ukraine, according to Ukrainian media. What he said: Trump's Truth Social post sounded at first like a major breakthrough. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" he wrote. It appears much more tenuous than that. Zelensky said the announced ceasefire "was news for me." State of play: After reaching a deal with Russia Friday to lift diesel sanctions, Trump remains focused on stopping Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. He believes the strikes are driving up U.S. gas prices. White House officials warn that Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries are hurting Zelensky's relationship with Trump more than they're damaging Russia. "Trump is really mad. He feels Zelensky is taking the U.S. for granted," the White House official said. Zoom in: Amid the crisis with Ukraine, presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have put their planned trip to Moscow on hold, at least until they get clarity on whether Ukraine and the Europeans are ready to agree to a new unified proposal for Putin. A Ukrainian official told Axios on Friday that during a meeting with U.S. negotiators in Miami on Friday, Witkoff and Kushner threatened that Trump could stop sharing U.S. intelligence if it continued to ignore his requests. A U.S. official denied that, saying Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainians that the U.S. was a strong partner, providing munitions and intelligence. Ukraine therefore shouldn't take actions that hurt American consumers, the two said. On Sunday, the Financial Times reported that the U.S. told European countries it might stop selling weapons to Ukraine through NATO if Ukraine continues to strike Russian refineries.

06daf636c421.text: By — Susie Blann, Associated Press Susie Blann, Associated Press By — Elise Morton, Associated Press Elise Morton, Associated Press By — Collin Binkley, Associated Press Collin Binkley, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/trump-claims-russia-and-ukraine-agree-to-energy-ceasefire-despite-continued-attacks Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agree to 'energy ceasefire' despite continued attacks World Oct 11, 2026 5:25 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but he offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement. Trump's brief social media post said only that the ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: "Do not break it!" Moscow did not immediately comment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that while his country "welcomed" the announcement by Trump as "good news for everyone," Russia was still hitting energy infrastructure in Kyiv and in the city of Kharkiv. "Unfortunately, Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian 'shaheds' all day today," he said in an evening address, referring to drones launched by Moscow . "There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too. A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening." The presidential office confirmed the Kharkiv attack came after Trump's ceasefire post. Zelenskyy said Ukraine was "ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure — and we count on the same readiness from Russia." Russia has sought to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as "weaponizing winter." Zelenskyy said Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps but Russian President Vladimir Putin "had one answer to all of them — 'nyet.' We do hope that he will finally say something different to America, Ukraine, and the entire world." He said Kyiv is maintaining contact with the U.S., and he thanked Americans for their support. He said on X that he had spoken about the development with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte. In an interview broadcast earlier Sunday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine's energy system, and he asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree. "We are asking President Trump, (to) give them (a) signal, not (to) attack energy infrastructure of Ukraine," he told ABC's "This Week ." On Sept. 14, Trump claimed on social media that both countries had agreed "not to hit" each other's energy infrastructure but offered no details on that proposal either. While Zelenskyy had said Ukraine was ready to comply if Russia did, nothing came of the proposal. Trump spars with Zelenskyy Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S. Zelenskyy said in response to Trump's comments that Ukraine could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire. "Give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections," he said, adding that Ukraine would be ready to accept whatever choice its people made. "With all respect to President Trump, it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader," he said. Holding an election during the war would be unlawful and that Ukraine would need security guarantees to allow for safe voting, Zelenskyy added. Ukraine has been under martial law since Putin launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the Ukrainian Constitution bars elections while it remains in force. Beyond the legal barrier, a nationwide vote would be vulnerable to Russian attacks, and organizing one is widely seen as logistically impossible, with roughly a fifth of the country held by Russia, millions of Ukrainians displaced abroad and soldiers on the front line. Zelenskyy's term formally expired in May 2024, but the constitution allows him to remain in office until a new president is sworn in. The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against Russian infrastructure, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, run by technology giant Yandex. It was the third strike on the company's facilities in four days. Russia and Ukraine have been waging a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line. Trump, who on Friday struck a deal with Putin to buy diesel from Moscow in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure. He has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia's war effort. Ukrainian strike on Russian data center triggers outages The Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data center in Vladimir caused outages across the company's services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra. "Operations at the data center have been completely halted. There were no injuries," said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel, which updates service availability. Moscow residents described disruption to everyday tasks. At least 72 civilians who had been prospecting for gold in a border region of Sudan have been killed in air strikes, a regional rights group says.
Emergency Lawyers, based in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, said jets targeted the so-called artisanal miners at a popular gold mining sites in Sudan's River Nile state on Saturday.
Neither the Egyptian government nor the de facto Sudanese authorities have so far commented.
Cairo has previously faced accusations of deadly strikes on gold prospectors as part of a crackdown on illicit activity along its southern border.
Emergency Lawyers noted the previous alleged attacks and said they represented not only a violation of Sudan's sovereign territory but demonstrated the government's lack of control over the region.
"The deliberate targeting of unarmed civilians violates international humanitarian law and the right to life," it said in a statement on Sunday. "These acts may constitute war crimes."
It noted that its death toll was provisional and could rise.
The Paris-based Sudan Tribune reported that the death toll could far exceed the number reported by Emergency Lawyers, citing a survivor of Saturday's attack who said many more people had been injured.
Eyewitnesses said the attack began around 06:00 local time (04:00 GMT), with the aircraft firing more than five missiles directly at the miners' camps, destroying them and excavation pits with people still inside, the newspaper wrote.
The Sudan Tribune reported claims in June that Egyptian forces had used drones and artillery to target artisanal mining sites in the same region, killing several, after sporadic incidents of Egyptian border guards of burning equipment, torching temporary shelters, and firing live ammunition to disperse mine workers.
Days later, Egypt's border agency announced that it and the military had begun a sweeping security campaign along the border to foil illegal migration, drug smuggling and illegal mining.
At the same time, Sudan's de facto leader announced an investigation into the alleged strikes, which were said to have killed dozens.
Gold lies at the core of the border tensions.
Sudan's ongoing civil war has led to a surge in artisanal mining - an often risky practice conducted by civilians with rudimentary tools and without official permission - particularly in remote areas near its borders.
Gold-rich areas such as those in River Nile state lie along porous borders in terrain historically associated with cross-border smuggling routes, with artisanally mined gold potentially feeding into those channels.
Egypt's border force said in June that it had seized 86 tonnes of gold ore along with amateur prospecting equipment.
Artisanal mining has also reportedly continued in Sudan's conflict zones and smuggled gold may be a source of income for armed insurgent groups.
This has raised concerns of illicit Sudanese gold undermining the legitimate Egyptian gold market.

People are being told to prepare for "the unthinkable" as flood response teams warn of a heightened risk over the autumn.
Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said it was concerned by long-range forecasts, external which indicated an increased likelihood of wetter, windier weather than usual over the coming months.
Those living in flood-hit areas told BBC Wales they were worried, and had started preparing.
One in seven properties in Wales is classed as being at risk of flooding, but NRW said just 27% of those eligible to receive flood warnings to their phone or email were currently signed up.
After a summer marked by drought and wildfires, the organisation has urged people "not to become complacent" and said conditions could change quickly.
Wales has seen a series of major floods in recent years, often in the wake of powerful storms such as Dennis in 2020, Bert and Darragh in 2024 and Claudia in 2025.
The threat comes from both rivers and the sea, while surface water flooding - where local drainage systems become overwhelmed during heavy downpours - is seen as an increasing danger.
NRW argues that the country's geography makes it particularly vulnerable - with a vast coastline and several so-called "fast-responding" rivers which can fill at speed as rain runs off steep terrain in places like the south Wales valleys.
More than 274,500 homes and businesses are currently classed at risk of flooding, with this figure set to increase significantly by the end of the century.
'People could have died'
On the high street in Monmouth, people told BBC Wales of "harrowing" and "dreadful" scenes when major flooding hit in November 2025.
Friends Malcolm Butcher, 82, Jim Tyler, 81, Brian Churches, 82 and Dave Blake, 82, said they had lived in the town all their lives "and never seen anything like it".
"At 2:30 in the morning when it hit it was unbelievable... absolutely raging," Malcolm said.
If it had happened in the daytime "people would have died", he added.
Eighteen cars on his road were lost to the flood waters - including his own, while the houses in the street behind were all flooded out.
"It is a worry, we have three rivers running into Monmouth... and the winters are changing," he said.
People could help prepare for floods by moving "the good stuff upstairs" and making sure they had sandbags to hand ahead of bad weather, he said.
"It's not back to normal yet but we're getting there," added Imogen Elliot, 82.
"Waitrose was four feet in water and it went right up the street - we've had flooding before but not like that."
Jane Roche, who runs a cafÃ© and fishmongers on the banks of the River Teifi in Cardigan, Ceredigion, has helped coordinate a community flood plan for the area.
"Flooding is something we've learned to live alongside for many years - we've seen first-hand the disruption it can cause for businesses, residents and visitors," she said.
"Developing a community flood plan has brought local people together, helped us understand what actions we need to taken when warnings are issued and given us confidence to support one another when severe weather is forecast."
More frequent and intense weather extremes are expected as a result of climate change, with Wales facing the prospect of wetter, wilder winters more often.
Meanwhile, this year scientists are monitoring the El NiÃ±o event over the Pacific Ocean - which set to be "strongest in living memory".
The powerful natural climate phenomenon pushes up global temperatures and can increase the risks of extreme weather.
While this does not automatically translate into bad weather in the UK it is "part of the picture" that is leading to concerns for the coming months, according to Jeremy Parr of NRW.
"We do invest in flood defences... but you can't stop all of the flooding all of the time," he said.
"So that means that people need to think the unthinkable really - or the unpleasant - and [consider] if it were to flood around where I live, what would I do?"
"Time and time again" the organisation was told by people who had experienced devastating flooding that "they'd never flooded before, and didn't think it would happen to them", he added.
NRW advises people to check their flood risk by postcode online, external, sign up for flood warnings and access advice about what to do, external if flooding is forecast in their area.
The organisation's flood warning service is available to 181,158 properties in Wales, but new figures show just 48,844 were currently signed up to receive the alerts via phone or email.
"It is low - 27%," Parr admitted, suggesting that people may be being put off by myths that signing up could affect their insurance premiums.
Cardigan's mayor Olwen Davies has bought a flood door for her own house, and also uses a flood gate for extra protection.
She said: "The river comes up once or twice a year... if there's a high tide, with a strong south-westerly wind that's what creates the most havoc.
"We work together and we know who to call on," she said.
Sarah Davies from the Met Office said long-range forecasts for October, November and December suggested "a greater chance of weather-related disruption".
"Weather patterns can change quickly at this time of year, and long-range forecasts describe broad seasonal trends rather than the timing, location and severity of individual weather events," she added.
"Whatever the season, understanding your flood risk and knowing what action to take if warnings are issued are sensible steps that can help you prepare should severe weather occur."
Additional reporting by Sara Dafydd

(AP) — People in the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama cleaned up after Isaias swept through as the storm's remnants brought the risk of flooding to the central Appalachians and the mid-Atlantic region on Sunday. Meanwhile, significant waves from Rachel, a former tropical storm, battered the coast of Southern California. "Major coastal flooding has already been occurring in some areas, with observed water levels running as much as 1.5 feet above predictions," the National Hurricane Center said, noting that high waves are coinciding with high tides. In western North Carolina, rivers overflowed as heavy rainfall raised the risk of flash and urban flooding, according to the National Weather Service. Tornadoes were possible in parts of Virginia and North Carolina, and life-threatening surf and rip current conditions were expected to continue along the Gulf and southeastern Atlantic coasts. At least four deaths were linked to Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, which came ashore as a Category 2 hurricane Friday near Destin, Florida, a Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops. The storm then roared into Alabama with tropical-force winds before heading farther north. In Florida's Escambia County, Sheriff Chip Simmons said a woman was killed when a tree fell on her home and a man died of carbon monoxide fumes from a generator running in his garage. One person died when a tree fell on a house in Birmingham, said Cory Moon, the city's fire chief. A second storm-related death in Alabama was attributed to a motor vehicle crash involving a downed tree in Barbour County, said Josh Johnson of the state's emergency management agency. Heavy rains cause problems in North Carolina In Burke County, North Carolina, an unhoused male and female were camping when floodwaters from the Catawba River caught them off guard. They were rescued, along with their dog, according to a spokesperson for the county emergency management agency. Separately, a woman trapped inside her car in floodwaters was freed outside of Morganton. People ride a golf cart through a partially flooded parking lot in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias in Gulf Breeze, Florida, U.S., October 10, 2026. Photo by Marco Bello/Reuters. In McDowell County, North Carolina, just west of Burke County, first responders said they dealt with five landslides and voluntary evacuations overnight Saturday into Sunday as they responded to flooded roads and streams overflowing their banks. "Despite a challenging night, we are thankful to report no known injuries or loss of life. We call that a success!" the county emergency management agency posted online. Nearly a dozen local weather stations in the western North Carolina county reported torrential 24-hour rainfall totals at 9 a.m. Sunday, from about 5 inches (13 centimeters) to as much as 9.57 inches (24 centimeters) at the fire/rescue station in Enola. The National Weather Service said rainfall was diminishing in the area but that rapid river rises and flooding remained possible. Dealing with Isaias aftermath in Florida Hurricane-force winds in the Florida Panhandle blew the roof off a Pensacola hotel, and the city's mayor said the airport "took some damage." The storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped away part of the facade of a high-rise in Panama City Beach. At a church in Pensacola where the United Cajun Navy was distributing supplies Sunday morning, a line of hundreds of cars stretched around the block. Yvette Haro said she arrived at 5 a.m. after being turned away the previous day because supplies had run out. A drone view shows a damaged apartments building in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias in Milton, Florida, US, October 11, 2026. Photo by Marco Bello/Reuters. With a 10-year-old son and a 5-year-old daughter at home, she said it's hard to go to stores and wait in long lines. She was looking for water, paper towels, toilet paper and cleaning supplies. "Anything that they're willing to give us is helpful," she said. While her home didn't suffer any damage, the loss of electricity was making things difficult, Haro said. "The biggest thing is our food going bad. It's really hard to keep grilling everything and then where do we store all this food?" Roughly 356,000 customers were without power Sunday at 2:30 p.m. ET in southern Alabama and the Florida Panhandle, according to poweroutage.com. Sarah Gatewood, a spokesperson for Florida Power & Light, said workers from all over Florida and from more than two dozen other states were mobilized to help restore power. Rachel brings wind and rain to southern California and the Southwest Rachel became a post-tropical cyclone overnight, bringing unusually big waves to Southern California, and it dissipated over Las Vegas as it drenched deserts across the Southwest. Waves battered a century-old wooden boardwalk on the Long Beach peninsula and forced homeowners to evacuate. The strip of multimillion-dollar oceanfront properties, along with much of the Southern California coastline, was already reeling from Hurricane Marie in September. "This area is completely shattered and vulnerable," Jack Gordon, a Long Beach real estate agent, said. "The fact that Rachel came and gave it the knockout blow — I don't want to say it can't get any worse for these houses, but it's really, really sad." 71124c1fd9ef.text: By — Fernando Llano, Associated Press Fernando Llano, Associated Press By — Martin Silva, Associated Press Martin Silva, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/hurricane-simon-hits-mexicos-pacific-coast Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Hurricane Simon hits Mexico's Pacific coast with damaging winds and rain World Oct 11, 2026 6:01 PM EDT PUERTO VALLARTA, Mexico (AP) — Hurricane Simon pounded Mexico's Pacific coast as a Category 4 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean. The hurricane's center swirled parallel to the coast, closing in on the Puerto Vallarta area, where its most damaging winds and rain were expected to hit around midnight and continue through Monday morning. The U.S. National Hurricane Center said it's not clear if it will make landfall, which could enable it to maintain its dangerous strength, sustaining winds of 140 mph (220 kph). That's not good news for people in and around Puerto Vallarta, a popular tourist destination in the state of Jalisco. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm. By midday Sunday, Simon's eye was moving within about 65 miles (100 kilometers) of Cabo Corrientes at about 7 mph (11 kph). A senior hurricane center specialist, Phillipe Pappin, said this westernmost tip of mainland Mexico is the area most likely to get a direct hit from the system. Cabo Corrientes is at the southern tip of Bahia de Banderas, the wide bay where Puerto Vallarta looks out to the Pacific. Waves hit the waterfront as Hurricane Simon approaches Mexico's Pacific coast, bringing heavy rain and strong winds to Manzanillo, Mexico, October 11, 2026. Photo by Daniel Becerril/Reuters. Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 25 miles (35 kilometers), and tropical-storm-force winds reach up to 80 miles (130 kilometers) from Simon's center, meaning the entire area between Mexico's western coast and the Sierra Madre mountains could be affected. "We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west-central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," Pappin said. "They're also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that's likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells." Meanwhile, the hurricane dumped rain over parts of southwestern Mexico. It could bring 10 to 20 inches (25 to 50 centimeters) of rain in many places, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 30 inches (76 centimeters). As the storm approached Puerto Vallarta, National Guard vehicles patrolled the streets while police used a megaphone to call out the few people who were jogging, walking their dogs or biking by the waterfront. Officers reminded people that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter. Not everyone followed the orders. Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas while asking the tourism sector to make sure workers and visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum took to the social platform X on Sunday to urge people in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to stay sheltered until the government issues a notification that the danger has passed. She also asked people to follow recommendations from civil protection officials and to avoid traveling on public roads. "Precautionary evacuation efforts to safe zones are ongoing; the priority is our safety," she wrote. Hotel worker Víctor Martínez went shopping for nonperishable food Sunday afternoon. He said he could not go to work because public transportation service was suspended and most of the hotel had been evacuated. Martínez found people's concerns about the hurricane comforting. "It happened to us before. It hit us years ago," Martínez said, referring to a Category 5 hurricane that hit the area in 2002. "People didn't expect it. We were very skeptical that it would ever hit us. Now, though, we're different. Precautions are being taken. It happened to us once, and we won't let it happen again." Despite the risks posed by Simon, tourists were still arriving in Puerto Vallarta. Visitors Ricardo Ramírez and Brenda Villarreal, who have never lived through a hurricane, went looking for food by the city's boardwalk and came across police urging people to take shelter. Ramírez said they were completely unprepared for the situation. "The boardwalk is closed. Be responsible. Understand!" police told passersby using a megaphone. Ramírez said he and Villarreal had planned their four-day vacation since last year and traveled from Guadalajara, Jalisco's capital. "We don't know the extent of the danger yet," Villarreal said. "We're just starting to see what's going on." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Regan Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/iran-calls-latest-u-s-proposal-to-end-war-insufficient-as-netanyahus-corruption-trial-resumes Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Iran calls latest U.S. proposal to end war 'insufficient' as Netanyahu's corruption trial resumes World Oct 11, 2026 5:43 PM EDT A senior Iranian official says Tehran finds the latest U.S. response to a proposal to end the war "insufficient" and warns of attacks on regional data centers and cables if fighting intensifies again. Meanwhile, Israel's former attorney general took the witness stand in corruption cases against Benjamin Netanyahu, as the political future of the country's longest-serving prime minister hangs in the balance with elections weeks away. Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Read our full coverage here. Iran says latest US response is 'insufficient' The head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council says Tehran finds the latest response from the United States "insufficient" as efforts at negotiations to end the war and fully open the Strait of Hormuz limp along. The comments by Mohsen Rezaei, a former Revolutionary Guard commander, were carried by Iran's state-run IRNA news agency. Rezaei added that Iran is no longer responding to the U.S. and said Washington must clarify certain issues, without giving details. He said the U.S. has accepted some of the seven conditions but others remain unclear. Iran's delegation to the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders last month proposed a sped-up agreement that echoed the memorandum of understanding that collapsed days after the U.S. and Iran signed it in June. The new proposal was rejected, but the two sides have remained in contact via mediation. Rezaei also threatened "cables, data centers, AI facilities and other sites in the region" if intense fighting breaks out again. Meanwhile, the Guard's navy warned that any ship on the strait that turns off navigation and identification systems would be "identified as hostile," according to an IRNA report. Attacks on ships transiting the strait have increased since Iran's proposal was rejected. One attack was reported Sunday. Former legal adviser testifies in Netanyahu corruption case Israel's former attorney general took the witness stand in Netanyahu's long-running corruption trial. Avichai Mandelblit indicted the prime minister seven years ago for fraud, breach of trust and accepting bribes. The charges were the first-ever against a sitting Israeli prime minister. Netanyahu was in the courtroom to hear Mandelblit testify. The prime minister handpicked Mandelblit, his former Cabinet secretary, for the attorney general job. His tenure ended in 2022. Netanyahu has been accused of offering or exchanging favors with wealthy associates and media moguls for political gain. He denies any wrongdoing. Saudi Arabia on alert as Houthis warn of new strikes A projectile struck the same passenger terminal at the Riyadh international airport that was hit on Saturday. The airport had been closed after Saturday's attack, which killed 12 people, but Saudi authorities reported injuries in the latest attack. Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed responsibility for both attacks on King Khalid International Airport, which has been targeted every day since Wednesday. Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis' military spokesperson, urged "everyone to take our warnings seriously" about the risks of flying in Saudi airspace. The attacks have marked a major escalation in the war between the Houthis and the kingdom, and complicated efforts to halt the U.S.-Iran war. Gaza residents return to rubble as strikes continue Residents in central Gaza returned home to assess the damage caused by Israeli strikes after they had been warned to evacuate the day before. Bassam Abed said at least 10 residences housing some 300 families were reduced to rubble, and families were not given enough time to flee. "Women slept outdoors. We did not take clothes," Abed said. Israel's military said it had targeted militant infrastructure, including a rocket launch site and a command center used by Hamas militants to attack soldiers. One year after Israel and Hamas reached a ceasefire deal, Israel continues to launch near-daily strikes. Netanyahu wants probe into 'NAZA' documentary Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has asked the attorney general and head of the Shin Bet security service to investigate people who participated in the new documentary "NAZA," in which Israeli military insiders describe what they say was the reckless killing of civilians in Gaza. Netanyahu said the film, which debuted at the Venice Film Festival to a record 25-minute standing ovation, tells "a false, misleading and biased story that slanders the State of Israel" and its military. The documentary has angered and unsettled Israelis, whose view of the war in Gaza differs sharply from that of much of the world, where criticism of Israel's actions in the Palestinian territory has grown. Netanyahu is fighting to stay in power in the Oct. 27 election, in which security is a major issue. Lebanese army says retired officer killed by Israeli shelling Lebanon's army said it had recovered the body of a retired army officer who was killed by Israeli artillery fire while checking on his property in the southern town of Yater. It said Ali Abdul Hassan Sweidan was "directly targeted by a hostile Israeli tank" and called it "a flagrant violation of existing understandings." An Israeli military spokesperson said they were not aware of the incident. Israel has occupied a large swath of southern Lebanon since the outbreak of its latest war with the Iran-backed Lebanese militant group Hezbollah in March. Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?
US President Donald Trump has said Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an immediate "energy ceasefire".
Moscow is yet to comment on the announcement and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky told US media it was "news to me".
Trump also recently announced a US deal to import Russian diesel, in an attempt to bring the fuel price down ahead of the midterm elections.
The price of diesel in the US has been high since the start of the war with Iran and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The BBC's Joe Inwood examines Trump's announcement and what might mean for the president ahead of the midterm election.

- Published
Nebraska rancher Yvette Mannon was already having a rough year.
In April, a wildfire destroyed 1,600 grazing acres and 13 miles (21 km) of fence along the ranch she bought in 2002. The ranch is nestled in a corner of Nebraska that's home to rolling green hills under sweeping Midwestern skies, the landscape dotted with grain silos and feedlots alongside fields and fields of bovines.
Mannon's 300 cattle survived the blaze - but the fencing needed to be replaced, and the herd still needed to be fed.
With steel prices at their highest levels in years, heavily affected by tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump, that meant spending $4.89 a foot - for a total exceeding $300,000.
On top of that, because so much good grazing land had been destroyed, Mannon also needed a tractor out every day delivering hay to her cattle - at a time when diesel prices, spiking due to the Iran War, were up more than 40% from the previous year.
Then in August, the Trump administration announced it would import 300,000 metric tons of duty-free foreign beef in a bid to lower consumer prices. The news hit right before the September-November window when most US calves are weaned and sold.
The cattle market tanked immediately.
'It felt like a betrayal'
"So we're 'Buy American', 'Let's Make America Great'," said Mannon, 63, who voted for Trump. "But for you guys over here, sorry."
"It just felt like a betrayal," she said.
Many farmers and ranchers across the US say they are being hit from all sides. Recent years have been difficult, with drought affecting crops and already historically low cattle herds. But they say government policies have added to the strain.
That has left some in Nebraska, which overwhelmingly backed President Trump during the last election, reassessing their political allegiances.
Dan Osborn, an independent candidate running against Trump-backed Republican Pete Ricketts, is performing surprisingly well in the polls ahead of November's Senate race.
Republicans seem keenly aware of the discord and frustration among farmers. Both Trump and Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen have in recent weeks announced relief policies aimed at lowering fuel costs for farmers and ranchers, who say they have been struggling for months.
The Iran War has sent diesel and fertiliser prices skyrocketing - both daily necessities for agricultural operations. Tariffs have affected machinery costs and repairs, as well as steel and lumber prices.
And decisions by the Trump administration - whether it be importing foreign beef or opening up the southern border to Mexican cattle - have sent already-volatile markets into overdrive.
Many producers are losing hundreds of dollars per head of cattle.
"All of this hit cattle markets, as a whole, negatively," said James Mitchell, an assistant professor and agricultural economist at the University of Arkansas.
Cattle markets run in 10-12 year cycles, he said, with some good years and some bad. The industry recently enjoyed a particularly lucrative period, where low supply and high demand drove up prices. But now, the market is clearly on a downswing.
Jake Wolfinger, 45, has been weathering the downturn at his feedlot near Lexington, Nebraska. He and his wife are both Ohio natives hailing from multi-generational farming families. They moved to Nebraska - which enjoys lush land and the most groundwater in the nation - to strike out on their own.
The Wolfingers bought a dilapidated feedlot in 2010, which they have turned into a sophisticated operation with 5,500 cattle. Neighbours point to them as an example of what hard work can still do in a tough industry.
But Wolfinger did not factor the Iran War, tariffs or foreign beef imports into his planning.
"Things were just chumming along pretty good," he said, selling cattle for $240 per hundredweight - but that's dropped to $225. That may not seem like much, but it means a loss of potentially hundreds of dollars a head.
Wolfinger is also contending with sky-high diesel costs, with some equipment going through 400-gallon tanks a day.
"It really makes a guy think," he said.
A Trump supporter, Wolfinger said he voted for the president because "we needed his spirit in this country". He also expressed frustration with what he called "woke DEI" policies on the left.
But he is unhappy with the way the president has intervened in the beef market.
"People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business, because it's harvest time," Wolfinger said.
'People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business'
Forty miles northwest, near Callaway, Nebraska, 54-year-old Duane Kimball stands in his shed surrounded by machinery - and a huge Trump banner along one wall.
"The daily upchargeâ¦ is kind of painful," he said.
"I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit."
Kimball believed the Iran War would have ended long ago.
But he does not blame Trump for all of his economic challenges. "To pin that on this administration, I don't think is a fair assessment," he said.
He pointed to cumbersome regulations as well as the rising cost of machinery and fertiliser - trends that began before Trump returned to the White House.
Mannon, who returned to her native Nebraska and bought the ranch after a career in banking, believes the agricultural industry will show its feelings at the midterms.
But like many around here, she prefers not to engage in too much political debate.
That is not a problem for her friend and nearby rancher Jim Jenkins. A former independent senatorial candidate, Jenkins is fiercely proud of Nebraska agriculture and his own ranch, which is on land his family homesteaded more than 150 years ago.
Jenkins has been so incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry that he wrote an opinion article over the summer in an Omaha paper.
He has felt the squeeze personally too, citing high diesel, fertiliser, lumber and steel costs - everything from barbed wire to fence posts.

The News
Despite increasingly critical media coverage of AI and the spread of data centers across the US, one news network has been painting a more positive picture.
More than half of the references to data centers on Fox News over the last two years would have left viewers with a favorable impression, compared to less than 10% on CNN and 5% on MS NOW, according to a new Semafor analysis of mentions of data centers on each network.
The mentions were pulled from closed captions preserved by the Internet Archive, which keeps a digital, searchable library of recorded TV news. A pair of AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI scored each reference on its content, with the networkâs name removed.
Mentions of data centers have, predictably, shot up across all three networks in recent months as political backlash against AI swells and the data centers themselves have become a salient issue ahead of the midterms.
But Foxâs opinion and morning shows, including My View with Lara Trump, Fox & Friends, and Life, Liberty & Levin, leaned on the promise of AI, economic investment and the race with China, skewing Foxâs coverage more favorably, the analysis showed. The networkâs news shows were more measured.
In an Aug. 23 monologue that at one point featured a chyron reading âThe case for data centers,â Fox host Brian Kilmeade acknowledged âreal concerns,â but argued that âsaying no to data centers nationwide also means saying no to the tax dollars that can flow into a community. â¦ If Americans donât build the infrastructure to meet the demand, somebody else will.â
On CNN and MS NOW, the criticism focused as much on the facilitiesâ political toxicity as on harms like power bills or water use, casting them as unpopular with voters and a liability for politicians who back them heading into the midterms.
Data centers âare driving up energy costs, sucking up water supplies, wiping out rather than creating jobs,â MS NOWâs Katy Tur said in May. âPoliticians beware.â
Polling shows that across demographic groups, Americans hold increasingly negative views of data centers: More than half of Americans say data centers are mostly bad for the environment, Pew Research Center found last month, compared with 39% in January.
Fox News did not comment for this story.
Maxâs view
The pro-data center programming on Fox News comes as the right tries to define its positions in an AI-fueled, post-Donald Trump future.
Foxâs favorable data center coverage mirrors Trumpâs position on their growth and the need for AI companies to help fuel the US economy.
âThe only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,â Trump wrote on Truth Social in August. âIf we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame.â
But anger about data centers and the rapid advancement of AI represents a faultline within the MAGA coalition that swept Trump back into office. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., have questioned some data centers in their states, while Texas Gov. Greg Abbott seems to have flipped from supporting data centers to looking to slow their growth in his state amid a tougher-than-expected reelection campaign.
Some on the right I have talked to in the last several months worry that Fox News, which Trump watches religiously, and other pro-data center voices are encouraging the president to take positions that are broadly unpopular with his rural and suburban base.
âThe Big Tech oligarchs, the guys driving AI, did a terrible job,â Steve Bannon, a staunchly anti-AI Trump ally, told the Daily Signal in September. âThey came in to try to muscle local communities, and particularly since President Trumpâs strongest base is in exurban and rural communities, thatâs where they were really the ugliest, and they havenât made their case, and they particularly havenât made their case at the local level about the economics of this, and the energy of this, and the water of this, and the manifestation of what these things are going to be used for.â
Room for Disagreement
Not all of Foxâs data center coverage has been rosy; its tenor grew slightly less favorable in 2026 compared to last year.
âItâs taxing our system way too much on water, agriculture land, or electricity. Weâre gonna implode,â the Texas agriculture commissioner said in an interview on a weekend Fox show in August. âWe just canât do it. Thereâs not enough.

The News
Hacked messages from an adviser to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu are providing a glimpse of his aidesâ close ties to the media.
The incumbent prime ministerâs reelection campaign has been repeatedly rocked by hacked and leaked documents, part of broad attempts to destabilize a wildly divisive leader both inside and outside his country ahead of Oct. 27 elections.
The latest breach comes from the WhatsApp account of Netanyahu aide Jonatan Urich, who appears to have exposed sensitive information through a vibe-coded media-monitoring app. Haaretz reported Sunday that it had âverifiedâ the leak.
The messages include conversations between Urich and Amit Segal, a central media figure who is chief political analyst for Channel 12 News, the countryâs leading broadcaster, and host of the program Meet the Press, an analogue of the US show of that name.
In the exchanges, Segal offers advice about the campaignâs videos and its messaging: Netanyahuâs management of the aftermath of the October 7 attack is his core political advantage, he suggests. Segal mentions he offered the same advice to Netanyahuâs campaign spokeswoman. In another message, Urich shares a speech Netanyahu is planning to give.
Segal declined to discuss the messages on the record. Urich, who is also enmeshed in a scandal over payments from Qatar, didnât respond to an inquiry, but in a lawyersâ statement posted to X confirmed that he had been hacked and threatened legal consequences against anyone who published the content of the leaks. Israelâs Privacy Protection Law prohibits republishing content obtained through illegal means.
Benâs view
Hacks and leaks are challenging to cover. The most important story in most hacks â including this one âÂ is the hack itself; this is part of the broad internationalization of the Israeli political campaign, in which actors across the region and in the US line up for and, mostly against, the leader who led his countryâs response to the October 7 attacks.
But Israeli commentators also professed shock, if not surprise, Sunday at how closely aligned the journalist and spin doctor appeared to be. Segal is a center-right figure broadly aligned with Netanyahu âÂ but heâs also a top journalist who appears on international platforms, like the American political figure Dan Senorâs widely-followed Call Me Back podcast, as an independent analyst.
One Israeli journalist compared Segalâs role in Israel to that of Fox News host Bret Baier, who maintains a journalistic independence despite working for a right-wing platform. The messages put a dent in Segalâs image, and offer a glimpse at parts of an Israeli media that has grown very close to its prime minister.
Room for Disagreement
Segal addressed the controversy on News 12, describing the messages as part of a âvery delicate tango between the journalist and the subject of their coverage.â He added that âany people Iâve covered over the years gave me drafts of speeches, saying, âThis will be our campaign, what are your thoughts?ââ
Notable
- The regionâs politics have been buffeted âÂ and illuminated â repeatedly by aggressive cyber campaigns for years. Semafor reported in 2023 on extensive, leaked Iranian government communications that revealed Iranian attempts to influence US politics.

The News
When ABC News removed a story about Donald Trumpâs sons from its website without explanation on Thursday, an unnamed company source told media reporters the article had been published âprematurely.â Nathan Lee, the investigative reporter who wrote the original piece, used the same language in emails to Powerus and Anduril, two of the companies at the center of the piece.
But emails between ABC News and its subjects, provided to Semafor, show the network seeking to downplay its errors by misrepresenting its own processes.
On Oct. 7, ABC News published an investigation into a new $6.6 billion deal between defense contractor Anduril and the US Navy to build a new high-tech submarine shipyard in Maryland. The piece largely focused on the financial ties between President Donald Trumpâs son and defense companies, noting that Donald Trump Jr. is a partner at investment firm 1789 Capital, which âclaimed a major stake in Anduril in June 2025 from a $2.5 billion investment into the company.â
After the piece was published, a spokesperson for Anduril reached out to Lee with several urgent requests for correction. The company â which had not responded to ABC Newsâ inquiries prior to its publication, according to an Anduril source â wanted the network to clarify connections between Anduril and 1789, noting that the firm had invested $50 million in Andurilâs latest round, a small percentage of the $2.5 billion total.
âToday, 1789 owns approximately 0.13% of Anduril and has no major investor rights. Any suggestion that 1789 financed the round or holds significant ownership, governance position or âmajor stakeâ in Anduril is inaccurate,â Andurilâs spokesperson wrote to Lee, according to emails obtained by Semafor.
After the story was published on Wednesday, Lee told Anduril that the network was slightly tweaking the language in its piece, but it was otherwise standing by its story.
âI have spoken to my editors and we have updated the story for accuracy,â Lee said in a note. âWe had pulled the âmajor stakeâ language from previous reporting. 1789 Capital did claim a stake from the $2.5 billion investment your company received, so we are standing by our language to that extent.â
Andurilâs PR team was not satisfied, and continued to press the network to clarify its story, saying that the piece misstated 1789 Capitalâs investment in Andurilâs fundraising round.
âItâs still not clear. I read your text and it reads as if they invested the full $2.5b. Would be much more accurate to list their actual investment of $50m and even more accurate to share that they own less than a percentage point in Anduril,â a spokesperson wrote.
In another email later Wednesday afternoon, Lee said ABC Newsâ editors had reviewed the language and were standing by the piece.
âApologies, but my editors said we are standing by the language. Iâll make sure to reach out to both of you directly for any future stories,â Lee said.
But by Thursday, the network had changed its mind. The network removed the piece without explanation, and Peter Charalambous, an ABC News producer in New York, reached out to Anduril and Powerus, a drone contractor mentioned in the story, saying the story had been âpublished prematurely and removed from our website.â
On Friday evening, ABC News republished a new version of the story re-reported by Charalambous, now without a byline. An editorâs note did not include language that the initial piece was published early.
âEditorâs Note: CORRECTION: A version of this story published on Oct. 7 contained errors in the description of certain company investments, government contracts and event chronologies. After subsequent reporting, this version contains corrected information and additional context regarding some of those investments, contracts and events.â
A network source told Semafor: âWe always review every situation in a thorough and thoughtful manner and will not be providing further comment at this time.â The source also noted that it was extremely rare for ABC News to remove a story.
Status reported Sunday that the article was mentioned during the networkâs regular 9 am editorial call the day it was published, âsuggesting at least some staffers were aware of its publication,â and it âcirculated it through its usual email distribution without raising any immediate alarms.â
Maxâs view
ABC Newsâ suggestion that its initial story was published prematurely is familiar spin to anyone who has dealt with crisis PR. It minimized the companyâs mistakes and made the situation seem like an accident.
But at a time when distrust in the news media continues to rise, deflections like this can damage the credibility of mainstream, nonpartisan American journalism. Tellingly, the network seemed to know the difference in its official response, acknowledging that the original piece contained errors.
Brett Velicovich, co-founder of Powerus, another company mentioned in ABC Newsâ initial piece, complained that the networkâs handling of the story reinforced his frustration with much of the media coverage of his company and the presidentâs administration.
âItâs destroying the integrity of what reporting is all about,â Velicovich said. âThe damage is already done.â
The Trump familyâs mix of business and governing, unprecedented in recent history, is an important reporting target, as journalists attempt to understand how companies and countries are attempting to influence policy by investing in Trump businesses or bringing the Trumps on as partners themselves. But ABC Newsâ decision to remove its story without explanation while misleadingly telegraphing that it was simply published on accident gave the presidentâs son and many on the right another opening to criticize mainstream news outlets.
If more and more people continue to believe that news organizations are willing to mislead or fail to take full accountability for mistakes, will they listen when outlets have legitimate stories?

Watch: Endangered orangutans released back into the wild after Borneo fires
Eight orangutans have been released into the wild in Borneo after being rescued from intense wildfires.

0081255f8795.text: Pete Buttigieg has been able to campaign for Democrats across the country more than many of his potential 2028 rivals this past year. One reason: He doesn't have a job. That's by choice. Buttigieg said no when top Democrats urged him to run for governor or the U.S. Senate in Michigan this year. Why it matters: That decision is a gamble for Buttigieg's presidential ambitions. He's been able to build a national network over the last two years but hasn't added to his relatively thin resume as a former mayor of South Bend, Ind., and Joe Biden's transportation secretary. Buttigieg, 44, became a national political figure without following the typical path. He ran for president in 2020 as a small-town mayor and won the Iowa caucus by offering an optimistic vision and impressing voters with his communication skills — including in hostile environments. Driving the news: In early 2025, Democratic lawmakers and strategists including New York Sen. Chuck Schumer and former Michigan Sen. Debbie Stabenow urged Buttigieg — who had moved to Michigan — to run for office in his new state. Winning such an office, they argued, would help Buttigieg build his resume for a future White House run and give him a chance to distance himself from the unpopular Biden administration. Buttigieg passed, citing both a desire to stay home more with his husband and young twins, and figuring that he could still get his message out without being in the Senate. Instead, he set about building a larger national network among Democrats — particularly with Black voters in the South, where he had struggled in the 2020 Democratic primary. Buttigieg has traveled to 37 states since he left the Biden administration, Politico reported last week. Democratic candidates in vital swing districts and states have welcomed him to campaign for them this year while resisting offers from other potential presidential candidates such as former Vice President Kamala Harris , New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and California Gov. Gavin Newsom. In Buttigieg, many Democrats see a surrogate who can draw attention and crowds without the degree of negative attention that other prominent Democrats attract. Buttigieg also will campaign in key races in the final weeks before the Nov. 3 election. He's scheduled to be in Michigan and Virginia — which happen to hold early contests in the 2028 presidential primary. Between the lines: Buttigieg has tried to position himself as a candidate of the next generation who also has enough experience in the executive branch to be able to deliver. He's betting that the traditional ladder of running for president — becoming a senator, governor, or vice president first — no longer applies, especially after the Trump era. What they're saying: Buttigieg "knows what no one else on the Democratic side does, which is what it's actually like to run for this office — the pacing, the pressures and imperatives," David Axelrod, a former senior aide to President Obama and an outside adviser to Buttigieg in the past, told Axios. "At a time when the party and country will be searching for youth and forward-looking vision, he has the capacity to articulate one in a powerful way," Axelrod added. Axelrod said that if Buttigieg runs, "it will be because he feels the timing is right for someone like him, and the big mission is more compelling than the statewide races on which he took a pass." A Buttigieg spokesperson said that "when Pete decided not to run for office in Michigan, he promised he would still get to work to help candidates everywhere. He's been doing just that."

e8812fa747bf.text: A federal judge on Sunday ordered the Trump administration to immediately halt taxpayer-funded ads featuring President Trump. Why it matters: The ruling temporarily blocks the ads weeks before November's midterm elections as multiple lawsuits challenging the Trump administration's use of taxpayer money play out in court. Sunday's ruling stems from a suit filed in the Southern District of New York by Washington, D.C.-based watchdog Common Cause, non-profit Democracy Forward and other plaintiffs. A similar lawsuit , filed by the Democratic National Committee, was filed in D.C. federal court earlier this month. The big picture: The Trump administration maintains that the ads are public service announcements and that previous Republican and Democratic administrations have used taxpayer-funded advertising to promote government policies. Trump pledged to pay for the ads himself after both lawsuits were filed, though the White House told Axios there were no plans to reimburse the government for millions already spent on the ads. Driving the news: The plaintiffs in the New York lawsuit allege that the Trump administration exceeded congressional authorization and violated restrictions on publicity and propaganda. In a brief order , U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon found that a motion filed by the coalition was "not moot." She found they had "demonstrated that they are likely to succeed on the merits, will suffer irreparable harm in the absence of an injunction, the balance of the equities tips in their favor, and an injunction serves the public interest," according to the order. The suit names the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles as defendants. Representatives for the White House and DHS did not immediately respond to Axios' Sunday evening request for comment. What's next: A hearing is scheduled for Oct. 13 to discuss next steps in the case.

Darline Graham (R) and pediatrician Annie Andrews (D) faced off in their one and only debate on Sunday in the South Carolina Senate race, and it quickly became testy as Graham sought to tie the physician to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) while Andrews suggested the GOP senator wouldn’t be able to stand up to the White House.
Graham, Andrews and libertarian Kasie Whitener, a radio host and professor, participated in a debate hosted by South Carolina ETV and Public Radio in Columbia, S.C.
Graham suggested Andrews was in favor of progressive policies like “Medicare for All” and called her a “radical liberal.”
Meanwhile, Andrews pointed to Graham’s past primary debate gaffe on Taiwan as an indication that the GOP senator was not up to the task of a full six-year Senate term and dinged her for dropping “Nordone” from her last name.
Graham is seen as the favorite to win in November, with Decision Desk HQ forecasting a 70 percent probability that the GOP senator wins next month.
Here are 5 takeaways from the lone debate in the South Carolina Senate race.
Graham, Andrews take swipes at each other
Graham and Andrews set the tone for the debate early, taking swipes at each other on policy issues and even their own personal names.
“I’ve been in the Senate for three months now. I’ve already co-sponsored several bills that protect farmers, that protect the American taxpayer,” the GOP senator said just minutes into the debate. “My Democratic opponent is pretending to be someone she is not. She’s the most radical liberal that’s ever run for state office in South Carolina.”
Graham also suggested that Andrews, a pediatrician, supported “government-run healthcare for all.”
“We are already $40 trillion in national debt. That will cost trillions of dollars,” Graham continued. “Our national debt will be through the roof. She will bankrupt our country with government-run healthcare for all.”
The Democratic candidate called Medicare for All in August “a policy from a few decades ago,” saying she was in favor of creating a public option for the Affordable Care Act.
Meanwhile, Andrews dinged Graham for dropping “Nordone” from her name after joining the Senate, insinuating that she was trying to ride on the tailcoats of her late brother Sen. Lindsey Graham’s (R) name.
“I told you my opponent was going to call me a socialist, and there she’s done it again. She’s been told to come out here and call me Bernie Ocasio Mamdani. That’s what’s in her script,” Andrews said. “But the truth is, my name is Annie Andrews, and there shouldn’t be any confusion about that because, unlike my opponent, I haven’t changed my name recently.”
Graham slammed Andrews over the statement, saying the name “Graham” appears in all of her signed documents and said she kept the name to feel close to her parents who died when she was young.
The Democratic pediatrician also suggested Graham wouldn’t be able to stand up to the president or White House while in the upper chamber.
“The job is to represent South Carolina. She considers the job to be to read their scripts and do their bidding, and we can do better,” Andrews said.
Graham defends Taiwan gaffe
Andrews referenced a gaffe the GOP senator made during her primary runoff debate against Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) in which she said that national security “is not my thing,” suggesting that the GOP senator lacked the experience needed to do the job.
“My opponent is the only one on this stage who had the opportunity to vote to end the war, but three times in a row she voted to continue it,” Andrews said at one point in response to a question about the war with Iran. “And several days after one of those votes, she had the audacity to walk out onto this stage and admit that national security isn’t really her thing. South Carolina, if your surgeon said that appendectomies aren’t really his thing, would you still hand him a scalpel? No.”
During a debate between Graham and Norman in August, the GOP senator was asked a national security question pertaining to Taiwan and the South China Sea.
“I’m just going to be honest here. … I’m not that informed on national security,” Graham said, adding later, “but I do support the military.”
Graham defended herself afterward, saying “I’m not a politician” and that voters care more about domestic issues than foreign policy. The GOP senator defended herself again on the debate stage, saying that constituents respected that she was honest about what she did and did not know.
“Your thing apparently is not being honest with the people of South Carolina,” Graham shot back. “At least I’m honest. If I don’t know something, I am glad to say it, and I’ll say it again tonight. But … you are deceiving the people of South Carolina.”
Andrews presses Graham to commit to more debates
The pediatrician pressed Graham twice to commit to another debate between the pair, arguing that voters should hear from the candidates again before the election, which is three weeks away.
“There’s a lot to talk about in this U.S. Senate race, and unfortunately, my opponent has only agreed to this one 60-minute debate. I’ve agreed to three additional debates. We have a lot to talk about. That is very clear,” Andrews said. “So I want to ask Sen. Graham this evening if she’ll commit to standing on another debate stage with me at least two more times before Nov. 3?”
Graham brushed off the request after she was pressed a second time.
“I’ve had a job representing the people of South Carolina in Washington, D.C., so I think it’s more important for me to hear from voters than to stand with you on this debate stage,” Graham said.

The GOP senator sidestepped a question about whether she supported a recent deal the president made with Russia on diesel. President Trump said on Friday that Russia had agreed to supply the U.S. and the global marketplace with 300,000 tons of diesel “immediately.”

Powderfinger, one of Australia's best loved rock bands, has unveiled details of a comeback tour â to take place 17 years after they broke up.
The Brisbane-based group, who confirmed their reunion last week, will kick off with four nights in their home city next September.
They will then play another 14 shows across Cairns, Sydney, Adelaide, Perth and Melbourne, with all gigs to be staged in a "stadium sized big-top" tent.
In a statement on Monday the band said they were "absolutely ecstatic" to be getting together and playing again.
"Over the years there have been tons of suggestions for us to go back on the road but, until now, it never felt quite right or lined up for all of us," they said.
"We have always been so grateful for the continued support from our long-term fans and over the years we've picked up a lot of new ones who have never seen us play."
"People often tell us that our music is connected to their most treasured and joyous memories," they added. "We hope to spread a little more of that joy when we make our way around the country with some of Australia's best established and upcoming talent, and to make some new memories for us all."
The tour schedule of only playing on Friday and Saturday nights is similar to that adopted by Oasis in their world tour last year. No gigs outside of Australia have yet been announced.
Powderfinger released seven studio albums during their career including 2000's Odyssey Number Five which was voted best Australian album of all time by listeners of Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) music station Triple J in 2011.
That included the single My Happiness, which was voted sixth best Australian song of all time by the same station in 2025. The group's other hits include On My Mind and These Days and Sunsets.
Since the band split, frontman Bernard Fanning has maintained a solo career while bassist John Collins has gone on to open two of Brisbane's largest live music venues.
