US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices.
Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments.
That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago.
The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws.
As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that.
This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries.
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended".
It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.
A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats â on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course".
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said.
They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine".
The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden.
Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products.
Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong.
Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel.
The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress.
Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.
The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.
The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (Â£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.
Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.
The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, which amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.
It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war.
Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow.

Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found.
During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force.
BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles.
Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones.
In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones.
The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives.
Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots.
Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures.
A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account.
The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute.
"The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said.
Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't thinkâ¦ somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment."
Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said.
Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home.
The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked.
After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful.
In total, three people were killed.
One of them was Evans Kiche, a 40 year-old-chef and father to seven children. BBC analysis shows he was around 60m from the confrontation when he was killed by a gunshot wound to the head.
The two other mourners killed, Vincent Ogutu and Jidah Burka, were at least 160m away, in the opposite stands, far removed from the pavilion.
Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head.
Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered.
Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons.
The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection.
The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium.
Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment.
Ogutu, a 36-year-old father of three, hadn't planned to go to Kasarani, his wife told the BBC. He was in central Nairobi on the morning of 16 October with friends when they saw the crowds heading to the stadium and decided to join.
Within hours, he was dead.
His widow Yvonne Akinyi described how the killing upended their family, saying their children were now orphans.
As she prepares to mark a year since her husband's death, Akinyi is no closer to understanding why he died while paying his respects at an event organised by the government.
"I will just try to be that strong woman. Very strong. But deep inside there is a hole," she said.
"It is very painful because sometimes you just sit down and ask yourself. At Kasarani there were so many people, so many of them. Why him."

The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found.
Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (Â£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.
Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents.
Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant".
Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals.
Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws".
The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism.
For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club.
Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, Â£5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years.
The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes".
Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers.
The evidence is contained in a leak that includes thousands of documents about the oligarch's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus - which used to be a tax haven popular with Russians - between 1995 and 2022.
The BBC and media partners including the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and the Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network - as well as the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, external - have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential, external investigation.
In 2022, Panorama also reported on how Abramovich had made his fortune from a corrupt deal to buy a Russian state-owned oil company in the 1990s, selling it back to the government a decade later for billions in profit. He has previously said allegations of corruption in the deal are false.
The profits from Abramovich's oil deals in Russia were funnelled into a web of offshore companies. They were administered from Cyprus by a corporate services firm called MeritServus, in Limassol, the island's second-largest city.
Until 2005, Deloitte - now the biggest of the "big four" firms which dominate the accounting industry - owned MeritServus. After they split, the two companies worked closely together with Abramovich's associates to manage his global fortune.
The leaked documents from MeritServus reveal some of their practices.
Panorama - Roman Abramovich: How He Hid His Fortune
He was the Russian oligarch who brought his wealth to the UK. But whatâs the truth about Roman Abramovichâs fortune? Panorama investigates the documents that were falsified to hide his wealth and evade tax.
Watch now on BBC iPlayer or on BBC One at 20:00 BST on Monday 12 October.
Our first example of backdated paperwork comes in 2006, after a new law in Cyprus meant that company accounts had to be made public. The new transparency law threatened to expose the secrets of Abramovich's vast wealth.
Deloitte Cyprus had prepared draft accounts for 2003 - but had not yet finalised them - for his Cypriot company Amiscan Investments. The accounts detailed $672m of luxury property.
A mansion in West Sussex, a luxury flat in London and an estate in the south of France were all included - plus helicopters, private jets and a small fleet of boats the oligarch owned at the time, including the $147.5m Pelorus.
To keep them secret, Abramovich's associates and Meritservus decided to rewrite history. They drew up a plan to circumvent the transparency law by transferring the assets to Amiscan's parent company in the British Virgin Islands (BVI), where they could be kept hidden. And they backdated the change by three years to make it look like the asset transfer had happened in 2003.
Deloitte Cyprus reviewed the backdated documents and said they were "adequate" to allow them to remove the assets from Amiscan's accounts.
When the 2003 accounts were signed off by Deloitte in 2006, the homes, planes and yachts disappeared at the stroke of a pen. Only $75,000 of assets remained.
Deloitte signed off the accounts even though the leaked documents show it knew they were completely misleading.
Lord Sikka, professor of accounting at the University of Sheffield, said it was a "violation of a statutory duty" and "pretty scandalous" to misrepresent transaction dates and not to publish true and fair accounts.
Panorama also found evidence that backdated documents had been used in a tax evasion scheme.
This involved another one of Abramovich's Cypriot companies, Kravin Investments, which had almost $2bn in the bank in 2003.
It had been earning large amounts in interest, so Roman Abramovich's company should have been paying tax on that interest to the Cypriot authorities.
But his advisers had another idea to rewrite history.

This story is a partnership between Dylan Baddour of Inside Climate News and Neena Satija of The Texas Newsroom.
Eight years ago, at the height of the shale-oil boom, a committee of industry giants and public officials unveiled a bold plan to make Corpus Christi “drought proof.”
With this plan, a consultant explained to city officials at the time, their semi-arid stretch of coastline in South Texas could finally overcome the economic limitations of its scarce water supply.
“Industry can continue to operate,” said a slideshow the consultant, Frank Brogan, presented to Corpus Christi City Council. “Industry can justify expansion. Community can attract new industry.”
The plan seemed simple. The region’s largest water users—Texas-based titans like OxyChem, Valero and Citgo—would pay Corpus Christi to build the state’s first-ever seawater desalination plant, which would produce millions of gallons of freshwater per day at minimal cost to the public. In exchange, the companies wouldn’t face pressure to throttle back operations at their refineries and chemical plants during future dry spells.
“We don’t want to have the reputation of having a water problem,” said Brogan, a former executive at the Port of Corpus Christi, the top U.S. port for crude-oil exports, in the August 2018 presentation.
City leaders unanimously approved the plan, hailing it as a breakthrough: Giant corporations had agreed to front the money for an innovative project that other communities could only dream of affording.
But instead of securing Corpus Christi’s water future, the plan pushed Texas’ eighth-largest city to the brink of a water-supply disaster, burned through tens of millions of public dollars, and engulfed the city in political turmoil.
The city has spent at least $50 million on the promised desalination plant, but it has yet to materialize—a victim of political dysfunction, the coronavirus pandemic, rapid inflation and frequent turnover in the city’s political leadership, among other factors. And the companies that had originally agreed to pay for it now contribute only a fraction of what the plant is expected to cost. Residents would have to pay for the rest.
Meanwhile, Corpus Christi has honored the commitment it made back in 2018: It has not pressured the companies to cut back on water consumption, even when the area slipped into a punishing drought.
By this spring, the region’s main reservoirs almost dried up entirely. The industrial giants raced to drill emergency water wells, the city’s credit ratings slipped, and local business leaders raised the specter of mass layoffs if the water ran out.
In the face of an unprecedented emergency, city officials debated meager measures like closing public pools and fining residents for washing cars, rather than imposing restrictions on the chemical plants and refineries that use more water than all 500,000 residents of the seven-county Coastal Bend region combined.
“The reason we were in the water crisis was because of their water usage,” said Isabel Araiza, a college professor and founder of a community group called For the Greater Good who has fought for a decade against the desalination project.
Bob Paulison, executive director of a trade group that represents the industrial giants, said they are not responsible for the crisis. He said the city’s leaders were tasked with building a drought-proof water supply with funding the companies provided, and they didn’t deliver.
Of Corpus Christi, he said, “you kept dragging your feet and thinking that everything was OK until it was too late.”
Gov. Greg Abbott also placed the blame squarely on Corpus Christi earlier this year, telling reporters in March that city leaders “squandered” massive state loans awarded to them for the project.
But a review of public records spanning more than a decade shows that the industrial giants also played a critical role in developing the failed plan.
Those companies initially sought to build a private seawater desalination plant solely for their own use. They later decided to team up with city officials on a public project, which allowed them to access hundreds of millions of dollars in low-interest loans from the state.
City and industry officials believed their partnership would guarantee Corpus Christi a prosperous future. Instead, it has become a case study into the pitfalls of tying an essential public resource to the growth ambitions of private industry.
Corpus Christi no longer faces an acute water crisis, thanks to heavy rain this summer. But its near brush with disaster has turned some residents against the same corporations that power the economy in one of Texas’ leading industrial hubs.
Now, a proposal to nullify the 2018 plan will be on the local ballot in November, following a successful petition campaign by Araiza and other activists. The proposal seeks to eliminate the protections from water restrictions that city leaders gave the industrial giants almost a decade ago and instead dramatically increases the price they would pay for water during the next drought.
If voters approve the measure, it would represent a dramatic about-face for governance in a port city that has long stayed faithful to private-sector leadership.
“It’s a referendum against the system,” said Roland Barrera, a fourth-term Corpus Christi City Council member, of the ballot measure. “I don’t think it ends well.”
Joe McComb, who was mayor when the city enacted the 2018 plan, said Corpus Christi’s wellbeing is at stake. The city needs industry, and industry needs water.
The activists, he said, want to break the economic backbone of the region.
“They’re wanting to try to punish the industry,” McComb said. “If industry shuts down, Corpus Christi will be just a fishing village again.”
Dreams of a Drought-Proof Water Supply
To McComb, the desalination project represented a generational dream to overcome the tiresome cycles of drought that have burdened Corpus Christi for as long as anyone can remember.

Tanzania is counting on increased investment to accelerate industrialization and create jobs for its young population, the prime minister said.
The government has targeted $15 billion in annual foreign direct investment, roughly triple last yearâs figure, as part of its long-term economic plans.
Mwigulu Nchemba, speaking on the sidelines of an investment forum in London, said the government had put money into rail and port infrastructure, as well as expanding power generation to create an industrial base. This was on top of cutting the cost of doing business, and strengthening supply chains.
Nchemba said increased industrialization would boost local processing of natural resources leading to more employment opportunities. Tanzania, like many African countries, has a rapidly expanding population. The UN estimates 42% of people are aged 14 or under. The prime minister said the path to creating work for all the countryâs school leavers rests on developing the private sector through investment.
âThere is no way you can absorb all those graduates,â the prime minister told reporters. âThe only way you can solve the issue of job creation is by empowering the private sector to create those vacancies for our youth.â
Know More
Tanzania has large offshore gas resources and deposits of minerals needed for the energy transition and digital infrastructure â such as copper, lithium, and cobalt â as well as precious metals and stones, including gold and diamonds.
In August, the country commissioned a 2,115 MW hydropower plant that more than doubled its electricity generation capacity and âcreated a surplus that officials said could support power exports and industrial growth.
Tanzania, like governments across the continent, is looking for ways to add value locally instead of raw minerals exports.
In neighboring Kenya, President William Ruto has focused on job creation through industrialization as a key plank in his campaign to secure a second term in next yearâs election.
Notable
- Liquefied natural gas development offers Tanzania its most obvious means of monetizing its giant gas reserves after the wars in Ukraine and Iran upended global energy markets, wrote Neil Ford in African Business.

62b403256e79.text:
The News
The $16 billion project to build Aliko Dangoteâs refinery on the Kenyan coast is at the center of a high-stakes political battle ahead of elections in 10 months.
President William Ruto is hinging his second-term bid on a series of major infrastructure developments. He has argued that the refinery could raise Kenyaâs annual gross domestic product by 12%. Additional expected benefits include 500MW added to the national grid and thousands of new jobs.
But mounting litigation, some initiated by his political rivals, is threatening to delay its construction, scheduled to be completed by 2030. Groups behind the legal action allege that the project is only the latest in a series of âsecretive dealsâ signed by Ruto and his administration.
The governmentâs refusal to make public key agreements related to the refinery has been criticized by opposition leaders, including one of Rutoâs main challengers, Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna. He has launched a bid in parliament for the documents, including the refinery contract, to be released.
Unanswered questions remain over the impact on the environment, the community living near the refinery, and taxpayers.
The president and his allies have warned that legal hurdles and uncertainty affecting key projects could dampen investor confidence.
Rutoâs government is no stranger to court challenges to its financial deals. Its plan to privatize the countryâs fuel pipeline company was eventually approved after various cases were dismissed. Last month, the $1.6 billion sale of a government stake in telecoms company Safaricom to UKâs Vodafone was declared illegal by the courts â the administration has launched an appeal.
Both deals are meant to fund Rutoâs infrastructure push, according to government documents.
Know More
Ekuru Aukot, leader of the opposition Thirdway Alliance,told Semafor he would âdefinitely file a suitâ if the government failed to meet an Oct. 23 deadline in his access to information request seeking more details about the refinery including the names of those who stand to benefit.
âWe are not opposed to investment. What we are saying is follow the law, follow the constitution,â he said.
âThe era of secretive deals negotiated in the dark will end when we kick this current regime out and return our country back to the rule of law,â Sifuna said on social media, adding that Ruto was frustrating his parliamentary push for more details. He insisted that the disclosure was âa constitutional imperative.â
The threat of protracted litigation also looms over a suit launched by more than 100 Lamu residents arguing that the site of the refinery is part of their ancestral lands, with a court halting construction until the matter is heard.
In addition, campaign groups have raised the alarm over the governmentâs failure to publish the environmental impact report, with Greenpeace threatening legal action. Last year, its five-year effort to block the construction of a $2 billion coal plant in Lamu ended in success for the activists.
Despite the legal cases, Dangote and Ruto, who broke ground on the refinery project on Sept. 30, have expressed confidence that the project will overcome the legal hurdles.
Step Back
Seen as the candidate for the young and downtrodden in the last election, Rutoâs popularity has waned especially among the youth after the deadly 2024 Gen Z-led protests in which dozens of demonstrators were killed by police. Instead, Ruto is now leaning heavily on his infrastructure plans and the promised opportunities to shore up support for his re-election campaign.
He has promised to move Kenya âfrom third world to first worldâ within 10 years, and unveiled a $38 billion infrastructure fund meant to finance various projects.
The View From Nigeria
Dangote is taking the objections in his stride. Speaking to investors in Nairobi ahead of the groundbreaking ceremony, Dangote said legal challenges were ânormal for us in Africa. In fact, this is small.â
He drew parallels with concerns over his cement plant in Senegal, which faced delays over land-related legal disputes. âThey stopped our factory for one year. We went up to the Supreme Court to get a judgment,â he said.

Former President Barack Obama has cut an ad for Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom, the latest sign of Democrats putting real effort behind boosting their candidate in the deep red state as they eye a potential upset next month.
The Colom campaign will run the 30-second spot on digital and radio statewide in Mississippi as part of a seven-figure media buy in Mississippi, according to details shared first with Semafor. In the ad, Obama tells voters: âMississippi, itâs time for a change.â
âYou need to send Scott Colom to the US Senate,â Obama continues in the ad. âScott made his community safer, prosecuting violent crimes as a district attorney and fighting corruption.â
Colom is running against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, a conservative GOP senator who blocked Colomâs nomination to a federal judgeship under then-President Joe Biden. Colom currently serves as a district attorney in Mississippi.
The race to defeat Hyde-Smith is not a must-win for Democrats to retake the Senate and Colom remains an underdog in deep red Mississippi. But national Democrats have been eying the race for months due to the stateâs large Black population, and Obamaâs ad is a clear effort to juice turnout.
Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., will appear with Colom on Wednesday in Jackson and Democratic Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, and Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware have also previously campaigned with the Democratic candidate.  Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has also listed Mississippi as a target for Democrats.
Democrats tried to beat Hyde-Smith in the past and failed. She defeated former Democratic Rep. Mike Espy by 7 points in 2018 and a wider margin in a 2020 rematch. But most Senate Democrats think Colom, a young father, is a stronger candidate in a tough environment for Republicans.

2b88adf31f73.text:
Army brings back ‘night court’ audit of programs, shifting more than $100M
The effort started this summer with science and tech efforts.
The Army may have a new take on acquisition and modernization, but senior leaders have brought back an innovation from the first Trump administration: top-to-bottom reviews of program spending.
“Night court,” as the Army calls it, started in 2018. Then-Army Secretary Mark Esper and Chief of Staff Gen. Mark Milley would meet up at the end of the day to hunt through reams of Army program documents for savings. Ultimately, tens of billions of dollars were reprogrammed to new priorities.
Over the summer, service leaders relaunched the effort to evaluate the Army’s many programs.
“Everything from basic research, all the way up—how is that lining into where we're actually taking the Army, from a modernization perspective?” Brent Ingraham, the Army’s civilian acquisition chief, told reporters Thursday of the new round of night courts.
They started with science and technology programs earlier in the summer, Ingraham said, ensuring that the Army’s basic research was aligned with larger goals in the new Portfolio Acquisition Executive offices, which are now responsible for the entire lifecycle of an Army program.
“We roughly found, I'll say, a little over $100 million of S&T funds that could better be realigned to match where the portfolios were headed,” he said.
Next they reviewed foreign military sales contracts.
“How can we improve on delivery of those capabilities?” Ingraham said. “And so it's really sort of looking at how we become better partners to our allies and partners on delivery of capabilities.”
Sustainment is the most recent bucket added to the review, he said. PAEs are reviewing their programs to realign what it will cost to sustain current and planned programs, what can be cancelled, and where they might save money by bringing maintenance in-house.
“The Army sort of fundamentally changed how we do budgeting, inside the department as well,” Ingraham said. “And so now the PAEs get to see the whole portfolio, not just traditional procurement and [research, development, testing and evaluation] dollars, but they see the [operations and maintenance] and the S&T dollars, so they can understand how it fits across the whole portfolio.”
Help us report on the future of national security. Contact Meghann Myers: mmyers@defenseone.com, meghannmyers.55 on Signal.

Saudi Arabia's energy minister has vowed a "serious" response to the deadly attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil and gas facilities by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement.
"The events of recent weeks are serious. Our response must be equally serious," Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh.
On Sunday, a Pakistani man was killed in an attack on a terminal at the capital's King Khalid International Airport, Saudi authorities said. It came a day after a Houthi missile hit another terminal, killing 13 people and forcing its closure.
The Houthis said they launched the attacks in retaliation for "brutal Saudi aggression" against areas they control in western Yemen.
The Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six other people were injured in a Saudi air strike on a home in the capital, Sanaa, on Sunday.
A Saudi-led coalition has been providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces battling the Houthis on Yemen's Red Sea coast and other areas.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The Yemeni government claimed it was behind that strike, saying it was trying to prevent an unauthorised Iranian plane from landing.
Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea.
They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports after the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
Last week, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.
Pro-government forces said they were quickly able to retake areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes, but the Houthis denied losing any territory.

Women's football is on course to become a billion-dollar industry, but many professional players are still earning low wages, working on insecure contracts and experiencing rising psychological stress.
That is according to the findings of a new global survey of more than 800 footballers by the players' union Fifpro., external
Players were asked why they might leave football early. The report stated 59% cited financial reasons, while psychological stress was another factor identified by 46%.
Alex Culvin, head of women's football at Fifpro, said there was no single explanation for the increase. She pointed to growing public exposure, financial insecurity and inadequate support systems as possible contributing factors.
"Players are now very visible," she said.
"Players are not only expected to be visible, but are obligated to be visible because of the low income to subsidise the lack of solid income they receive."
While awareness of mental health issues has improved, Culvin explained many players felt they were being left to cope alone.
"Players also reported, whilst having a higher psychological stress, that they didn't have the support they needed in a mental health sense, either at the club or internationally," she said.
In total, the report shows 57% of women who responded to the survey struggled with their mental health and half of them were not provided with support by their clubs.
The report states that global revenue in the women's game is expected to rise from about $581m (Â£439m) in 2024 to over $1bn (Â£756m) in 2027.
It also highlights emerging psychological pressures facing professional women's footballers.
In an increasingly digital world, players are more accessible than ever through social media, bringing them closer to fans but also exposing them to online harassment and abuse.
The Fifpro survey suggested that although salaries, visibility and investment have risen significantly since 2017, much of the professional game still operates in precarious conditions.
For Culvin, the sport's commercial growth is not yet being matched by safeguards for the players driving it.
"The economic case for women's football has been made," she said.
"I think the institutional regulatory and policy case needs to catch up quickly to protect and enhance our women's players and enable them to perform maximally."
Players don't see themselves as 'professional'
One of the report's most striking findings is how players view their own professional status.
Under Fifa's definition, a professional player has a written contract and is paid more than the expenses incurred playing.
In the survey, 62% of players described themselves as professional, 27% selected semi-professional and 12% chose amateur.
All players in the survey were playing for clubs in the top tier of their country, yet only 78% reported having a written contract and 82% said they were paid by their club.
However, just 57% said that payment was enough to cover the costs of playing football.
"Players who are professional but don't see or feel themselves as professional are not receiving the full benefits of being an employee," Culvin said.
The report also highlights the limits of salary growth. Although mean average monthly earnings have tripled since 2017 to $2,601 (Â£1,970), the median salary is just $1,669 (Â£1,250).
Average monthly pay varies considerably by region, from $6,450 (Â£4,886) in North America and $3,982 (Â£3,016) in central/Western Europe, to $878 (Â£664) in Eastern Europe and just $480 (Â£363) in Africa.
While salaries have risen sharply in leagues such as those in the USA and Mexico, average pay in 10 Eastern European countries remains below the national minimum wage.
Even in regions such as Western Europe and Asia/Oceania that span some bigger football markets, average pay is not significantly higher than national minimum wage levels.
Fifpro was unable to provide average salaries per league as the report focused on regions rather than individual countries.
Short-term contracts and late payments
Average contract lengths have also increased from about one year in 2017 to 19 months, but many players still face periods without guaranteed income.
"Only two-thirds of players are paid for the whole 12 months," said Culvin.
"There's a lot of players who are on seven-month contracts, nine-month contracts, which means that they've got to work to make up the rest of the calendar year."
She believes the rapid commercial growth of women's football has helped to obscure some of these realities.
Despite the rapid growth of England's Women's Super League, Fifpro says conditions at the top of the game could obscure the reality for many players elsewhere.
Culvin warned the economic boom in women's football could "mask some of the realities that players face and actually endure on a day-to-day basis".
The report also found that 24% of players had experienced late payments over the past two seasons, while 42% were not provided with a pension.
'Wake-up call' is needed, says Culvin
Culvin argues there is a growing disconnect between expectations and reality.
"I think there's a wake-up call needed for the ecosystem, that our players are suffering and that there is not the kind of wraparound support and accountability that's needed for players," she said.
However, not all trends were negative.
One significant improvement being felt in the game concerns parenthood.
In 2017, nearly half of respondents considering leaving the game early said wanting a family could drive them out of football.
That figure has now fallen to 19%, which Fifpro attributes in part to maternity regulations that were introduced by Fifa in 2021 and updated two years ago.
"What we've concluded, which I think is incredibly important, is that targeted regulatory intervention works - maternity regulations were introduced in 2021," said Culvin.

India's opposition parties are marching to the Supreme Court in Delhi to demand the resignation of the election chief over alleged voter fraud.
This will be the latest in a series of demonstrations in Delhi, with thousands of security forces deployed and roads barricaded in the capital.
Attempts to hold a protest by the Cockroach Janata Party pressure group over the weekend led to thousands of demonstrators being detained.
Opposition parties allege that under Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, India's voter rolls are being manipulated to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the Election Commission and the BJP have rejected the charge.
The opposition lawmakers want to submit a memorandum to Chief Justice Surya Kant, but he has told reporters he declined the meeting citing "certain reasons".
He did not provide the reasons, but media reports citing the letter have said that he pointed out that some of the issues the opposition wanted to raise with him were also pending before the court. The BBC has not seen the letter.
"Every Indian citizen has the right to approach the court, and we will hear their concerns and grant whatever is due under the law," he told reporters.
Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, meanwhile, has called "all opposition parties, civil society groups [and] all those who believe in democracy" to join Monday's march.
In a press conference on Monday, he shared a letter that he and Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge had written to the Chief Justice, laying out their concerns with Kumar's alleged conduct and with the contentious electoral roll revision.
He said that Kant had asked them to file a petition, which they would do at the end of their march.
Authorities in Delhi have announced heavy restrictions on traffic and on entry and exit at some key metro stations. There is also heavy security deployment in central Delhi and along the route of the march.
Several thousand people were on Barakhamba road, where the march began, as a bus carrying Rahul Gandhi and other opposition leaders arrived just before 15:30 local time. Supporters waved flags and chanted his name as the Congress MP and others waved through the windows. Seated a few rows behind Rahul was Neha Bora, a leftist student leader who has gained prominence for participating in the protests.
Over the past week, top opposition leaders, including Rahul Gandhi, have been briefly detained several times while leading protests in central Delhi.
On Sunday, the CJP - which is not a registered political party - said it would continue protesting until Kumar stepped down.
The CJP, which successfully led a protest over the summer that culminated in India's federal education minister's resignation, had called for a march on Saturday to Jantar Mantar - the best-known protest site in Delhi where the last set of sit-in demonstrations had also happened.
But authorities in Delhi imposed overarching restrictions that made it almost impossible for protesters to travel and reach Jantar Mantar - trains were cancelled, dozens of metro stations were shut down and tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were on the roads to detain protesters.
The CJP leaders - founder Abhijeet Dipke and co-convenors Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were dramatically detained from a plane as they landed in Delhi to join the protest.
They were only released a day later - while Dipke has returned home to attend his grandmother's funeral, Das and Ranka held a press conference where they said the protests would continue. Both leaders, however, did not join the protests on Sunday but have said they will seek a new protest date from the police.
Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses.
The BBC also captured visuals, external of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi Police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters.
In a statement, Reporters Without Borders condemned the detention of at least 16 Indian journalists.
"Covering events of public interest is not a crime. It is their job. The police's actions against the press are unacceptable," it said.
Congress leader Gandhi said that young Indians who had come to peacefully protest with "love in their hearts, not hatred or anger" had been beaten up.
BJP President Nitin Nabin accused opposition parties and the CJP of trying to destabilise India "at the behest of foreign forces" without elaborating on who the forces were.

5b6e6fc966a6.text:
- Published
It is one of cricket's oldest and most frustrating problems: bad light.
A fascinating passage of play halted when things get too gloomy.
The issue has reared its head again this week in the fascinating first Test between South Africa and Australia in Durban, wiping out more than 60 overs across the first three days.
The fact a solution was added to cricket's rules just last week, an option so far unused around the world, only adds to the frustration.
Bad light in mid-afternoon - what's gone on in Durban?
Play is already starting at 09:30 local time in Durban. This is the first October Test at Kingsmead, where the sun sets shortly after 18:00 at this time of year on South Africa's eastern coast.
Still, on day one, play was halted at 15:23 local time after clouds built. Only 65.2 of the scheduled 90 overs had been bowled and the players were unable to return.
Day two was slightly better with play continuing until 16:25, but that finish was still 35 minutes earlier than it could have been. Day three's end came at 16:31.
On each occasion, the first two sessions have been played in hot, sunny conditions, only for clouds to build in the afternoon - a familiar weather pattern in Durban.
"Very quickly in the morning, as temperatures have risen inland as the sun heats the ground, a sea breeze has formed with winds coming from the sea into Durban," said BBC weather presenter Chris Fawkes.
"This has increased humidity levels through the morning and brought some cloud in. As temperatures have started to fall again towards the evening, this has increased the relative humidity with the air getting increasingly saturated.
"That has caused the cloud to get thicker and lower."
What about the change in playing conditions?
Following a trial earlier in the year, the International Cricket Council amended its playing conditions to allow the pink ball to be used in Tests.
It was supposed to help in these exact scenarios.
Crucially, it does not allow a red ball to be switched for pink when the light becomes poor - something previously suggested by former England captain Michael Vaughan.
Instead, if problems with the light are expected, it allows teams to agree before a Test starts to use the pink ball throughout.
No such discussions were held between the Proteas and Australia before the Durban Test, however.
'There is a stigma around the pink ball'
The pink ball has been a fixture of day-night Tests because it is easier to see than the darker red in night-time conditions.
Former South Africa bowler Shaun Pollock was part of the ICC committee which recommended the change and he believes there is a "stigma" around the pink ball in the game.
"They say it moves too much," Pollock said.
"If Australia were 124-6 [as they were on day one] and we were using the pink ball, everyone would have said it was the pink ball's fault.
"If Australia were 124-6 and got to 390 [as they did in their first innings] everyone in South Africa would have said it was the pink ball's fault, that it got soft.
"The pink ball would have meant we played 45 more overs of Test cricket and that is why I am keen to introduce it, and not just for day-night games."
Why might teams not want to use the pink ball?
One narrative exists that the pink ball moves more under floodlights, though that is not backed up by ball tracking data.
Instead, various batters have spoken about the pink ball being more difficult to see. Batting averages are lowest in the evening of day-night matches.
Australia have also played in 15 of Test cricket's day-nighters - 10 more than anyone else.
Unsurprisingly, the four leading wicket-takers in day-night matches are all Australians. Left-armer Mitchell Starc's haul of 89 wickets in 15 Tests has positioned him as the undisputed pink-ball king.
You would not blame teams if they would rather face Australia with the red ball.
Former South Africa bowler Vernon Philander said he prefers the idea of switching balls during the match if conditions require it, but that would raise questions over the Test's integrity.
Is the potential injustice of one team having to face a pink ball outweighed by the need to get more action of the field?
"They have to take it out of the hands of the players completely and enforce it from the umpires' point of view that the pink ball will become in play when the light has faded enough," Philander said.
"You are always going to have the argument of who is ahead of the game.
"I would like to see the ICC enforce it on to the officials to make that call."

Robert Pattinson is having quite the year.
The British actor has already starred opposite Zendaya in The Drama, and played a key role in summer blockbuster The Odyssey.
But his new film, Primetime, takes him in a completely new direction - as he portrays the real-life host of American TV show, To Catch a Predator.
The show, which aired from 2004 to 2007, involved hunting alleged child abusers.
For Pattinson, who became a father almost three years ago, the film's plot is particularly concerning.
"It's both the most terrifying thing that can happen to you, whether you're a parent, or even if you're not," he told BBC News at the film's screening at London Film Festival.
"It's the most unimaginable sin possible," he added.
The new A24 crime thriller depicts the show's host, NBC journalist Chris Hansen, carrying out sting operations on would-be predators.
The show was a ratings hit.
But it also led to questions over where to draw the line between investigative journalism, police activity and reality television.
Speaking on Sunday night, Pattinson reflected on the show's complicated legacy.
"The show was this kind of microcosm of saying, 'oh, we can do something about [child abuse], and we can do something about it really, really, really quickly," he said.
"And in some ways, that's correct, but it also makes for incredibly powerful TV, and that's when it gets into slightly dicey territory."
When asked whether he thinks attitudes towards entertainment have now changed, Pattinson paused.
"I think on mainstream TV, but then it's just been replaced," he replied, pointing out that similar content has since appeared on social media.
"That's why I was interested in the show, because I could see the beginning of a new wave of 'predator catching' in pretty much the same format that it was in the early 2000s," he said. "And I was just interested as to why that was happening."
"And it got bigger and bigger and bigger, and now it's one of the most massive things on social media."
Hansen himself has been critical of the film, calling it "bizarre" and "detached from reality" in a video posted on X, external.
Addressing his criticisms, director Lance Oppenheim said: "I agree, that was by design.
"I always thought of this movie as more of a fever dream than something that was representational portrait."
Oppenheim added there was something "ancient" about the desire to watch people getting publicly punished.
"It's happened for thousands of years," he added. "I wanted to make something that interrogated that."
Oppenheim, who is also currently co-directing with Nathan Fielder a highly anticipated documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, said separately of that project: "I want everyone to see it. It's a really special movie."
From Twilight to the Oscars?
Pattinson, 40, became something of a pin-up after playing vampire Edward Cullen in the Twilight series, alongside American actress Kristen Stewart.
Before that, he stole young hearts as Hufflepuff hunk Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire.
He has since starred in major films including Christopher Nolan's Tenet, as well as a range of eccentric, indie films.
This year, he has been on a roll, with Dune: Part Three still to come.
Heâs also got the next Batman film in the pipeline, although production on that has reportedly paused, external. When asked when they'll be back to work, Pattinson didnât give much away ("We don't know yet, but yeah, working on it.")
Primetime has also led to speculation that this could be the year that Pattinson gets his first ever Oscars nomination. Is that likely, I wonder?
"I am eternally grateful that I got these jobs," he responds.
"But then [to have] been able to even do them, this is one of the best years of my life."

- Published
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) chief has defended a plan to livestream the execution of convicted killer Nidal Hasan, rejecting claims that it could fuel radicalisation or make him a martyr.
"I don't see an elevated risk," Markwayne Mullin said on Sunday. "I think people need to understand that if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime."
Hasan, a former US Army Major, is due to be executed by firing squad in December for shooting dead 13 soldiers at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.
The Trump administration has said it plans to livestream his death, prompting shock and concern from both Republicans and Democrats.
President Donald Trump has said he signed off on the execution, but while he approves of the livestream plan, a final decision is yet to be made.
It would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century.
The plan, which was announced by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth last week, has been heavily criticised by politicians, academics and experts.
Alaskan Republican Senator, Lisa Murkowski, called the decision "gruesome" and said livestreaming an execution was something she would expect "from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America".
"It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks," she wrote on X, external, adding that "how we carry out justice matters just as much as the justice itself."
Virginia Democrat Mark Warner said that allowing the public to tune into the execution could heighten the national security risk.
"Beyond the profound moral concerns, a public execution could hand terrorist organizations a propaganda victory, fuel radicalization, and put American service members, diplomats, and citizens overseas at greater risk," he wrote, external.
But speaking to CBS news programme Face the Nation on Sunday, the DHS secretary rejected these concerns, and insisted the risks had been considered.
"[Hasan] killed 13 individuals on Fort Hood. I have no sympathy for him, and I give absolutely zero thought to the way that this man dies," Mullin told presenter Margaret Brennan.
Nidal Hasan, a former US Army major and psychiatrist from Virginia, admitted to fatally shooting 13 unarmed troops at a crowded medical building at the Fort Hood military base. A further 32 others were injured in the attack.
In court, Hasan apologised for "any mistakes" and said he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. Hasan was shot during the attack and now uses a wheelchair.
His execution would be the first by the US military since 1961, and the first execution by firing squad since World War Two.

ec7df0b6f44e.text: Both parties will be pressured to intervene more in markets after the midterms as economic frustration animates the new Congress, according to an FGS Global sketch of 2027 Washington scenarios, shared first with Axios. Why it matters: In a Trump-dominated Washington, Congress ceded much of its power and relevance. That'll change three weeks from Tuesday if Democrats win the House, as expected, and perhaps the Senate in the midterms. The new analysis by FGS , a worldwide strategic leadership advisory with huge clients, is a sequel to a popular FGS report that Jim VandeHei and I used as the basis for a series of popular "Behind the Curtain" columns before the 2024 elections. FGS bills "Alternative Futures: Beyond November" as a framework for processing the epic battles ahead: how power will get used, how both parties will evolve, and how business leaders can navigate the uncertainty. "The 2026 midterms will begin — not end — a 27-month period of unusually high strategic uncertainty," the report says. Zoom in: Michael Feldman — FGS partner and co-chairman, North America — tells me that for Republicans, "intervention may mean tariffs, industrial policy, domestic manufacturing incentives, and other measures aimed at strengthening U.S. production capacity, economic security, and competitiveness." "For Democrats, intervention may mean affordability policies, labor protections, antitrust enforcement, plus regulation designed to reduce costs, curb concentrated corporate power and address inequality." "Everyone is focused on who controls Congress," Feldman added. "We think the more important question for business is what happens next. The midterms are the beginning, not the end, of a period of significant political and policy uncertainty." Left: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) campaigns in Linden, N.J., last year. Right: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) campaigns in Davenport, Iowa, last week. Photos: Getty Images Zoom out: Three structural shifts will drive the post-midterm operating environment for businesses of all sizes, FGS warns. " Voter dissatisfaction may be the most important force pushing both parties away from established policy orthodoxies. A frustrated electorate could push both parties toward more populist, interventionist and less predictable approaches to business." "Technological disruption could reshape the political agenda as profoundly as traditional partisan conflict. AI and related technologies are becoming a political variable — not merely a sector-specific policy issue." "Generational turnover will weaken established political assumptions even where ideology remains unchanged. The next generation of leaders may inherit existing parties without inheriting their relationships, orthodoxies or governing style." The bottom line: "Divided government does not necessarily mean lower political/legislative risk," FGS writes. "It may mean that policy/political conflict moves in less predictable ways." Get the 16-page FGS report .

Proposals to install a major battery energy storage system have been rejected after an appeal by the developer was dismissed.
Sky UK Development's plans for the battery system site (BESS) on land near Raymond's Hill in Axminster were refused by East Devon District Council's planning committee last year.
The applicant appealed the decision with the Planning Inspectorate, proposing changes to mitigate concerns around groundwater contamination and the risk of battery units catching fire.
In her decision, inspector RC Kirby said such mitigation "would not be effective" in ensuring an acceptable balance between harm and benefit", stating the proposal was "not suitable for its location".
A key risk highlighted during the planning debate for the proposed BESS revolved around what could happen if one of the battery units caught fire, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service, external.
Opponents claimed the amounts of water needed to contain such blazes and prevent their spread could mean any water running off into a nearby local waterway.
The appellant said it believed it would be about eight years before water used to fight a notional fire at the BESS would reach the drinking water source, but the inspector said there had been "insufficient evidence" to substantiate this.
The appeal decision notice stated the appellant had put forward revised plans that East Devon had not had put before it.
These included an increase in the size of the water tanks, relocation of some of the tanks, the separation distance between pairs of containers being 6m (20ft) apart, and other alterations.
Campaigners from Devon branch of the Campaign to Protect Rural England (CPRE) and the Hawkchurch and Monkton Wyld Action Group said they were "massively relieved" plans for the site had been blocked.
Devon CPRE energy spokesperson Dr Phil Bratby added: "For years, Devon CPRE has been highlighting the risks from the hazardous materials that could be released and contaminate the groundwater."
Kirby said that, while the benefits of the scheme would "outweigh the moderate harm that would be caused to the Dorset National Landscape", they were "insufficient" to outweigh the "very substantial, overriding, unacceptable risks in respect of pollution of the water environment".
Proponents of BESS systems highlighted their benefits in helping the nation reach net zero aspirations, notably because they could store energy.
The UK government noted BESS systems used batteries, for example lithium-ion batteries, to store electricity at times when supply was higher than demand.
"They can then later release electricity when it is needed. BESSs are therefore important for "the replacement of fossil fuels with renewable energy", it stated.

71cba14b7542.text: President Trump has privately shared misgivings about livestreaming the firing-squad execution of a former Army major who murdered 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas, according to four people who have spoken with the president. Why it matters: Trump has been deluged with "negative input" about the idea from a bipartisan chorus of lawmakers as well as advisers inside and outside of his White House, a senior administration official said. A livestream of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan's execution on Dec. 3 "might not happen," Trump told one confidant, who doesn't work in the administration and shared the comment with Axios. "He didn't sound particularly enthusiastic" about webcasting the execution, the source said. "That's why he's calling around, doing the Trump thing, asking people what they think." Zoom in: Hasan faces a firing squad at Fort Hood, where he went on his murderous shooting rampage 17 years ago. He would be the first person in the U.S. whose execution would be livestreamed. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the norm-shattering idea Thursday on Real America's Voice. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it — that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said. Zoom out: The idea was roundly condemned domestically and internationally . In the ensuing days, Trump started to publicly shift his positions: At first, Trump was full-throated in his support. "Absolutely, I approve," Trump told reporters early Friday evening. Later that night, Trump was more nuanced : "They want to do that because they want to set an example. I wasn't involved in that decision, but I understand the decision." On Saturday, Trump took control by telling reporters he would have the final say: "There are two thoughts: Don't show it and show it. 'Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won't be doing what he did. So I'll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we'll make a decision," the president told reporters at the White House. Behind the scenes: Vice President Vance has signaled where he thinks the president is going with the decision, according to a source. "I don't know if that's actually going to happen," Vance, speaking off the cuff, told reporters Friday. He has privately repeated that to others. "I'm not going to be watching it," Vance said. Between the lines: Trump, Vance and everyone else in the administration is clear about supporting Hasan's execution. But the president is grappling with competing pressures. "The president wants the bastard to pay, and a public execution might be that extra humiliation [Hasan] deserves," another confidant who spoke with the president said. "At the same time, he doesn't want to make the guy a martyr." Said another: "This is an old dude in a wheelchair we're shooting. We want to livestream that?" (Hasan, 56, was permanently injured when he was shot during his capture.) Friction point: The divide in opinion over livestreaming the execution is another point of disagreement between Vance and Hegseth. They've been on opposite sides when it comes to the use of military force in Yemen and Iran , to the leadership of the Army . Advisers say the men have a good relationship. Context: Whether at the state or federal level, executions often are witnessed only by family members or select media. They haven't been livestreamed. Executions used to be viewed in public squares, but that practice was discontinued in the 1930s, according to NPR . Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh's 2001 execution was viewable to loved ones and bombing survivors via a private closed-circuit telecast. Flashback: Yelling "Allahu Akbar!" Hasan fatally shot 13 people — including a pregnant woman — and wounded 32 others on Nov. 5, 2009, when they lined up for medical checks at Fort Hood's Soldier Readiness Processing Center. The rampage was the worst terrorist attack on U.S. soil since 9/11. A special Senate Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee report criticized the military for "political correctness" that blinded authorities to the major's increasingly clear Islamist radicalization. The bottom line: Hasan will be executed unless something unexpected happens. The only real doubt is whether private citizens with no attachment to the case will be able to witness it. "If I had to bet, I would bet the president doesn't authorize this," said one administration official. "But I'm not gonna get ahead of the boss and try to predict what he'll do." "Hasan will be executed for his crimes," the official said, "and that's what matters."

Israel has produced more tech unicorns per citizen than any country in the world, twice as many as the US. Ittai Ben-Zeevâs job is getting them to stay there.
The CEO of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange is tasked with convincing the next Wiz, Monday.com, and Fiverr, which all went public in New York or sold to US rivals, to list at home instead. Heâs also courting global investors whose money will help boost trading and valuations.
His biggest tailwind, he said, is the takeover of US markets by a handful of AI giants. Israeli startups worth a few billion dollars canât get the attention of investors rhapsodizing about trillion-dollar IPOs from SpaceX, Anthropic, and OpenAI.
âNew York is no longer an option,â said Ben-Zeev, the exchangeâs CEO since 2016.
After the Oct. 7 attacks, 7% of its workforce was called up for military service and the bear case for its stock market was obvious. Since Oct. 8, 2023, the TA-125 has beaten the S&P 500 by 50 percentage points and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite by 23. The country is on track this year for a record 30 IPOs. Foreign holdings of Israeli shares more than doubled from September 2023 to the beginning of this year.
Ben-Zeev dismissed wartime nationalism as a reason for Israeli founders to list at home, or for Israeli investors to buy their shares. âIsraelis will be patriotic about certain issues, but thatâs not the way they view the exchange,â he said. But he said the Jewish diaspora has increased its investments. Bill Ackman and his Israeli-born wife, Neri Oxman, bought 4.9% of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange in 2024 after a 45-minute meeting with management, Ackman said in an interview.
âOwning a stock exchange is the purest way to bet on a country,â he said, taking a minute to run the numbers: His $23 million investment is worth $230 million today. He said AIâs productivity-enhancing potential will overcome Israelâs economic weakness, its small population. âThere will be a trillion-dollar company coming out of Israel, and that value will be shared among a tiny country.â
The war also gave TASE cover to move its Sunday-to-Thursday trading to Monday through Friday. It wasnât an easy pitch in a country that takes Shabbat seriously, but a way âto signal the world that we are part of itâ and gain entry into global indexes that have long snubbed it, Ben-Zeev said.
Anti-Israel sentiment and antisemitism are fueling campaigns at many US institutions to divest from Israel. Politicians will politick, he said, but âinvestors, at the end of the day, want to make a return.â

Six or seven years ago, if an Israeli company couldnât do an IPO on Nasdaq or NYSE, they were looking at Singapore, Toronto, Australia. We managed to change the perception. And I believe that in 2027, maybe before the end of 2026, weâll start seeing global investment banks leading global IPO offerings on TASE, and only for TASE.
Iâm mindful, speaking to you the week of the anniversary of Oct. 7 â is patriotism part of the pitch?
No. Post-Oct. 7, I see a genuine change in the way that Jewish people in the diaspora, especially in the States, want to invest in Israel, not only to make a return but also to get a broader connection to Israel. But thatâs not the case with the Israeli entrepreneurs. Israelis, I have to tell you, will be patriotic about certain issues, but thatâs not the way they view the exchange.
Then whatâs the pitch?
You are Israeli. You donât understand the American mentality. The American market can be brutal. You miss your estimates by one cent, your share price goes down, and then what? Start in the Israeli market and, once youâre ready, you can always do a dual listing. Think about TASE as a stop on the way to New York.
Youâve also courted global companies to dual-list in Tel Aviv. Palo Alto Networks did that after buying [Israeli startup] CyberArk, but why would most companies bother?
We have data that shows you get more liquidity and more demand for your shares. You can argue that itâs not significant enough, but itâs a free option.
And not too many people are aware of it, but if you look at the amount of money Israelis have in cash deposits in Israeli banks and you compare it to GDP, we are No. 1 of any western society. Thatâs money that is just ready to be invested.
Youâre in New York this week, selling the Israeli economy to investors. But the Middle East is a volatile place to invest right now, and there are big anti-Israel divestment campaigns at some US institutions.
In the old days, people would ask me: What will happen to Israel if something happens in Iran? I remember being in New York a couple of years ago, telling one of those American investors that if something happened in Iran, you should be more worried about your American portfolio than your Israeli portfolio. Israel is more well-positioned than it used to be, and Iâm not sure that everybody fully understands it.

Itâs not only about facts; itâs also about storytelling. As a country, this is something we need to do better.

b9dc26bf8181.text:
The Scene
Riyadh Season â the Saudi capitalâs biggest suite of events that had been key to its tourism push â opens next week with concerts, UFC, the Epcot-esque Boulevard World, and the worldâs top ranked tennis players set to compete at the Six Kings Slam.
Since 2019, it has been the capitalâs answer to anyone asking whether Riyadh is the place to be. After the Houthi strikes over the weekend, residents are asking themselves the same question.
Traffic on King Fahd Road is lighter and some companies â mostly those based in the King Abdullah Financial District â told staff to work from home on Sunday. Schools in the city have moved to remote learning for the week, with no clear date yet on when students will return to class.
When I ask Saudis â friends, relatives, and sources â how they are doing, most say: Alhamdulillah, thanks to God, the catchall for everything from the greatest blessings to the mantra mourners repeat when family members die. Itâs the same expression they used in March when Iranian missiles first reached the capital, but the tone now is different after more than a dozen people were killed and hundreds wounded in attacks on King Khalid International Airport.
Fear is breaking through. Social media and WhatsApp group chats have been filled with eulogies for Captain Hamoud Alkalthami, the Saudia Airlines pilot killed on Thursday, and for Saturdayâs dead â eight of them foreign residents from countries including Bangladesh, Egypt, and Sudan. People are posting about and queuing to donate to blood banks. The crown prince himself did so last week, part of an annual campaign, and that image was used to spur urgently needed donations. The captainâs death in particular has become a symbol for many Saudis: The war now has a martyr, with a name and face that looks like theirs.
Manalâs view
Saudis broadly trust their government. When they wrap themselves in the flag, or share statements of solidarity after attacks (at least for those who use their real names), itâs genuine and reflects how people speak in private.
But there has been a shift. Some are talking about leaving, which a few months ago would have been seen as a betrayal. Most are still confident and say the kingdom has come through worse. Whatâs pretty universal is the desire for the disruption to be over and to get back to living.
While the conflict with Iran was clear â we have been told to be wary of the Islamic Republic from the time we understood what an enemy was â the confrontation with the Houthis is more complex. Riyadh has tried a mix of strikes and diplomacy for more than a decade, and the UN-brokered truce in 2022 held long enough for people to stop thinking about the issue. Itâs clear now that itâs a forever war, and few people I speak to can describe what winning would look like.
Without public polls, itâs impossible to gauge exactly what the Saudis think. Speaking to more than 25 people this weekend showed a split. One camp wants the Houthis finished for good, whatever that may mean. Others worry about the toll on Yemenis, our poorer neighbors, who make up the kingdomâs largest foreign community and share ties of kinship and history with Saudis.
Over the past six months, those who lived through the 1991 Gulf War used it to explain why they werenât worried. Those six weeks of Iraqi strikes had one Saudi business leader âmore frightened of the uncertainty of the Scud than anything else.â Uncertainty is again, 35 years later, the greatest fear.
Notable
- The strikes sharply raise the risk of Saudi Arabia being drawn into a wider war, after a decade in which Riyadh worked to contain the Yemen conflict rather than escalate it, Bloomberg reported.
- Eulogies for the 12 killed in Saturdayâs strike filled Saudi social media, among them a Flynas flight attendant killed on duty and a university student in her final year, Arab News reported.
