Claims that Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centres reduced Kremlin-linked bot networks have spread widely online, but experts have told BBC Verify there is no evidence the attacks have significantly reduced them.
Viral social media posts have claimed there has been a significant drop in influence operations in recent days, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky suggesting on Monday there was "less hate, less division and fewer provocations" online because of "fewer bots".
Russian influence operations, which promote pro-Kremlin narratives and spread disinformation, have been tracked by researchers and journalists including BBC Verify for more than a decade.
These campaigns push disinformation on to people's social media feeds on issues like the Ukraine war or post messages in support of Moscow's interests.
Ukraine has struck three of Russian tech giant Yandex's five data centres since 8 October in response to Moscow's attacks on Ukrainian internet hubs.
The second of these strikes on Thursday caused Yandex, often referred to as Russia's Google, to announce it was struggling to maintain its services.
But claims these attacks have affected Russian disinformation operations, including accounts posting supportive messages about groups including the Make American Great Again (MAGA) movement in the US and the far-right AfD party in Germany, appear to have come from a misinterpretation of data produced by tech firm Cloudflare.
Some social media users have been sharing charts of Cloudflare data which show bot activity using Yandex's network has declined.
While bots are commonly associated with fake social media accounts that may post false, divisive and inflammatory content, they are also used to automate tasks like scanning web pages so they appear on search engines.
Cloudflare clarified its data includes all automated internet requests to websites hosted on its network, including bots crawling websites for information.
The company also said the drop off was "not necessarily bot behaviour on social media platforms".
TomÃ¡Å¡ ZdechovskÃ½, a Czech member of the European Parliament, shared a post on X which has been viewed more than four million times, that said: "If confirmed, this is telling: Russian data centres get hit, and online activity around AfD suddenly plummets."
He has since said he "did not present it as a clear fact", but the post remains pinned at the top of his X profile.
Researchers from dTeam, a US-based group that tracks Moscow-linked influence operations, told BBC Verify there has not been "any traffic change from known Russian accounts and bot clusters on any platform".
They added that if the offices of known groups involved in these operations "were in flames then we would see a change".
Bots linked to pro-Kremlin influence operations like Storm-1516 and Matryoshka - both of which BBC Verify has previously reported on - were still active on social media on Tuesday, evidence shared with BBC Verify by dTeam shows.
Zelensky's office told BBC Verify the president was "talking about the atmosphere on social media" rather than a fall in bot activity. It added it had seen "reports of fewer provocative and hateful comments" from many social media users.
Mikhail Klimarev, an independent internet analyst, told BBC Russian that while Cloudflare can establish whether bots or real people have visited a website it does not reflect what these bots are doing.
He added that Yandex uses bots to "essentially crawl the entire internet once a day" and index websites for search engine purposes, so it is most likely the company switched these off in response to its computing resources being severely degraded.
Yandex has said the use of its cloud services for "large-scale manipulation on social media, spam and other improper activities" are against its rules and that accounts which violate this are blocked.
While there is no evidence to conclude the strikes on Yandex's data centres have had an impact on Russia's influence operations, they have disrupted internet services for many.
Isik Mater, director of research at the internet monitoring group Netblocks, told BBC Verify disruptions related to Ukrainian strikes "affect all users" globally and "websites which rely on Yandex may be partially or entirely unusable".
She said that following Ukraine's attacks there has been a clear impact on the company's cloud services and platforms relying on them, adding that an entire area remaining "out of service indicates a significant infrastructure-level incident rather than a brief service interruption".
Additional reporting by Paul Brown, BBC Verify, and Sergey Goryashko, BBC Russian
Graphics by Tom Shiel

The Hungarian parliament has voted to amend child protection laws, scrapping measures that stigmatise gay and transgender people. LGBTQ and human rights activists warmly welcomed the move, but called for changes to other OrbÃ¡n-era laws.
The 2021 Child Protection Law, passed by the large Fidesz majority of then-Prime Minister Viktor OrbÃ¡n, banned the "portrayal or promotion of homosexuality or transgenderism".
Since OrbÃ¡n's April election defeat, the Tisza government of PÃ©ter Magyar has been working to dismantle the previous government's legacy.
Minutes after Tuesday's vote, Budapest said the EU had agreed to release â¬4.2bn (Â£3.5bn) of funds frozen in the last years of the Fidesz government.
The European Commission said last month that the Magyar government had addressed a number of "rule of law breaches affecting the EU budget", and urged EU leaders to unlock the funds , externaland readmit Hungary to two key EU programmes - Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe.
Hungary's 2021 law had affected a wide range of other laws, including education and the right of assembly.
Magyar's Tisza party commands the same two-thirds majority that OrbÃ¡n's party used to have, and the measures passed on Tuesday were bundled together by the new government in a package of laws designed to unravel the Fidesz legislation.
"We are very happy that this got adopted," TamÃ¡s Dombos of civil rights group the HÃ¡ttÃ©r Society told the BBC. "We've been fighting this so-called child protection law for five years. There have been problems with the bill submitted to parliament, but most of those problems have been fixed."
Both the Fidesz and Tisza governments made child protection central to their image.
But while Fidesz under Viktor OrbÃ¡n appealed to the conservative electorate by identifying gay and transgender people as a threat to public morals, Tisza under Prime Minister PÃ©ter Magyar is trying to remove or soften legislation, without actually identifying as a liberal-minded government in favour of full equality.
In June 2025, the Gay Pride march through Budapest drew an estimated quarter of a million people, despite a promise by then-Prime Minister Viktor OrbÃ¡n to his supporters that he would prevent it happening.
Police stood aside despite an official ban, and proceedings against the city mayor and others for organising the festival were later dropped. This year's event went ahead without restrictions.
The child protection issue turned from being a strong card in OrbÃ¡n's hand to become his Achilles heel, when the public found out that his government had supported the pardon of the deputy head of a children's home who had been found guilty of covering up the paedophile crimes of his boss.
In his own election campaign, PÃ©ter Magyar presented his party as a champion of the rights of children in state care, while painstakingly avoiding the issues of gay and transgender rights, for fear of alienating right-wing voters.
"We are still knocking on a closed door," Dombos told the BBC, "but at least they are listening on the other side."
This marked a major improvement on the OrbÃ¡n years, he said, where his community felt constantly targeted. Other issues he wanted addressed include the full recognition of same-sex marriage, same-sex couples' rights to adopt children, and the restoration of the right of transgender people to change their names in official documents.
"I'm very cautious," Magyar said in an interview published in Finnish daily Helsingin Sanomat on Saturday. "As prime minister, it's my duty to represent all Hungarians, and we have sensitive issues, such as the situation of sexual minorities."
Fidesz and its sister party, the Christian Democrats, voted against the new amendments to the law on Tuesday.
"There is no place for the promotion of LGBTQ content in schools or the media," the Christian Democrats said in a statement on their website.

His comments reflect the growing role of foreign investors in the regionâs energy industry, already expanding even before the Iran war. The contradictory tangle of energy policy actions taken by US President Donald Trump toward Russia over the weekend risks repeating mistakes that he and his allies often slammed his predecessor for.
On Friday, Trump announced the US would waive sanctions on Russian diesel exports until the spring and permit it to release 300,000 metric tons of diesel into the global market, before announcing an energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv.
The diesel deal was quickly condemned by a bipartisan group of senators, who argued that the volume was too small to make a difference â equal to less than a day of US consumption â and extended a âfinancial lifelineâ to Russian President Vladimir Putin. This, they said, contradicted both a 2022 US ban on Russian energy imports and the spirit of the new sanctions law Trump signed last month, which seeks to penalize countries like China and India for the very same kinds of purchases the president is now pursuing. The diesel relaxation, former State Department energy diplomat Geoff Pyatt told me, is âenough of a sweetheart deal to encourage [Russian Direct Investment Fund CEO Kirill] Dmitriev and Putin to keep fighting in hopes Trump will deliver Kyiv.â
As for the âceasefire,â Russia seems to have violated it almost instantly. A Ukrainian official told me on Monday that Kyiv was temporarily holding off on further long-range drone strikes against Russian refineries while it assessed Moscowâs behavior and was waiting for a chance, potentially later this week, to clarify details of Trumpâs proposal with US officials. Axios reported the deal could apply only to refineries, which would make little sense for Ukraine to participate in given that it has only one barely-functional refinery. Kyiv is more worried about the power sector, which a recently leaked Russian military planning document makes clear is still directly in Moscowâs sights.
Dangling a limited ceasefire deal that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy canât accept sends the same message to the Kremlin as the diesel deal: Ukrainians are the problem in this war, and US resolve in support of Ukraine is barely paper-thin. The past few years have shown repeatedly that accommodating Putin pushes him away from the negotiating table, not toward it.
Trump and his energy officials have criticized Biden often and loudly for authorizing, in 2022, a record release of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which they framed as an irresponsible stab at tamping down US fuel prices ahead of an election at the expense of long-term American security interests. They also criticized Bidenâs decision in 2021 to relax sanctions on the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline in the interest of repairing relations with Moscow, which helped embolden Putin to undertake the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. With just three weeks until the midterms, Trump is clearly riled about diesel prices and the slow recovery of exports of refined products from the Persian Gulf. But itâs counterproductive to capitulate to Putin: In addition to the uncountable human toll, a longer war in Ukraine means more energy market distortion ahead.
Notable
- A new poll found that even if Trump managed a political feat like ending the Iran war or bringing down gasoline prices by $1 ahead of Novemberâs midterms, a majority of voters would not be more likely to vote Republican.

The News
Inflation tied to the AI boom is âjumping out of its laneâ and starting to push up prices in unrelated corners of the economy, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said.
âPrices are going up in spaces that are not just components in data centers and the directly adjacent industries,â he said on Semaforâs Compound Interest. âIâm getting increasingly nervous that thatâs just straight, old-fashioned overheating demand.â
Prices for land, electricity, water, construction, and electrical components used in data centers have surged. Those spikes donât appear to have yet hit consumer pain points â for example, the cost of groceries or a haircut â but economists are closely watching how AIâs wealth, from paper millionaires in Silicon Valley to higher-paid construction workers, is being spent.
Fed Governor Lisa Cook warned last month about âsome economy-wide pressure from AI-fueled demandâ but said that so far the boom looks like âa shift in demand toward AI-related sectors rather than an increase in economy-wide demand.â Fighting that kind of sector-specific inflation with rate hikes âcould be a mistake,â she said.
Goolsbee isnât a member of the Fed committee that sets interest rates, but will join it in 2027. He and other economists have been trying to parse how much of todayâs stubborn inflation â 3.4% in August, with Septemberâs numbers due out this week â is from higher oil prices triggered by the war in the Middle East, which the Fed canât do much about, and how much is coming from hotter demand across the economy for goods and services.
âIf inflation remains persistent, then I think itâs clear what the Fed has to do,â he said, when asked whether the central bank should raise interest rates again when it meets later this month.
Lizâs view
The Fedâs problem is that its best tool for fighting inflation doesnât seem to be denting the demand for AI inputs. Hyperscalers arenât slaphappy consumers who might be deterred by higher interest rates. They are locked in a must-win battle and donât seem to mind higher debt costs. Companies like Alphabet and Meta have cash-cow advertising businesses that can support a few extra basis points of interest.
Itâs a broader problem for the Fed: Big parts of the US economy no longer respond to rising interest rates. There may be a pain point for the hyperscalers, but itâs likely to be intolerable for the rest of us.

Hereâs what I think four months from now the interest rate should change.â Most of the discussion about communication seems to have been about that, and I kind of agree with we should phase out that kind of communication. Liz: Getting to those numbers that you would all like the market to put more stock in and make their own decisions about, even if they were prepared to be weaned off the commentary, does the data that youâre seeing right now lay out a clear picture?
I like how you phrased that. I would say no, not a super clear picture because inflationâs still way too high. I have been worrying publicly about the potential for supply shocks like tariffs, like oil prices to shove us into a stagflationary kind of a trade-off. There is one sense in which it hasnât been ambiguous. It hasnât been stagflationary. The job market still looks very stable to me. Growth has been solid, consumer spending solid. 524228311da7.text: President Trump is turning to Vladimir Putin to help ease a global diesel crunch, setting up a clash between Washington's energy priorities and its efforts to pressure Russia over its invasion of Ukraine. Why it matters: The fuel shortage is among the most severe effects of the Iran war and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. Average U.S. diesel prices remain far above $6 per gallon, adding to GOP headwinds in the midterm elections. Trump says his deal will help bring costs down. Catch up quick: Trump on Friday claimed an agreement to bring escalating Russian exports, and the Treasury Department waived sanctions to help enable it. A few things to watch... The campaign trail. So far a few Republicans in close races — including Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers and Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan — have criticized the agreement. Republicans already saddled with Trump's unpopular policies in the midterms now face another awkward choice: whether to back his diesel deal with a dictator many of them despise, Axios' Andrew Pantazi writes. The market. Diesel futures dipped after the announcement. But analysts expressed doubt that the levels Trump is claiming will meaningfully sway prices in the U.S. and elsewhere — if Russia indeed delivers. Per Trump's claim, Russia will "immediately" provide what amounts to 2.24 million barrels, followed 3.73 million next month (equivalent to around 124,000 barrels per day spread over a month), and then roughly double it thereafter. "In the near-term, it's hard to see the waiver helping global fundamentals for diesel much," writes economics and geopolitics analyst Rachel Ziemba. The global market currently has a deficit of about 1 million barrels per day, per market intel firm Kpler, and "Russia's ability to deliver additional barrels remains uncertain," writes Kpler's Michelle Brouhard. Capitol Hill. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.), one of those lawmakers in a close reelection fight, will try and force a House vote to block Russian oil purchases. The law. It's not clear if any Russian barrels will reach U.S. shores — or whether it's legal if they do. A bipartisan group of seven senators, in a statement , say the decision runs afoul of a 2022 law barring U.S. imports of Russian oil and petroleum products. Treasury's Office of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence said it is acting "in compliance with all applicable laws." Meanwhile, the White House faces an Oct. 18 deadline to begin implementing a more recent law — named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham — that imposes fresh sanctions on Russia and trade penalties on buyers of Russian energy. But the law gives the White House discretion to waive key provisions. Ukraine. Trump is pushing Ukraine and Russia to ease attacks on energy infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has criticized Trump's deal, said Russia has continued its barrages even as he maintained Ukraine held back early this week. Afghanistan's Taliban government has suspended the transmission of BBC broadcasts from FM radio sites across the country.
A Taliban government spokesman said the BBC had been suspended because of "repeated violations" but did not elaborate.
The BBC has been the only international news organisation to broadcast inside Afghanistan since two US outlets were banned from operating in the country in 2022.
"Millions of people across Afghanistan rely on the BBC for accurate news and information and we are working with the authorities to address the situation," the broadcaster said in a statement.
The BBC said it was "continuing to report fairly and independently in Pashto, Dari and English to our audiences in Afghanistan, on shortwave and medium wave radio, online and via satellite".
It reaches more than 20% of the adult population in Afghanistan each week with news and other output, including educational programming aimed at girls who have been banned from secondary schools.
Taliban Ministry of Information and Culture spokesman Khubaib Ghufran told local media: "Due to some repeated violations by the BBC media outlet, it is decided that for time being its activity is suspended across the country."
The Taliban government has a tight grip on media operating in the country.
Music is not broadcast and women are less visible on screen than before the Taliban retook power in 2021. Women no longer appear on air together with men.
People can still use some social media platforms, but a lack of electricity in large parts of the country, high costs and low literacy rates remain major barriers.
The BBC's Afghan service has been operating since 1981.

Barn owl chicks have been ringed in Purbeck for the first time to help track their movements and if the area's conservation-focused farming is working.
The 15 chicks and one adult were ringed at nest sites across three farmland sites in a partnership between Birds of Poole Harbour, Carey Ringing Station and the National Trust.
Mark Singleton, Purbeck's National Trust countryside manager, said: "This is an exciting project and a first for us in Purbeck. Although barn owl numbers have fallen significantly over the past century, there are encouraging signs they may be recovering locally."
Set to run every year, the project hopes to expand with more nest boxes put up next year.
Singleton said National Trust tenant farmers were managing the land to support wildlife with areas of longer grass, maintaining hedgerows and patches of scrub.
He said: "These habitats support the voles and other small mammals that barn owls rely on.
"By monitoring ringed birds over many years, we'll be able to assess how effective these measures are and continually improve what we're doing."
Kate Fox, licenced bird ringer and ornithologist from Carey Ringing Station, said: "Ringing provides invaluable scientific data about these birds, which can't be gained from observations alone.
"Barn owls are striking birds, but it's very difficult to tell individuals apart. If birds move to a different nest box, we won't know whether it's a new pair or birds we've recorded elsewhere unless they have been ringed."
The ringing was carried out under a special licence and follows strict guidance from the British Trust for Ornithology (BTO).
Barn owls are a Schedule 1 breeding species, meaning it is illegal to disturb them during the breeding season without a licence.

- Published
El NiÃ±o has continued to strengthen to what some scientists are calling "unprecedented levels", weeks before its expected peak in December.
Several key measures are now in record territory.
In its latest update, Australia's Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) said average weekly sea-surface temperatures in the central Pacific have reached their highest level on record, external.
It comes after scientists declared a new record for daily sea surface temperatures in the central-eastern Pacific in September, exceeding the previous record set during the very strong El NiÃ±o of 2015.
Temperatures above 30C have also been recorded for the first time in parts of the tropical Pacific, while record sea-surface temperature anomalies and exceptional subsurface warmth have been observed.
These measurements come from the region of the equatorial Pacific used to monitor El NiÃ±o.
El NiÃ±o is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year.
However, the Pacific is also warming due to human-induced climate change and this is starting to mask the strength of the natural warming during El NiÃ±o.
To remove this additional warming signal, Australian and US official forecasters are now using a Relative Ocean El NiÃ±o Index (RONI), to enable better comparison to historical events.
Using that measure, the BOM's average weekly data - while only going back to 2008 - is significant as it now exceeds levels during the record-breaking December of 2015.
"We are currently witnessing an El NiÃ±o event that is unprecedented in the historical record," Dr Zeke Hausfather, a climate scientist at Berkeley Earth, told the BBC.
Strong El NiÃ±o in a warmer world
The warmth across the Pacific now extends well beyond the tropical region normally used to monitor El NiÃ±o.
Comparisons with previous major events in 1972-73, 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16 show much more widespread ocean warmth across the Pacific and into the Gulf of Mexico.
Part of this reflects the long-term warming of the oceans but scientists say it is not the whole story.
"The strength of El NiÃ±o this year is spilling out of the traditional El NiÃ±o region," Dr Hausfather said.
The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says there is currently no evidence that climate change is making El NiÃ±o events stronger or more frequent, external. However, it remains an active area of scientific research.
What is clearer is that El NiÃ±o releases additional heat from the oceans into the atmosphere.
Historically, global temperatures during El NiÃ±o years are typically higher than during neutral years.
Combined with human-driven climate change, that extra heat is expected to help make 2026 one of the warmest years on record, with unusually high global temperatures likely to continue into 2027.
No two El NiÃ±o events are exactly alike
Although the most widespread impacts are expected later this year and into 2027, El NiÃ±o's influence is already being felt across parts of the world.
The strength of an El NiÃ±o does not automatically determine the scale of impacts in any one location. Regional effects can vary considerably from one event to another.
However, some common patterns are emerging when compared with previous super El NiÃ±os.
During the 1997-98 event, severe drought across south-east Asia contributed to extensive peat and forest fires, while parts of East Africa experienced devastating floods.
The event also helped make 1998 the warmest year on record at the time.
A similar pattern developed during the 2015-16 El NiÃ±o.
Severe drought and wildfire activity returned to parts of south-east Asia, while southern Africa experienced one of its worst droughts in decades, triggering a major humanitarian crisis.
Another recurring signal is tropical cyclone activity. Strong El NiÃ±o events typically suppress Atlantic hurricanes while boosting activity across parts of the Pacific, a pattern that has also been observed during 2026.
The World Meteorological Organisation says drought and flood-related disruption is already being reported in several regions, with growing concerns over food security in parts of East Africa and the Asia-Pacific.
Forecasts from both the European Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasts and the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration indicate El NiÃ±o is likely to peak in December.
Dr Hausfather said the latest projections were "astonishing" and are likely to set new records "by a remarkable amount".

5e3583338dbf.text:
Andyâs view
The Australian sinologist Geremie R. BarmÃ© wrote that âautocrats and patriarchs share a fateful dilemmaâ: Once in power âthe countdown to their demise is on.â
Mao Zedongâs long descent into ill health and madness brought China to the brink of civil war. Deng Xiaoping went out peacefully, though the decade before he died was marked by political upheavals, including the Tiananmen Square protests. Now, the Xi Jinping âdeath watchâ has begun.
Of course, the big difference is that today China is at the center of everything.
As it drags on, the Xi âdeath watchâ will become a global spectacle, moving markets, affecting investment flows, and shaping defense priorities. Chinaâs internal risks are now the worldâs risks.
Xiâs physical condition is one thing. At 73, heâs visibly slowing; he looked fragile descending the stairs of his plane at Air Base Andrews when he arrived for a summit with US President Donald Trump last month, clasping the hand of his wife, Peng Liyuan, for support. The Wall Street Journal reported that Chinese officials made a highly unusual request for a âhold roomâ for Xi at the White House where he could take breaks between meetings, and his talks with Trump were surprisingly brief.
But the pressures building inside the Chinese system are largely unseen: Leadership politics, including the health of the top man, are as much a black box today as they were in the Deng era. But we can assume that from now on, everything that happens behind the high red walls of the leadership compound in Beijing will be connected, one way or another, to the vexed issue of how a post-Xi China will be governed.
Political transitions are the midnight hour for all autocratic regimes. But Xiâs dilemma is particularly acute: If he names a successor now to carry forward his policies and protect his legacy, he risks triggering a political knife fight years before heâs ready to relinquish power.
Wait too long, though, and he creates a dangerous political vacuum.
Either way, Xi will have to pick a relative unknown â all the current members of the Politburo Standing Committee are too old to step into his shoes â raising a host of troubling questions. Would a designated successor catapulted to the top be strong enough to command the loyalty of the powerful military? Could he hold the Party together?
Or could Xi himself turn on the chosen one? One of Maoâs designated successors, Liu Shaoqi, died of diabetes and pneumonia in solitary confinement, lying in his own filth. Deng cycled through two successors before settling on Jiang Zemin.
Xi has grown paranoid about those around him, his ruthless purges targeting some of his oldest, and most trusted, comrades. That doesnât bode well for any potential second-in-command.
China now faces a period of prolonged political uncertainty. Carl Minzner, a US legal scholar and senior fellow for China studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, predicted a âlong twilightâ with the economy sagging, social discontent rising, and the state using âgrid managementâ â surveillance techniques used to maintain control over Xinjiang and other restive border areas.
A succession struggle is unlikely to remain within Chinaâs borders, Tyler Jost, a professor at Brown University, and Daniel Mattingly of Yale University argued in Foreign Affairs last year, noting that Xiâs prize goal is unification with Taiwan and âif he hears the succession clock ticking, he could become more willing to gamble on war.â
Iâm betting that the end of the Xi era will look a lot less like Dengâs, whose passing created hardly a ripple â by then, heâd handed over power and put in place a system to ensure smooth leadership transfers â and more like Maoâs, a drama that involved a bloodless coup (the arrest of the so-called âGang of Fourâ led by Maoâs widow), intervention by the Peopleâs Liberation Army, and show trials.
We had a foretaste of this kind of turmoil when Xi took power in 2012. A carefully constructed power transfer was upended by the arrest of Xiâs main Politburo rival, and there were wild internet rumors of a military coup, tanks in the streets of the Chinese capital, and gunfire near the leadership compound.
Xi has wrenched China back to an era of one-man rule. But having attained the pinnacle of power â next year heâll likely get a fourth five-year term in office â Xi now has to reckon with the consequences for his country. As Deng himself warned, âbuilding a nationâs fate on the reputation of one or two people is very unhealthy and very dangerous.
Notable
- In 2025, during Russian President Vladimir Putinâs visit to Beijing, a hot mic picked up a conversation between Putin and Xi in which the two discussed organ transplants and the possibility of living forever. Musing on such procedures, Putin told Xi (through a translator) that with modern technology organs could be transplanted again and again so that â(you can) even achieve immortality.â While a largely hypothetical conversation, it hinted that staving off old age and death â maybe for eternity â is top of mind among the worldâs most powerful autocrats.

Missiles and drones have been intercepted over Riyadh after the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen struck a fuel depot near the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa, its spokesperson says.
Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki said several projectiles targeting the Saudi capital and other cities were intercepted after the coalition carried out a strike on the Yemen Petroleum Company's al-Sabaha facility on Tuesday night.
The Houthis warned they would target the airport and Aramco refinery in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and Aramco's headquarters in the eastern city of Dammam.
Al-Maliki later said missiles targeting cities including Dammam had been intercepted, while shrapnel had fallen in a residential area in Dhahran.
An Armaco administration building in Dhahran was also targeted, resulting in "limited fire", Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy said in a statement.
No casualties were reported, the statement said.
It came as the Saudi cabinet, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said the Iran-backed group would "bear the consequences" of its recent deadly attacks on the kingdom.
Thirteen people were killed when a missile hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday, while another person was killed in a similar attack there the following day.
On Tuesday, the coalition said its forces had destroyed three drones north of Riyadh.
The Houthis have said they are targeting airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones in response to deadly Saudi strikes on territory that they control in western Yemen, including Sanaa.
The Saudi-led coalition has been providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces mounting an offensive on Yemen's Red Sea coast and several other front lines.
A correspondent for AFP news agency reported that queues formed at petrol stations in Sanaa on Tuesday afternoon following the coalition's warning of an impending operation against the al-Sabaha oil facility, with many residents worried about shortages.
The Yemen Petroleum Company, which is run by the Houthis, issued a statement that sought to reassure them, saying the facility "does not contain any stock of petroleum products".
The company also said it had "taken all necessary precautionary measures to address any emergency, ensuring the stability of the supply situation and the continued meeting of citizens' needs in a normal manner".
After al-Maliki confirmed the strike, first reported by Houthi media, explosions were heard over Riyadh and other Saudi cities, with al-Maliki reporting four missiles and two drones had been intercepted near the capital.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social on Tuesday the Houthis were "behaving very badly... and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices".
Speaking to reporters, he did not answer a question on whether he'd made a decision to help the Saudis retaliate against them, but said he "might" ask Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan to intervene.
Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes.
Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed in Yemen since August. The UN's human rights office says they include at least 54 civilians, half of them children.
More than 216,000 people have also been displaced across the country, and suspected cholera cases have tripled in three weeks, rising from 217 to 647, according to the UN.

1edfeb38365c.text: By — David Fischer, Associated Press David Fischer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/florida-executes-a-prisoner-who-killed-his-cellmate-in-hopes-of-getting-a-death-sentence-its-the-states-17th-execution-of-the-year Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Florida executed a prisoner who killed his cellmate in hopes of getting a death sentence. It's the state's 17th execution of the year Nation Oct 13, 2026 6:27 PM EDT STARKE, Fla. (AP) — A Florida prisoner who said he killed his cellmate specifically to get on death row was executed Tuesday, nearly 18 years after the attack. James Robertson, 63, declined to offer any last words before receiving a three-drug injection and was pronounced dead about 10 minutes later. It was a stark contrast to the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee two weeks ago, where she was rushed to the hospital after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. WATCH: Botched execution reignites debate surrounding death penalty Robertson's execution, the first in Florida since Pike, comes at a time of escalating attention on the death penalty in the United States. The Pentagon said last week that it would livestream the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, drawing criticism from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers. "Florida has a sound lethal injection process and protocol," Jordan Kirkland, a state Department of Corrections spokesperson, said at a news conference before the execution. Although he couldn't speak to Tennessee's lethal injection procedure, he said Florida would make sure its process was "humane and dignified." Florida executes people by injecting them with a sedative, a paralytic, and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections. Robertson wanted to be executed Robertson had pleaded guilty to first-degree murder for strangling Frank Hart while he slept in 2008, and waived all appeals. He told investigators that he did it so he wouldn't have to live out his days in prison. Hart was killed just eight days before he was due to be released, his daughter, Rebecca Hart, told reporters at Florida State Prison. She stressed that her father was not just a piece of Robertson's story. "When someone you love is taken from you in such a violent way, the world keeps moving, even when a part of yours feels like it has stopped," she read. "Other people go on with their lives, but you carry your loss into every tomorrow." Robertson was 17 years old when he went to prison in 1980 for burglary and assault. Years of convictions for escape, battery and weapons while in prison kept adding time to his total sentence. Hart had been sent to prison in 2003 following a sexual battery conviction. A rare reprieve leaves another Florida prisoner on death row Robertson was supposed to be one of two executions carried out by Florida on Tuesday, but Gov. Ron DeSantis withdrew a death warrant last week for William Lee Thompson. The Republican governor did not provide a reason but had temporarily stayed the execution last month pending a psychiatric evaluation. Records show this was the first time DeSantis withdrew a death warrant. Thompson, 74, will remain on death row, and a new death warrant could be signed in the future. His attorneys say he has dementia and failing health, and they want him transferred to a medical facility. DeSantis is the third Florida governor to sign a death warrant for Thompson. Bob Graham and Bob Martinez both scheduled executions for Thompson in the 1980s, but years of appeals and stays allowed him to avoid the electric chair, the state's method of execution at the time. Thompson was convicted of first-degree murder, kidnapping and sexual battery in the 1976 killing of 23-year-old Sally Ivester. Florida has the nation's busiest death chamber DeSantis oversaw 19 executions in 2025, more than any other Florida governor in a single year since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Robertson was the state's 17th execution of 2026, with two more already scheduled, not counting Thompson. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has made few public comments about the unprecedented number of executions but explained previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims' families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out. William Reaves, 77, is scheduled to be executed on Oct. 20, followed by Jesse Guardado, 64, on Nov. 5. Reaves was convicted of fatally shooting a deputy after dropping a gun in front of the law enforcement officer in 1986. Guardado was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004. A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. in 2025. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half the 31 total executions in the U.S. so far this year. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — David Fischer, Associated Press David Fischer, Associated Press

Schools closed. The internet partially shut. Roads blocked by shipping containers. And the army arriving in town.
Imran Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, is under a state of emergency, his party's provincial government suspended. It's another dramatic escalation in the standoff between the former prime minister's supporters and Pakistan's state - and one that some fear could lead to more instability, not less.
According to the federal government this step, allowed by the constitution, was needed to provide protection for the province's population from the threat of terror.
"The PTI KPK government was hand in glove with the terrorists," Attah Tarrar, federal information minister, told journalists on Sunday. He did not elaborate or provide evidence, but promised to do so soon.
Two days later there had still been no update from him - but schools had reopened in Peshawar and most parts of the province, and internet services had been restored.
While police would not confirm any detentions, there is clearly a crackdown under way to prevent protests. Most PTI leaders in the province have gone into hiding.
On Tuesday dozens of PTI supporters took to the streets in Bara, Khyber district, hometown of provincial Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. There were reports of tear gas shelling in the area.
To many observers, the timing of Sunday's announcement of emergency rule is not coincidental.
For the last week, thousands of Imran Khan's supporters have marched through Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where the PTI have been in power for 13 years, demanding Khan's release.
"The charitable response would be to say that it sounded disingenuous," says Farzana Sheikh, associate fellow at Chatham House.
"I do not see the link with terrorism," says Arifa Noor, journalist and commentator. "I'm not even sure if it was the long march itself [that led to this]. Perhaps it was the last straw or perhaps it's just a case of saying, we don't want to deal with the government being in the hands of an opposition party."
The protests were led by Chief Minister Afridi, whose whereabouts are still a mystery. His party says he has been arrested; the government says that he is in protective custody.
Before the march had begun, there had been a crackdown. Three of Khan's sisters were arrested in September, accused among other things of mobilising supporters, and have been detained ever since.
Khan has barely been seen by his family or lawyers in the last year; two of his sisters saw him in August, one in prison, another as he was checked over at a hospital visit after concerns were raised by the Supreme Court about his health, before he was returned behind bars again where he has been held for more than three years.
The PTI leader, who is widely believed to have lost power because of a rift with Pakistan's powerful military, has been imprisoned since August 2023. He is convicted in several corruption cases which he says are politically motivated.
With the party already weakened, why this reaction from the authorities?
"The PTI rank and file has been becoming increasingly restless in recent months amid growing concerns about Imran Khan's health," says Michael Kugelman, senior South Asia fellow at the Atlantic Council.
"There is a sense that perhaps now is the time to send a very strong message to the party and make it more difficult for them to be able to put pressure on the government."
The government has previously argued that Khan was going against jail rules by using his meetings to discuss politics.
Tarar has said of the state of emergency: "There was no political agenda. They could have gone on with their march," and pointed to the talks the two sides had in the run-up to the decision as an indicator that they did try discussion.
But others see this as just another attempt to restrict Khan and his party.
"The government has less and less space for disagreements or dissent and they do not want to negotiate their way out of any kind of conflict," Noor says.
Zahid Hussain, Islamabad-based author and defence analyst, is clear about who is behind the decision.
"The balance of power is completely shifted to the military establishment," he says.
Sheikh thinks that Pakistan's military is feeling confident because it believes it has a good relationship with the White House, its international credentials burnished by their role in the US-Iran peace talks.
"The mode is very much, this is the moment, let's seize it," she says. "There is a sense that, we have all the cards in our hands. We can ride this out internationally."
But Pakistan has plenty to contend with. Militancy is rising. The country was ranked number one in the Global Terrorism Index 2026 as the country which had been affected most.
The country is at loggerheads with two neighbours; it has repeatedly hit Afghanistan with air strikes accusing the Afghan Taliban government of harbouring militant groups, a claim it denies. It would take little to reignite its long-running simmering conflict with India.
Meanwhile, it has promised to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against attacks as the conflict against the Houthis has become increasingly dangerous.
Short of solving one problem, some have warned this state of emergency could lead to more challenges. It risks increasing political instability, with Islamabad taking responsibility for a province without a buffer - the provincial government - they can blame.
"I would argue that this could actually backfire," Kugelman says. "You're playing with fire because if this move ends up adding to the anger and the discontent among so many there, then you have a very big problem on your hands."
"It is reckless, given the challenges, multiple challenges the country is facing," Hussain says. He fears that more of these powers could be used across Pakistan.
Attempts to combat militancy with more active army operations could come with its own perils too, Sheikh argues.

"The biggest difficulty really was the loneliness. Sometimes, if I wanted to talk to someone I'd talk to the TV."
Yang, 91, lives on the outskirts of China's bustling capital Beijing. Following the death of her husband, she was so lonely that she says she even considered the possibility of voluntary euthanasia.
"I asked my son about it but he told me it was banned. I told him that if it ever becomes legal I want to do it - I didn't want to live any longer."
Suffering glaucoma, with failing eyesight, she was unable to even do basic things like adjust the controls on her air conditioner.
Cases such as Yang's have become increasingly common in Chinese cities which Associate Professor Teresa Kuan, from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, says is "exacerbated by the structure of society and the modes by which people interact".
There are many causes of isolation in China. Most of it happens when rural migrants pursue economic opportunities, leaving behind close-knit support networks for urban centres where loneliness and uncertainty can be difficult to overcome, or when graduates uproot themselves chasing employment on the other side of the country.
But now a growing "loneliness industry" has emerged to try to fill these gaps in people's lives.
Yang says her life has been transformed by one of these services - Wang Yingwei and his electric scooter delivery team - who started coming over twice a day with hot meals but whose help extends far beyond that.
"We see ourselves as community children," Yingwei told the BBC. "It means putting yourself in the shoes of older people and carefully considering their needs.
"For example, they may be drinking tap water which can be cloudy and contain a lot of lime. I can fix this problem with a filtered water tank. Such a small thing can make them much happier. Maybe they can't shower because their equipment is broken. I'll buy a part, replace it and their shower is fine."
"The elderly treat us like their children, and we treat them like our own parents," he added.
Yingwei's services cost less than half the price of employing a caregiver.
The former mobile phone salesman says he started his company to help seniors remain at home without having to move into retirement facilities. He was inspired to do this after his own father-in-law, who had developed Alzheimer's, had to go into a nursing home. Yingwei said he felt that the conditions there were so sub-standard he wanted to make sure others could stay out of institutions like this for as long as possible.
His small business currently employs four people but he says there is a possibility he will expand as demand grows.
There is still a shortage of solid data on the size of this sector â which operators say has exploded in recent years â but securities company Sinolink valued it at around $7.4 billion in 2025. And this is only expected to grow given the trajectory of modern lifestyles.
Zheng Ruizhi, another client of Yingwei's who lives in Beijing's northern outskirts, welcomed him at the door with a big smile.
"After retiring, I don't have much opportunity to hang out with others," the 75-year-old, whose son lives two hours away from her, told the BBC.
She was recovering from a recent injury which she said was making everyday tasks more difficult.
But the arrival of Yingwei â who she calls her "dear boy" â lightened her mood.
"I call you 'dear boy' because I am so fond of you. I genuinely like you from the bottom of my heart. I also admire and trust you. When you help me out, I don't have a single worry or fear," she told him.
Yet the services offered by those in this sector are not limited to home visits.
Twenty-three-year-old Liu Yanyan, for instance, works as a "medical escort". She acts as a friendly face taking clients to see the doctor, or picking up their test results or medication from city hospitals, which can be intimidatingly large and bureaucratic.
"Some of my customers are people in their 20s who came to Beijing to build a career. They might not have friends here or feel awkward asking colleagues to accompany them because of the concept of social reciprocity in Chinese culture," she said. "If I accompanied you to a doctor's appointment for free, you might feel obligated to buy me a meal or a movie ticket afterwards."
She said that, because of this, there are many people in modern Chinese society who tend to keep to themselves.
"So, they hire someone like me to accompany them to the hospital. If they had to go alone, they could feel scared or anxious."
At the core of many businesses catering to loneliness in China is a simple offering: human connection.
Teresa Kuan said that some people prefer the option of pouring their hearts out to a complete stranger for a fee.
"If there is a companion you have paid for, the relationship is not exactly equal. It is a service relationship, so you don't have to deal with the unpredictability of a standard relationship. The thing about friendship is that it can be unpredictable. You don't know when someone might disappoint you. But, in a service relationship, you have a better idea of what to expect."
Wang Zhoutao runs a hiking business to help people who want to climb China's famous mountain Huangshan in Anhui Province.
"We provide emotional support, like cheering them up, taking their photo or telling jokes. It's really a service based on companionship," he said.
The former soldier added that he normally hikes up the mountain with clients 10 to 15 days a month. When fully booked, this could be as many as 30 times a month.
He gave an example of a young woman he once accompanied who felt ostracised at work. "She felt useless and wanted to prove something to herself," he said.
"We started climbing but it was a tough trek as the weather was really hot and we were sweating a lot. There were moments she wanted to give up but I told her, 'If you quit now and can't get over this mountain how will you handle anything else in life?'. I kept encouraging her."

As Indonesia battles its worst wildfire season in a decade, a toxic smog is choking millions of residents in the region.
The air on the islands of Kalimantan and Sumatra have turned an ominous amber, with air quality recorded at hazardous levels.
The smog - also known as the haze - has also drifted beyond Indonesia's borders to neighbouring countries, raising public health concerns. It has obscured Singapore's skyline and forced some schools to close in Malaysia.
Now, anger is mounting at the companies accused of burning farmland - as well as the authorities who have struggled to stop them.
The annual dry season wildfires have been especially intense this year because of an unusually strong El NiÃ±o - a natural climate phenomenon which changes weather patterns around the world.
According to independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas, 1,043,377 wildfire hotspots have been recorded in Indonesia, burning a total of 900,000 hectares of land.
Slash and burn
Many of these fires in Indonesia's forests and peatlands are caused by the razing of vegetation to clear land - a practice known as "slash and burn".
This is an agricultural method that has traditionally been employed by farmers in Indonesia to create nutrient-rich soil for new crops.
But today, many of these fires are associated with commercial farming and are taking place on a much larger scale - and are harder to control. Activists and government investigations have repeatedly accused some companies of using fire as a cheap way to clear large swathes of land.
While slash-and-burn farming is illegal in Indonesia, enforcement of a ban has long proven tricky.
But persistent haze this year has prompted Indonesian authorities to step up efforts to punish offenders.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has called for tougher sanctions against slash-and-burn farming, describing the practice as "ecological terrorism".
Last month, Indonesian authorities announced they had suspended the operating licences of 26 companies linked to the wildfires and launched investigations into others. Cases involving criminal elements would be taken to court, officials vowed.
But it's not just Indonesian companies that have been embroiled in controversy amid the haze problem.
A Greenpeace report published this month identified businesses based in Singapore and Malaysia which are linked to plots of land in Indonesia where wildfires are burning.
This includes First Resources, a Singapore-based palm oil company. Between August and September more than 30 haze source points were recorded on land managed by its two Indonesian subsidiaries, according to Greenpeace.
First Resources told the BBC in a statement that it maintained a "strict zero burning policy across all planting activities and implement robust fire prevention, monitoring and firefighting measures throughout our operations".
Greenpeace also named Malaysian plantation group Kuala Lumpur Kepong, whose subsidiary PT Menteng Jaya Sawit Perdana managed land in Indonesia where 19 haze source points were recorded.
Kuala Lumpur Kepong said in a statement that a "majority" of the fires originated from beyond its concession area and had all been extinguished.
"We do not condone or permit the use of open burning for land preparation or any other purpose across our operations," it said.
'When there is no smoke, we send oxygen'
It remains to be seen how effective governments can be in sanctioning offending companies.
In 2014, Singapore passed the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act which allows the government to take action against local and foreign firms found to be contributing to the haze.
The following year when Singapore saw a bad bout of haze, authorities issued summonses to several Indonesian companies thought to have cleared land by burning, in a bid to prosecute them under the new law.
But that drew sharp ire from Jakarta, which said the move harmed bilateral ties. And with Indonesia refusing to cooperate, Singapore authorities said they could not obtain information about the suspected companies.
Also in 2015, Indonesia's then-Vice-President Jusuf Kalla angered Singaporeans when he said that "for 11 months, they enjoyed nice air from Indonesia and they never thanked us... they have suffered because of the haze for one month and they get upset".
Similar tensions surfaced again last weekend when Syahganda Nainggolan, who leads Indonesia's government communications agency, said the raging wildfires were beyond human control and added that the oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests".
"When there is no smoke, we send oxygen," he added, in a video that has been widely circulated on social media, triggering criticism and ridicule from Malaysians and Singaporeans.
But Indonesia has in the past also apologised to its neighbours for causing the haze.
This year, Indonesian officials have thanked Singapore and Malaysia for offering to help tackle the wildfires - though it has not officially requested international support.
In Indonesia, there have been efforts by civil society to force the government to take action.
In Pontianak in the West Kalimantan province, several groups have filed a class action lawsuit against the Indonesian government and Prabowo, accusing them of "gross negligence" over recurrent toxic haze.
They want the government to declare the haze a national disaster, which would allow for recovery measures such as the coverage of healthcare costs.
A similar case was filed last year in South Sumatra, but it was dismissed.
Meanwhile, on the ground in Kalimantan and Sumatra, air pollution levels have remained at dangerous levels for weeks.
There are many who have no choice but to brave the toxic smog every day.
"I'm short of breath and have a headache breathing air now. But I still have to work," Imrayedi, a 63-year-old motorcycle taxi driver in Pekanbaru city, on Sumatra island, told BBC Indonesian last week.

Why the lonely in China are hiring 'temporary children'
In China's cities, despite the huge crowds, or maybe because of them, residents can feel very isolated.
Now, a new industry being dubbed the "loneliness economy" has emerged, with people hiring themselves out as companions to help the elderly.
The BBC's China correspondent Stephen McDonell visits a company that does just that, to see how their business works.

Susie Walker-Munro is one of a handful of tea growers in Scotland.
She says the acidic soil creates ideal conditions for the perfect artisan brew.
Costing about Â£40 per packet for her most expensive product, it's not going to replace the supermarket brands any time soon.
Droughts, intensive downpours and diseases have created challenges for tea growers across the world as they deal with the impact of a warming planet.
But some experts believe Scotland's relatively settled climate could give the tea industry here a helping hand.
As the picking season draws to a close, Susie plucks the last few leaves before proudly pouring me a small glass of her Kinnettles Gold, which is grown in a walled garden on the family farm near Forfar.
She believes Scotland's latitude â sitting 57 degrees north - will always be a bar to having a year-round crop like those countries close to the equator.
But she says wetter weather could help boost production.
"Our yields are never, never going to be high," she says.
"Maybe with climate change they might come up a bit, it depends if we get enough rain. Scotland could be absolutely ideal."
Susie isn't convinced tea will ever be a major crop for Scotland.
But others say it could be one of a numbers of options in the future, as farmers are forced to diversify and adapt to a changing climate.
Rethinking the way we farm the land might be one way to extend the range of crops produced.
Countries like the Netherlands are already embracing glass houses, which could become more commonplace in Scotland. Susie says they would be a good way of growing more tea.
They would also allow Scotland to produce more Mediterranean vegetables like tomatoes, cucumbers, aubergines, and even melons, according to Pete Ritchie from campaign organisation Nourish Scotland.
He says an abundance of renewable energy from wind farms later in the century will make heating them relatively cheap and will cut down on air miles.
"We're going to be able to produce those plants with a lower carbon footprint and provide secure all-round jobs for people on brownfield sites in the cities and also on the islands and remote parts of Scotland," he says.
The James Hutton Institute already has a large number of glass houses â but it is going even further by artificially creating the sort of conditions that may exist in 75 years.
Climate modelling shows that Scotland can expect hotter, dryer summers and milder, wetter winters by the end of this century.
The institute's new advanced plant growth centre is effectively a climate simulator.
It's able to control plants' light, water and nutrient intake to test how they cope with stresses - and then select species which are likely to fare best against all that climate change can throw at them.
For the past three months they have been experimenting with fava beans, which are photographed daily so scientists can monitor their progress.
Dr Robert Hancock says they need to switch from breeding crops for specific environments, such as hot or dry climates, towards ones which are more generally resilient.
"We need to start breeding those crops now and start understanding what Scottish farming's going to look like," he says.
"Farmers need time to plan, we need to get those crops out to the farmers and registered.
"Ultimately it's about what those guys do in the fields that matters, not what we do inside a climate simulator."
The farmers of the 22nd Century are probably only a generation away from those starting out in the industry today.
That means the current crop of young farmers will have to give the closest consideration to the businesses they hand on to their own children.
And that means more precision farming, more artificial intelligence, and automation.
Modern tractors and combine harvesters are so high in technology such as GPS steering that it's no longer such a leap to consider autonomous harvesting.
But the chair of the Scottish Association of Young Farmers, David Murdoch, believes traditional skills will always be important.
"There's no point in doing it if you don't know your cattle, but embracing the technology is what keeps us competitive.
"Working with larger herd numbers and larger machinery to keep us producing more with less people - that's the way the world's going," says David, who farms dairy with his father at Beith in North Ayrshire.
But it's not just food production that will drive future changes in farming.
Protecting and enhancing nature, offsetting carbon emissions, and renewable energy production are already shaping the farms of tomorrow.
Health innovations may also play a growing role, with obesity drugs already showing a demand for proteins and nutrient-dense foods.
Soya, flax and legumes could become a more common sight as conditions for growing them become more favourable and that desire to grow them locally continues.
Prof Wayne Powell - the principal of Scotland's rural college, the SRUC - predicts that Scotland will become "the bread basket of Europe".
That title is currently used to describe Ukraine, because of its abundance of fertile agricultural land and exports of crops including wheat, maize and barley.
"Climate change is redrawing the farming map of Europe and Scotland could become one of Europe's most important climate resilient food regions," he says.
"The possibility of access to cheap renewable energy could also transform the economics of Scottish farming from irrigation, refrigeration, food processing, so that we can capture more value from our land and food."
Scotland's rural communities have seen major changes over the past 75 years which have resulted in far fewer people working the land.
Pressure to keep food affordable for consumers while farms remain profitable will be a key driver of innovation.

The stark assessment years ago from Nancy Pelosi echoed anew after Trump's surprise announcement last week that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import tons of Russian diesel to the U.S. as a way to ease sky-high prices at the pumps for Americans ahead of the midterm elections. Trump's diesel deal with Putin has been criticized by both Republicans and Democrats as fueling Russia's war against Ukraine, violating existing U.S. laws and drawing the U.S. closer to Russia. It joins a growing list of instances in which the Republican president has sided with Putin, often at the expense of Ukraine — and America's own standing. "The harm to the Ukrainians is real," said William Taylor, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine, now a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, in an interview Monday. "And the cost to us, the United States, is high." It's not at all clear the Trump-Putin deal will deliver the supply boost the president is seeking to bring down prices. Energy experts have said the flow of Russian diesel is unlikely to lower prices in the U.S., which have escalated largely due to disruptions from the U.S. war against Iran. But the agreement underlines a message at home and abroad that Trump is an unreliable ally as Ukraine battles Russia. A bipartisan group of six senators urged Trump over the weekend to reverse course, saying the U.S. "should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline." Trump, however, held fast to his deal with Putin and lashed out, blaming Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for America's high diesel costs and asserting he should step aside — something Ukraine's leader has no intention of doing. "Anything that could help our farmers, our ranchers, I like," Trump said Monday outside the White House. Asked about Republican criticism of the Russia deal, Trump said they "can't really be serious." But a dozen senators weighed in with a letter to Trump on Tuesday. The six Republican and six Democratic senators said allowing Russian diesel into global markets would have a negligible impact on fuel prices while the revenue Russia gets will "undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition" and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran and North Korea. WATCH: How the diesel price spike is rippling through nearly every part of the economy "It will also endanger servicemembers operating overseas in support of Operation Epic Fury," they wrote. Trump also insisted that an energy ceasefire is in place for Ukraine and Russia, despite Zelenskyy saying that Moscow continued to strike his country's energy sites. An AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll published Oct. 1 found that Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the Iran war and blame him for higher prices. Congress voted to halt Russian imports, but Trump has other plans Congress swiftly approved legislation at the outset of the Russian invasion of Ukraine in spring of 2022 to ban the import of Russian energy products, which are widely viewed as providing the financial fuel for Putin's military assault on Ukraine. The bill passed the House on an overwhelming 414-17 vote and the Senate without a single senator opposed. The law says the president can seek to lift the prohibition if an agreement has been reached to withdraw Russian troops from Ukraine and cease military activity. Such a proposal would need to be reviewed by Congress and to have been "accepted by the free and independent government of Ukraine." "Trump is directly violating that law," said Rep. Lloyd Doggett, D-Texas, the bill's chief sponsor, in a statement Monday. He said Trump "illegally rewards his pal Putin while once again blaming Zelenskyy for not capitulating to Putin." More recently, Congress last month approved a sweeping Russian sanctions bill, named after the late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham, that would slap tariffs on countries that continue importing Russian oil. Trump signed the bill into law. The bulk of the law's provisions go into effect Oct. 18, the end of the administration's 30-day review period. But such action now appears to be in question since Trump's diesel deal with Putin will allow the flow of Russian energy. In a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senate leaders from both parties last week said the most urgent priority for the U.S. must be to tackle the "shadow fleet" of tankers that Moscow is using to transport oil and bypass America's sanctions. But that was before Trump announced his deal with Putin, which he said would unleash hundreds of tons of diesel. A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.
OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee.
Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.
OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired.
According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.
Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product.
Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say.
On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said.
OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier".
According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment.
Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege.
He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'".
On 5 October, prosecutors say he allegedly returned to inspect the device in the office room. Prosecutors used CCTV camera footage to link him to the scene.
That same day, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different part of the building. A security team for OpenAI opened it to find his wallet and ID, as well as another recording device that was similar to the one found in the office conference room, prosecutors said.
Alfozan appeared in court on Tuesday. It's unclear whether he has legal representation.
If found guilty, he faces up to five years in prison and a fine of $250,000 (Â£187,000).

35a5e553cd13.text: By — Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/cvs-agrees-to-pay-315-million-to-settle-justice-department-case-over-opioid-prescriptions Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter CVS agrees to pay $315 million to settle Justice Department case over opioid prescriptions Nation Oct 13, 2026 5:02 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — CVS Pharmacy Inc. and various subsidiaries have agreed to pay $315 million to resolve a Justice Department case alleging it unlawfully dispensed medically unnecessary prescriptions of highly addictive opioids, officials said Tuesday. The settlement resolves a lawsuit brought in 2024 that accused the healthcare giant of providing massive amounts of opioids and other controlled substances "to fuel its own profits at the expense of public health and safety." WATCH: Leading researcher explains how viewing addiction as a brain disorder improves treatments It's the latest effort by the federal government to hold accountable companies that officials have alleged helped fuel the U.S. addiction and overdose crisis. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "Today's settlement is a significant milestone in the Justice Department's efforts to combat the opioid epidemic by cracking down on pharmacies who unlawfully fulfill prescriptions for controlled substances," Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said in an emailed statement. WATCH: Opioid crisis renews focus on expanding access to methadone treatment CVS said in a statement that its pharmacists were trained "in the safe and appropriate use of all medications" and that it had implemented "best-in-class" programs to help them "make the best decisions on behalf of patients." The company said it strongly disagreed with the claims made in the lawsuit and that the settlement admits no wrongdoing. The company said in 2024 that pharmacists were being held to "vague, undefined, and ever-changing standards of practice" when it comes to filling prescription opioids. READ MORE: CVS, Walgreens announce opioid settlements totaling $10 billion The lawsuit filed under President Joe Biden's administration accused CVS of violating the Controlled Substances Act by filling illegitimate prescriptions for high doses of potent opioids that "fed dependence and addiction." The Justice Department alleged it dispensed large quantities of opioids based on prescriptions from known "pill mills," or providers that hand out prescriptions for drugs without a legitimate medical purpose. It alleged that poor staffing levels coupled with performance metrics and incentive compensation policies implemented by the company led to pharmacists racing to fill prescriptions without confirming they were legitimate. The prescriptions were often billed to and reimbursed by Medicaid and other federal healthcare programs, the lawsuit says. Under the settlement, CVS must also "implement additional safeguards to ensure that prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances are dispensed only when medically appropriate," Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate, who leads the Justice Department's Civil Division, said in a statement. Over the last decade, drugmakers, wholesalers, pharmacies and other companies have agreed to settlements with governments in the U.S. totaling over $50 billion. Most of the money is intended to go to address the crisis, which has been linked to more than 100,000 deaths in the U.S. some years, though the numbers have fallen sharply recently. Most of the settlements -- and dollars -- have been with state and local governments, but the U.S. has reached several deals, including in the last two years with the pharmacies Walgreens and Walmart. Associated Press reporter Geoff Mulvihill contributed to this report from Philadelphia. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 70c1d9fad782.text: U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said her office is probing Rep. Ilhan Omar's (D-Minn.) financial disclosures, the day after federal agents searched the congresswoman's Washington, D.C. home. The big picture: It's another example of the administration's escalating fight with the progressive lawmaker, who has clashed with the White House over its immigration crackdown — and whom President Trump has labeled as "crooked." Driving the news: Asked about a prior ethics probe into financial filings from the Office of Congressional Conduct, which her office said cleared Omar, Pirro said Tuesday on Fox News' "America Reports" that "is subject of an investigation as well." "It doesn't matter what the House does. It doesn't matter, you know, what this agency or that does. We're looking at the facts. Based upon the facts, we'll follow them wherever they take us," she said, and confirmed her office is handling the probe. Catch up quick: Federal agents searched Omar's home before dawn Monday as part of a separate immigration probe, Axios' Ben Berkowitz reported. Omar described the search in an X post as "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement." Trump has repeatedly lashed out against Somali immigrants, including Omar — who he described in a post last year as "always wrapped in her swaddling hijab" and "the worst 'Congressman/woman'" in our Country." Zoom out: Omar's office pointed Axios to The Wall Street Journal's reporting last month that the Office of Congressional Conduct recommended that the House Ethics Committee dismiss allegations that she possibly violated House rules or law by reporting false or incomplete information in her financial disclosures. A disclosure filed last year listed Omar and her husband's assets as ranging from $6 million to $30 million. She later amended the form to reflect a much lower range, the Journal first reported, citing what her team said were accounting errors. Pirro's office did not respond to Axios's request for comment. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.
