NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft has been breaking distance records for decades. Launched almost 50 years ago, it became the farthest human-built object from Earth when it overtook the pathfinding Pioneer 10 probe in 1998. It was the first spacecraft to leave the solar system’s protective bubble, and it will be humankind’s first emissary to the stars.
The cameras on Voyager 1, along with those on its twin spacecraft, Voyager 2, captured powerful megastorms in the outer solar system, the first images of dozens of moons and never-before-seen details of the gossamer rings around Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune and Uranus. The images and data sent home have shaped theories of how the solar system formed and evolved, inspired subsequent missions and posed enough new questions to keep space scientists busy for decades.
And this month, Voyager 1 will set another big record. On November 18 at 5:16:07 a.m. Eastern Standard Time, it will become the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth: the distance light travels in 24 hours. That’s a journey of 25.9 billion kilometers, or more than four times the distance from the sun to Pluto. At that point, signals from Earth will take a full day to reach Voyager 1; it will take another day to hear back.
“I just never imagined [the mission] would last that long,” says Linda Spilker, a planetary scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., who began working on Voyager shortly before the probes launched in 1977. Spilker was in Cape Canaveral, Fla., for the first launch. She even planned the births of her children, now in their 40s, around mission milestones. After stepping away to lead another mission, she is now back as Voyager head scientist.
Two other scientists have been with Voyager since the beginning. Others weren’t yet born when the spacecraft launched. “Voyager, to this day, is a multi-generational mission,” Spilker says. But it isn’t a mission of nostalgia. There’s still a world of discovery out beyond the solar system’s edge.
“Every piece of data, every day that goes by that we get data from the Voyagers, tells us something new,” says physicist Jamie Rankin of Princeton University, who started her Ph.D. in August 2012, the same month that Voyager 1 left the solar system for the cold, calm seas of interstellar space. “Every day, it’s in places nobody’s ever explored before.”
Exploring our neighborhood
The original mission of the Voyager probes was to explore the outer parts of our solar system, which until then had remained largely mysterious. A rare planetary alignment meant that a spacecraft launched in the late 1970s could swoop past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, getting a gravitational boost from each planet that it passed. With these gravitational assists, the spacecraft could complete the tour in less than 15 years. Such an alignment won’t happen again until the 2150s.
The project was a bold step for its time. When work began in the early 1970s, no spacecraft had gone farther than Mars. NASA set a conservative goal for the mission: flybys of Jupiter and Saturn. In 1972 and 1973, NASA launched two Pioneer probes, which made sure the trek was possible and gathered data along the way. As with Voyager, there were two spacecraft in case one failed.
After nail-biting launches and a wait of nearly two years, the Voyagers began uncovering many of Jupiter’s and Saturn’s long-held secrets, including the volcanoes on Jupiter’s moon Io, details of Jupiter’s Great Red Spot and hints of geologic activity on Saturn’s moon Enceladus.
Mission accomplished, Voyager 2 went on to pass Uranus and Neptune. It took the first images of the planets’ rings and discovered more than a dozen moons along the way. The spacecraft also spotted a perpetually churning storm on Neptune and erupting geysers on Neptune’s moon Triton.
“The highlights of Voyager were clearly the planetary encounters,” said Ed Stone, the mission’s original head scientist, in a NASA interview before his death in 2024. “We had a lifetime of discovery packed into each one.”
The uncontested stars of these encounters were the images shared in news reports and TV broadcasts as the planets and their moons came into view. Jupiter’s moon Io turned out to be a shocking splotchy orange color that looked like a pizza.
A humble navigation image of that moon led to one of the most surprising discoveries of the entire mission. Four days past Voyager 1’s closest approach to Jupiter, after the excitement had died down, project astronomer Linda Morabito of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory started processing additional images of Io. These images had been taken after the flyby, when Voyager was looking back over its shoulder.
As Morabito enhanced one image’s brightness, she spotted an odd bulbous formation protruding from Io’s edge. “What’s that?” she asked herself. Her supervisor had the same reaction: “Jesus, what’s that?” she later recalled him saying.
The bulb turned out to be a volcanic plume — an erupting fire fountain extending 250 kilometers above Io’s surface. It was the first discovery of active volcanism anywhere other than Earth, and it transformed our view of the outer solar system. Instead of a cold, inert icebox, this was a bubbling and dynamic region.
The findings inspired many future missions. While visiting Jupiter from 1995 to 2003, the Galileo probe found that Europa may have a subsurface ocean that could be hospitable to life. When the Cassini probe orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017, it discovered that the moon Enceladus also has a potentially habitable ocean that spews icy geysers into space.
In 1990, with Voyager 1 about 6 billion kilometers from the sun, astronomer Carl Sagan convinced mission leaders to turn the spacecraft backward for one last look at the planets. Formula 1 will return to Africa for the first time in more than three decades with a Grand Prix in Rwanda in the early 2030s, the sportâs governing body confirmed.
The FIA, which has committed to a 10-year race deal, linked the move to expanding the global reach of F1, highlighting the âexciting growth opportunitiesâ of the continentâs young fan base.
After Rwanda beat South Africa to the honor of hosting a Grand Prix, President Paul Kagame said at the launch in the capital, Kigali, that âtoday belongs to Africa.â The race forms a significant addition to Rwandaâs growing portfolio of international events as it raises its global investment and tourism profile.
But rights group Amnesty International has accused the FIA of handing the country a âsportwashing prize.â It accuses the authorities of arbitrary detention and torture of opponents, as well as stoking conflict in neighboring DR Congo â all of which Kigali denies.

Malawi launched a nationwide crackdown on fuel hoarders and black market sellers as the nation struggles with shortages that have left truckers queuing for up to a week and bus fares doubling on some routes.
Diesel and petrol have been scarce for weeks because the country lacks the hard currency to buy fuel supplies, sparking a scramble for dollars that has seen the central bank sell off gold to pay suppliers and the government return to the IMF for a bailout.
Malawi, which has among the highest fuel pump prices in Africa at more than $3 a liter, highlights the impact of a $100-plus per barrel crude price on import-dependent economies with thin buffers. Unlicensed resellers face arrest, and stations caught hoarding can lose their license under the new measures.
The IMF last week said it was making âconsiderable progressâ in designing a âpackage of macroeconomic policies.â Its last program was a $175 million loan that expired in May last year, the latest in a string of support packages for one of the continentâs poorest countries, whose agriculture-based economy has been hit hard by extreme weather patterns.

DR Congoâs former President Joseph Kabila has formed a new rebel movement incorporating Rwanda-backed forces, openly taking charge of the insurgency despite US sanctions against him.
The move deepens the political and security threat to President FÃ©lix Tshisekediâs government and challenges Washingtonâs efforts to end fighting and secure access to the countryâs critical minerals.
UN experts reported in June that Kabilaâs growing prominence appeared intended to obscure Rwandaâs role by portraying the rebellion as a Congolese movement addressing a national problem. Rwanda has acknowledged defensive âsecurity coordinationâ with the M23 insurgents, who have held large swaths of mineral-rich eastern DR Congo for more than a year. US sanctions against rebel leaders and Rwandaâs military, a Washington-brokered peace deal, and talks mediated by Qatar have so far failed to end the fighting.
Insecurity has complicated DR Congoâs hopes of profiting from rising demand for copper, coltan, and cobalt used in digital infrastructure and the energy transition. Washington has paired its peace efforts with a bid to loosen Chinaâs grip on mining in the worldâs largest cobalt producer.

The IMF raised its 2026 growth forecast for sub-Saharan Africa to 4.5%, cementing its position as one of the worldâs fastest growing regions.
The IMF said the new projection, marginally higher than Julyâs 4.3%, âmasks substantial divergence,â with oil-importing economies the most exposed to higher energy and food prices driven by Iran-war-related supply chain shocks.

Tokenmaxxing may have been the shortest-lived corporate try-hard hustle in history, but many of Wall Streetâs year-end bonuses still hinge on AI use. Applicantsâ AI skills are nearly four times as important in hiring decisions as where they went to college, and a quarter of US financial firms have tied raises, promotions, and bonuses to AI proficiency, according to a survey of 500 companies by financial recruiting firm Selby Jennings. Breathe easy, bulge-bracketers: The practice is more common among fintech startups and smaller firms than brand-name banks and trading houses, Jacob Summers, Selby Jenningsâ head of tech recruiting, told Semafor.
Nearly a third of firms surveyed have created new roles or departments to track AI use, where total token burn is less important than wringing some actual value out of all the token use. (âTokenmaxxing is dead, long live valuemaxxing,â proclaims an IBM blog post from June.) But in many organizations, monitoring that work falls to managers, turning them into part-time AI accountants.

The Scoop
Saudi Arabiaâs sovereign wealth fund is preparing to inform organizers of the 2034 menâs soccer World Cup that it plans to drop five new stadiums it proposed to build to host the tournament, according to people familiar with the matter.
Public Investment Fund will likely narrow its focus to three new stadiums as it cuts spending on some of its signature domestic investments, the people said. Dropping the five venues would leave the kingdom with 10 stadiums for World Cup matches. The changes are part of a revised plan the kingdom is preparing to submit to FIFA, the tournamentâs organizers, the people said.
PIF is looking to drop plans to develop stadiums in King Abdullah Economic City and Qiddiya Coast, both near Jeddah; Roshn and New Murabba in Riyadh; and NEOM, in the kingdomâs northwest. Several of the cancelled stadiums are attached to broader real estate projects that have been halted or where work has slowed.
Saudi Arabian officials are still working on the updated proposals and the plans could change, the people said. PIF and the Saudi Ministry of Sport didnât respond to requests for comment.
Know More
Reuters earlier reported on the cancellation of the NEOM stadium, which was envisaged as being on the roof of The Line, a 500-meter-tall skyscraper. Work on The Line has effectively ground to a halt, and NEOM has not allocated any funding for the project until after at least 2030, Semafor previously reported.
Saudi Arabia had also proposed a 45,000-seat stadium at Qiddiya Coast, a planned entertainment and tourism destination north of Jeddah. That development has also been put on hold. Another 45,000-capacity stadium in Riyadhâs New Murabba district is also set to be dropped. Work on the wider development has slowed after the departure of Chief Executive Michael Dyke and the suspension of work on the projectâs centerpiece, a 400-meter-tall, cube-shaped skyscraper with screens lining its interior, similar to The Sphere concert venue in Las Vegas.
The kingdom is still proceeding with plans for other new stadiums including one in Dhahran being developed by Saudi Aramco, and the King Salman International Stadium and Prince Mohammed bin Salman Stadium in Riyadh.
The cuts could leave Saudi Arabia developing just six new stadiums and refurbishing four existing ones for the World Cup. Four of the stadiums it plans to use in 2034 are also due to host matches for the 2027 Asian Cup, which starts in January.
The outlook for that contest going ahead in Saudi Arabia has been thrown into doubt by the kingdomâs involvement in the war in Yemen against Houthi militias. The group has launched multiple attacks against Saudi cities in recent weeks, shutting down the capitalâs airport and killing at least 18 and injuring hundreds.
Qatar also previously dropped four of the stadiums it had planned to build for the 2022 World Cup as it got closer to the tournament.

AI agents, meet double agents. OpenAI said it identified, fired, and reported to the FBI an employee who bugged its office. The employee, a Saudi national later identified by law enforcement as Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested last week and charged with illegally recording company communication. (He appears to have some ties to members of the Saudi business elite.) Among the evidence against him: chatbot logs about how to install recording devices.
Startup espionage has been pursued for far less (see: the Deel-Rippling drama over corporate HR software), but the FBIâs quick work and public rollout of the arrest shows how high the stakes are for the US government and frontier labs. The arrest comes days before the White House AI task forceâs first meeting. Its chair, Jay Clayton, cited the case as proof the group is needed.

A little-noticed deal this week for senior-care clinics is the first shot fired in a Wall Street turf battle. BlackRockâs HPS credit arm is essentially lending $2.8 billion to Humana, marking Larry Finkâs entry into a space that Apollo has had to itself until now.
Apolloâs dryly named âcapital solutionsâ business, launched in 2024, was a bet that asset managers could cosplay as banks. Their money could go places that banksâ deposit funding couldnât, especially after post-2008 regulations. Apollo has since made big loans to companies including Intel and Keurig Dr Pepper, notching $800 million from the business last year on its way to a $1 billion target.
Two years ago, I wagered that BlackRock and Apollo would be the winners of the weird debt world that limped, then sprinted, out of the global financial crisis. Apollo got there first, but BlackRock just threw its hat in the ring.

Spainâs king said his countryâs control of exclaves in Africa was ânon-negotiable,â after the cities became flashpoints in territorial disputes with Morocco and Europeâs anti-immigration debate. Ceuta rose to international prominence in July, when more than 70,000 people swept into the tiny exclave in a matter of hours. Most have returned to Morocco, which Spainâs prime minister accused of entering its territorial waters during the crisis.
But European far-right parties have seized on the crisis as evidence that Madridâs welcoming stance toward foreigners â it previously vowed to regularize hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrants â has backfired: âThe future of Europe is being decided in Ceuta,â the leader of Franceâs hard-right National Rally party said while visiting the Spanish territory.

India cracked down further on anti-government protests that have grown substantially in recent months, escalating from attacking the authorities over education to frustration with what critics see as broader threats to the countryâs democracy. Three leaders of an upstart political party were jailed and an historic protest site in central New Delhi â âthe countryâs most recognizable stage for public dissent,â per AFP â was shut down.
The latest demonstrations have centered around a review of Indiaâs electoral rolls that has led to an estimated 130 million people being barred from voting. Opponents of the effort say it has targeted minorities and critics of the ruling Hindu nationalist party; in Delhi, for example, The Hindu reported that Muslims were disproportionately affected.

c6a1b77d9b50.text:
Iran-backed Houthi fighters reportedly hit the headquarters of Saudi Arabiaâs national oil company in overnight strikes, stoking a conflict that risks spiralling into a wider war.
The attacks follow a Houthi onslaught that killed 13, injured hundreds, and forced Riyadhâs airport to shut at least through Saturday, denting the kingdomâs reputation for stability and piling pressure on the countryâs de facto ruler.
Analysts fear the conflict could expand beyond the Arabian Peninsula: The Houthis are reportedly building an advanced missile using Chinese parts. US President Donald Trump has accused the group of âpurposefully trying to drive up Oil Pricesâ ahead of Novemberâs midterm elections; Tehran is reportedly targeting crude tankers in a bid to keep prices elevated.

aa9f5150a01b.text:
The threat of a workerâs strike â which has since been averted â at Chileâs La Escondida, the worldâs biggest copper mine, sent prices for the metal near record levels, underscoring the Latin American countryâs growing role in the industry.
Other recent temporary closures in some of Chileâs copper mines, which are responsible for almost a quarter of global output, because of worker accidents and benefits disputes have also pushed up international prices.
Demand for the metal has surged on the back of the AI data center and EV production boom, with countries globally racing to lock up supplies. But despite production rising to record levels in 2025, UBS nonetheless expects shortfalls to reach an all-time high next year.

f82feb5cee65.text:
The CEO of ASML, the worldâs only provider of the machines that make cutting-edge chips, said AI demand would outstrip supply for years to come, easing investorsâ worries of a spending bubble. His comments come after Europeâs most valuable company reported bumper profits that far exceeded analyst expectations, boosting its share price.
Investors globally have grown concerned that AI spending may be cresting as borrowing costs surge, with the International Monetary Fund warning that a market correction posed a threat to the global economy. But, for now, spending on the technology remains strong: Goldman Sachs expects AI infrastructure investment to drive a $7.6 trillion boom through 2031.

6cf27150b50f.text:
Chinese exports jumped 36% year-on-year in September, a bumper figure that is likely to vex the countryâs trade partners, who have demanded Beijing address imbalances and alleged domestic overproduction. Faced with US and EU restrictions, which have dented Chinese imports in the West, Chinese companies have turned to other markets, sparking criticism from producers in Southeast Asia and Africa, who say their industries risk being hollowed out.
The latest figures pushed Chinaâs trade surplus in 2026 to almost $1 trillion, nearing the entire figure for last year, underlining the countryâs continued reliance on exports, with domestic consumption weighed down by a long-running real estate crash and rising youth unemployment. Beijing has so far resisted calls for a significant stimulus package.

4c1c12063fba.text:
The News
Kenyan investors hoping to participate in the Dangote refinery initial public offering now have access through a financial instrument being used for cross-border African investment for the first time on Nairobiâs bourse.
The use of global depositary receipts (GDRs), which allow backers to buy a stake in a foreign company without leaving their home market, bypasses regulatory barriers that have held up intra-African investment. The use of GDRs offers a template for exchanges across the continent to expand pan-African trade and broaden their investor bases.
After an extension of the IPO period was announced on Monday, Kenyan individuals and institutional investors will have until Oct. 27 to buy into their countryâs $300 million allocation of Africaâs largest public offering.
The minimum entry price in Kenya was slashed from $824 to $4.12, matching what Nigerians were being offered. Announcing the extension, Dangote said he wanted greater African participation and highlighted the Kenyan arrangement that he hoped could be replicated.
African policymakers are keen to deepen capital markets as a way to mobilize more of the continentâs domestic resources to fund infrastructure projects and reduce borrowing costs.
Know More
The refineryâs stock market debut was touted as a way for African investors to own a stake in the continentâs largest refining plant. But the prospectus for the $1.6 billion share shows it was not registered as a public offering outside Nigeria, Reuters reported. That has left investors relying on their own countryâs regulations or finding workarounds using the few eligible online financial platforms. Reuters reported patchy take-up outside Nigeria, reflecting low levels of cross-border investment.
The Nairobi Securities Exchangeâs (NSE) approach is structured around Standard Bankâs Kenya subsidiary Stanbic, which will hold the shares and issue the GDRs. These will be traded on the NSE in Kenyan shillings, and Stanbic will manage the foreign exchange conversion and pay out dividends.
Karimi Warui, vice president of investment banking at Renaissance Capital, which is overseeing the IPO in Kenya, told Semafor that the Dangote Group initially intended to pursue a conventional cross-listing approach to get on the NSE and other stock exchanges, but ultimately settled on GDRs for ease. Trying to deal with the rules and regulations of 10 different jurisdictions âbecame a bit onerous for them,â she added.
She said this approach in Kenya could inspire others. âI wouldnât be surprised if companies that are already listed like [Kenyan telecoms company] Safaricom pursue GDRs in the future to tap into markets like South Africa and Nigeria,â she said. âI actually think we will see more of this now,â saying the IPO would âshow regulators the need to work with financiers and issuersâ to accelerate growth and integration of Africaâs financial markets.
Warui also emphasized the need for regulators to customize policies to fit African markets instead of copying Western regulators.
The use of GDRs comes amid a significant push to enhance retail investing in the country. Safaricom this year rolled out NSE trading on the mobile money service M-Pesa, helping drive retail participation in the IPO of the state-run Kenya Pipeline Company (KPC). Warui told Semafor that Renaissance Capital was copying the KPC blueprint for the Dangote IPO â with an online platform for share purchases during the offer period, and trading on the M-Pesa platform expected once it is listed on the NSE.
Besides Kenya, Ugandaâs markets regulator has approved a restricted offer limiting participation to high net-worth individuals and professional investors. Botswana has been selected to host the southern African portion of the public offering, Bloomberg reported.
Step Back
Some analysts have cautioned that the GDRs could leave Kenyan investors exposed to FX risks as the GDR tracks the Lagos share price, which is in naira, meaning currency devaluation could significantly affect investors. Acknowledging the concerns, Warui noted that Dangote Refineryâs revenues were dollarized and that dividends could also be paid in dollars, mitigating the potential impact of naira devaluation.
Previous GDR listings by African companies have been outward, where issuers list the underlying shares on exchanges outside the continent â mostly on the London Stock Exchange (LSE) to attract Western capital.
Room for Disagreement
Sultan Mwangi, a Nairobi-based investor and financial researcher, predicted that participation in the Dangote IPO among Kenyan investors would be far lower than expected, especially among retail investors.
He attributed this to the handling of the IPO which he said had left investors âdisappointedâ despite initial excitement. Among issues he cited were inadequate investor education and a need to address concerns regarding the use of GDRs, especially over whether this will leave people exposed to fluctuations in the value of the naira. According to Mwangi, the extension of the IPO offer as well as lowering the minimum investment were a response to low uptake among retail investors.
âPeople were not convinced, and the amount of time available to explain it has not been enough,â he told Semafor. Dangote Industries has yet to respond to enquiries from Semafor on whether the lowering of the minimum investment was a response to underwhelming participation among Kenyan retail investors.

7914b4ca937b.text:
- Published
Police in Mauritius imposed an overnight curfew overnight to quell the worst riots to break out on the Indian Ocean island in decades.
Peaceful protests over water shortages and the high cost of living that started a week ago erupted into violence on Friday when a woman was shot and wounded by police at a roadblock.
The circumstances of the shooting are not clear, but the officer has since been arrested and remanded in custody.
Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam ordered the curfew on Tuesday, warning against those "acting against the interests of the country", which is a tourism and financial services hub.
"Those who have carried out these actions will have to face the very heavy consequences warranted by their anti-patriotic acts," he said in an address to the nation.
Protesters burned tyres and blocked âroads as the unrest escalated over the weekend, with police stations and other public infrastructure properties being vandalised.
The mayhem prompted the closure of schools and public transport, with foreign embassies issuing alerts warning its nationals to be cautious.
Despite the curfew, police said there had been several incidents overnight and some arrests.
But the police assured people that by Wednesday morning traffic was again moving throughout the island and said people should resume their normal activities.
When protests over the shortage of water initially started, the government had responded proactively by providing more water to households, according to ZoÃ« McCathie, an analyst at South Africa-based Signal Risk.
The escalation had presented a more "unusual situation for the country's security situation", with the government resorting to closing schools and imposing a curfew, she told the BBC's Newsday programme.
"Protests to this scale and to this extent haven't been seenâ¦ since around 1999. So the government's response to this in that case is logical and is necessary," she said.
While the government had managed to "curtail the worst of the unrest" there was still a possibility that protests could return in some areas, with water shortages expected to persist until the rainy season in December, she said.
The cabinet is due to meet on Wednesday afternoon to reassess the situation and decide on the next steps.

6cfbc32dc3e3.text:
Waelâs view
In June 2008, I sat in a Jeddah Hilton conference room packed with ministers from more than 100 countries waiting for King Abdullah to arrive. Oil was closing in on a record price. Saudi Arabiaâs message that day: The world had enough oil. It offered a modest increase in output and told governments to cut taxes and rein in speculators. Less than three weeks later, on July 11, crude hit about $147 a barrel.
This week in Riyadh, another ministerial gathering took place. The man now leading the kingdomâs response, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, was an assistant oil minister two decades ago. This time the crisis is different â and so is his answer.
Then, the argument was about speculation. Saudi officials said investors had pushed prices well past what supply and demand justified, and that financial trading in oil had grown many times larger than the physical market. Washington thought OPEC should pump more. Riyadh replied that it would not build capacity for buyers who did not exist. Now the argument is about geography.
Gulf crude is trapped behind the Strait of Hormuz, and the kingdomâs answer is to build around it. Prince Abdulaziz told the World Petroleum Congress that Saudi Arabia may lift its East-West pipeline capacity from about 7 million barrels a day to 10 million within three years, and he wants more international involvement. His logic is that the more countries have a stake in the line, the better it is protected.
Both responses share one feature. Saudi Arabia cannot solve the crisis alone, and it ends up paying for the attempt. In 2008 it built rarely used spare capacity and has carried its cost ever since. A new pipeline will follow the same pattern. When the war ends it will not run full, and Riyadh will keep it as insurance.
The oil market has also shifted. In 2008, OPEC was dominant and no one else could add meaningful supply. Some consumers searched for substitutes, and ethanol was an answer then. Today, itâs the electric vehicle. But neither remedy has removed the need for fossil fuels and no price spike has changed the thirst for oil.
The biggest difference is Washington. In 2008, the US relied on OPECâs oil. Today, it has plenty of its own, a reality that may not be felt by Americans paying more at the pump. If America needed OPEC barrels as badly as it did in 2008, the politics of this current crisis would look very different.
Geopolitical risk has been the main factor driving $100 oil this year, with shipping and insurance comprising more than a third of the price of the global crude benchmark. Even if Hormuz is opened tomorrow, the new logistics of moving crude will weigh on producers. It will also change the relationship between states: Iraq is planning to build a pipeline through Syria to the Mediterranean, while Kuwait and Qatar may lean on their Gulf neighbors to reach ports outside the strait.
Ultimately, much of the bill will go to the same address: Riyadh. The kingdom has carried the cost of a largely idle pipeline for decades, and will soon have to revert to its role as the global swing producer, keeping prices fair to producers paying for new infrastructure, and consumers who wonât tolerate high prices forever.
Wael Mahdi is an independent commentator specializing in OPEC and Saudi Arabiaâs economy, and co-author of âOPEC in a Shale Oil World: Where to Next?â
Notable
- Saudi Arabiaâs oil supply could still be threatened even after the end of the war. This report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies looks at what options there are.
- Despite the oil shock, the Saudi economy can remain resilient, according to this briefing from the Atlantic Council.

aaa68af6fcab.text:
President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putinâs deal to deliver Russian diesel to global markets may be sending shockwaves through the GOP â but donât expect it to do the same to prices.
Already, multiple House Republicans; key GOP candidates; and two bipartisan groups of senators have pushed back on the move.
The planned imports will âhave very little unnoticeable impact on domestic US diesel prices, even if it happens â and I think thatâs a big if,â given legal complications and Russian constraints, Bloomberg economist Chris Kennedy, who served on the National Security Council during the Trump and Biden administrations, told Semafor. He said that the amount of diesel Russia has pledged to release for the month of November represents only âone day of US diesel demand.â
He pointed to heating oil futures, observing that âtraders appear to be pricing in very little near-term impact.â
The White House pushed back: One official insisted to Semafor that âmassive amounts of supply will lower costs for American farmers, truckers and workers.â
âTheyâre not releasing that [diesel] to us, theyâre releasing it to the entire world,â Trump told reporters Tuesday. âBecause the world market suffered with high prices â and when you knock out diesel refineries, thatâs not a great thing.â

17ab65c23eb3.text: Apple's big new hardware bet for the AI era is here, and it's a...smart display? Why it matters : Cue the time machine and let's head back to 2014, when Amazon's Alexa shocked the tech world and led us to imagine a Jetsons-style home would be ours in the near future. It wasn't, but Apple believes it could come soon. The iPhone maker is betting that modern AI can finally make good on that vision, unveiling a slew of new smart home devices Tuesday. Between the lines: While the smart home has largely failed to live up to its promise, modern AI could help address its biggest shortcoming: Getting devices to just work without requiring users to become amateur IT experts. Apple's new products emphasize easy setup and integration with its existing ecosystem, while AI could help diagnose problems and coordinate devices. "The capabilities that AI would bring in helping make sure that these devices can solve their own problems and work together is really interesting to me," Paul Gagnon, a vice president at market research firm Circana, told Axios. Driving the news: Apple's announcements Tuesday included a new smart display, a revamped speaker, an updated streaming device and a collection of connected home accessories developed with partners. HomeView: Apple's new $299 smart display features a 7-inch screen and an AI-powered Siri that can respond to requests, control connected devices and recognize different household members to deliver personalized information. It will ship next month and comes in two versions, one that can hang on a wall and the other, a tabletop device reminiscent of the iMac G4. Apple Home Collection: Apple worked with LG and Schneider Electric on smart locks, doorbells, cameras and thermostats designed to work together through Apple's Home app and Siri. The big picture: The AI hardware race is taking two different paths: Making familiar devices substantially smarter and creating entirely new kinds of gadgets. Amazon and Google have been incorporating more capabilities into their respective assistants and accompanying smart home products, efforts that were three years in the making . Meanwhile, others are betting that the AI era needs new kinds of highly personal devices. OpenAI is expected to release its first AI device soon, and Meta recently teased plans for Charm , a Tamagotchi-like device meant to bring its Muse assistant to the masses. Reality check: Apple has a loyal customer base and a history of making complicated technology easier to use. But that doesn't guarantee consumers will spend more on a category that has struggled to generate sustained demand. U.S. smart speaker dollar sales fell 9% in 2024 and another 7% in 2025, and smart displays fared poorly as well before rebounding somewhat this year, according to Circana. "We have definitely been in a, we'll call it, an enthusiast phase or early adopters phase for quite a while now," said Circana's Gagnon. Zoom out: Better AI doesn't necessarily mean consumers will rush to buy more smart home devices, particularly when increasingly capable AI assistants are already available on smartphones. Apple could benefit from its large installed base of iPhone owners and its ability to simplify setup, but it remains unclear whether those advantages will expand what has remained a niche market. "The new smart home products could appeal to consumers who have previously resisted buying smart home devices because they are perceived as difficult to set up and sometimes hard to use," Ben Wood, chief analyst of CCS Insight, told Axios. The bottom line: A decade ago, the smart home promised to change how we live. AI may finally make that possible. But Apple still has to convince consumers that the home needs another screen or speaker — not just a smarter phone.

dd9326e49e8d.text:
Watch: Block of flats destroyed in Russian strikes on Ukraine
A key energy facility and a residential building in the outskirts of Kyiv have been hit by overnight Russian missile and drone strikes.
In the capital, at least three people were killed and 21 injured, Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS said. At least 600,000 people across the country are without electricity after strikes hit critical infrastructure in the Kyiv region and the north-eastern city of Kharkiv.
The strikes come after US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that an "energy ceasefire" was in place between Russia and Ukraine.
Russia's defence ministry said its "massive" strikes had targeted communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military.
BBC Ukraine Correspondent Dan Johnson explains.

674f9298fcd3.text: Cities and researchers are using AI to map and predict extreme heat risk, but new research suggests it's used far more to identify where people are in danger than to help officials respond. Why it matters: As climate change intensifies extreme heat, better predictions won't protect vulnerable communities unless governments can turn them into action. U.S. deaths associated with high temperatures rose 53% from an annual average of 2,670 in 2000–2009 to more than 4,000 in 2010–2020, according to a 2025 Yale study . Driving the news: A study published in Climate Risk Management examined existing research on how AI and machine learning are being used to manage extreme heat. Of the research papers reviewed, 98.4% focused on prediction and 59.2% on prevention. That's compared with just 10.4% on response, 3.2% on recovery and 1.6% on preparedness — a disparity the authors call a "research-to-implementation gap." The research is heavily focused on using AI to forecast dangerous heat and identify who's at risk, with far less attention on how it can help officials decide what to do next. "Where AI can actually add value is where prediction is central to the decision-making, and that's in scale or providing more granularity," said Karishma V. Patel, a RAND policy researcher who co-authored the study. State of play: Turning sophisticated heat predictions into government action requires more than advanced models. Cornell researcher Jennah Gosciak told Axios that having "robust data systems" that can ingest data from a variety of sources and then make it usable to practitioners "is most of the battle here." Case in point: Google in June announced it had expanded its AI-powered Heat Resilience data from an initial 14-city pilot to more than 50 cities worldwide, giving urban planners building-level data to help target heat interventions. The data uses AI and high-resolution imagery to map roof reflectivity down to individual buildings. Google said data from the pilots helped inform decisions in several cities, including cool-roof ordinances and adaptation plans. Reality check: Better information doesn't necessarily equal better outcomes. Gosciak, who spent time as a Public Interest Technology Fellow with New York City Emergency Management, recently compared simpler heat-vulnerability indexes with more complex predictive algorithms for government heat decisions. She described one important distinction as "slow versus fast data." Predictive algorithms may be more useful for time-sensitive decisions "tied to a specific trigger event," while simpler indexes can be better suited to longer-term planning. One advantage of simpler indexes is that officials can explicitly choose which vulnerable populations to prioritize, added Gosciak, a PhD student in Cornell's Information Science Department. What's next: The next frontier may be less about making heat forecasts incrementally better and more about connecting predictions to interventions. AI's value could lie in helping officials make "near real-time decisions" by integrating changing signals and providing "hyperlocal forecasting at granular levels," Patel said. That could help officials respond to heat risks in real time and better understand compound threats involving heat, air pollution, wildfire smoke and drought, she said. The bottom line: "What is important is not just that we can build AI-enabled technology, but it actually solves a problem or removes a bottleneck," Patel said.

7202223420e7.text: President Trump is indulging his fondness for Vladimir Putin at a moment of acute political peril, forcing Republicans in the midterms to take cover as he showers Moscow with one-sided concessions. Why it matters: With just three weeks until the election, Trump is rekindling a decade-long, scandal-scarred relationship with a dictator reviled by most Americans — including his own supporters. Driving the news: Since speaking with Putin on Friday, Trump has embarked on a remarkable five-day campaign of diplomatic concessions and cover for Russia — sparking bipartisan blowback just as voters prepare to cast their ballots. On Friday, Trump announced a deal to unleash millions of tons of Russian diesel onto global markets, easing sanctions designed to starve Moscow's war revenues. On Saturday, Trump lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky for striking Russian refineries and demanded that Kyiv replace its leader. On Sunday, Trump blindsided Zelensky by declaring an immediate "energy ceasefire." Russia has continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, with no apparent consequences from Washington. On Monday, Trump dismissed months of intelligence-based reports that Russia was enabling Iran's war effort by supplying information about U.S. military assets. On Tuesday, Trump doubled down on the diesel deal and brushed off concerns that the proceeds could finance Russia's war machine, even as GOP senators labeled it a "betrayal" and "a gift to our adversary." Between the lines: The benefits to Russia are clear. Far less apparent is what Trump's concessions accomplish for American security, European allies or his own political fortunes. For America: Energy analysts doubt the diesel deal will meaningfully ease fuel prices sent soaring by the Iran war. For Europe: Washington is breaking ranks with a NATO alliance confronting a historic threat environment , as Russia escalates its hybrid campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions. For Republicans: With control of Congress hanging in the balance, Trump is embracing a dictator viewed unfavorably by 81% of his own 2024 voters, according to a January YouGov poll . The big picture: Trump's warm relationship with Putin has haunted his political career since 2016, when Russia interfered in the presidential election to help him defeat Hillary Clinton. From the Mueller investigation to the Helsinki summit , Trump's deference toward Putin has long divided Republicans and put him at odds with his own national security establishment. A decade of investigations, scandals and Washington outrage has done little to shake that affinity. If anything, the scrutiny appears to have hardened Trump's determination to defy the foreign-policy consensus. What they're saying: On Monday, Trump again suggested that Russia was more interested in ending the war than the country it invaded, telling reporters: "I think, actually, Putin wants to make a deal more than Zelensky." "The President's diesel deal will help lower prices for farmers, truckers, and families across the nation as he simultaneously urges both sides of the Russia-Ukraine conflict to stop strikes against refineries, which are driving up costs and hurting American consumers," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement. The bottom line: Losing control of Congress could paralyze Trump's legislative agenda and expose his administration to years of investigations and subpoenas. But as polling alarms pile up , the president appears increasingly willing to follow his raw political instincts, regardless of the consequences for Republicans fighting to keep him in power. In a Truth Social post Tuesday, Trump made clear that he sees himself as personally immune from the results of the midterms, writing: "I'm not running in the Elections, I've already won, IN A MASSIVE LANDSLIDE."

87a7bf92b1db.text: Advocates for AI safety and regulation are emerging as a force in U.S. elections, spending nearly $50 million this election cycle on candidates who favor regulation, a new analysis shared exclusively with Axios shows. Why it matters: The safety spending points to the unusual power dynamics in the AI race, where researchers shape policy and regulation in ways that differ at times from the priorities of the companies where they work. The researchers add to the advocacy and giving of an array of AI safety groups that have been well-funded for years, including from Coefficient Giving, a philanthropy with close ties to many top AI executives, especially at Anthropic. Driving the news: AI safety groups and individual donors have spent $48 million this cycle on Democratic and Republican races, according to new figures shared first with Axios. That includes donations from researchers, such as OpenAI's Juan Felipe Cerón Uribe and Redwood's Aryan Bhatt. It also includes Guardrails Alliance, a tech-worker backed AI safety group, which has raised $11.7 million between its super PAC and 501(c)(4). The big picture: Taking AI industry money has grown complicated due to viral warnings of catastrophic AI risk from the very same industry developing it and data center NIMBYism mobilizing communities in blue and red districts alike. OpenAI President Greg Brockman pulled a planned second $25 million donation from Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by tech execs and investors, in part because of an internal revolt at OpenAI. Forces favoring AI acceleration — who earlier in the year appeared to favor veiled threats to pro-regulation candidates — haven't spent as much as opponents expected, and safety advocates see an opportunity to fill the void. Zoom in: Jacob Eliosoff, who runs the cryptocurrency investment fund Calibrated Markets, said he decided to engage in political giving related to AI after he saw early fundraising and candidate advocacy from Leading the Future. Eliosoff, an active participant in New York's effective altruism community, said he didn't want to see a repeat of 2024, where crypto industry funding had outsized influence on the regulatory positions of most candidates. "If politicians feel like they can't say anything because there's a very deep-pocketed and ruthless political entity that's going to go after them, that motivates me to step in," Eliosoff said. Between the lines: Eliosoff has donated to Democrats and Republicans who he says appear to be open to taking AI risks seriously and could be well positioned to pass regulation. Donors told Axios they are not primarily motivated by party affiliation or specific policy positions but by fears that industry spending will silence candidates on an unpopular technology. The other side: Leading the Future had retained more than $31 million at the end of the second quarter and has supported more than 15 Democrats and more than 25 Republicans. In a statement, the group said AI regulation will need 60 votes to pass in the Senate, so anyone serious about safety "and harnessing the benefits of AI for all Americans should be focused on building a broad coalition for action." What's next: This cycle will be a test of whether candidates who take AI industry money and oppose real regulation lose and whether that is clearly understood as a central factor in their loss, Guardrails Alliance Executive Director Shaunna Thomas said. "Republican leadership and the Trump administration are on the other side of the majority of Americans on AI," Thomas said. "That's a very important place for Democrats to be stepping into – boldly." Yes, but: Guardrails faces pushback from some Democrats who warn its strategy, which includes opposing some Democrats, could help elect Republicans less inclined to regulate AI. The bottom line: Trump allies have opened a new front against Anthropic and safety advocates affiliated with the EA movement, but their political giving — as well as the insistence of AI insiders — shows that the political clout of pro-safety AI advocacy is set to grow.

28128ddd0c69.text:
Kristin Martinelli began her workday at 7:30 a.m. on a recent Monday, completing an online Medicaid recertification form for a client in a nursing home in Austin, Texas.
Next, she drove to meet an 85-year-old and her daughter, who had come in from out of town. The older woman had “pretty advanced dementia” and was scheduled to move into the secure memory care unit of a senior living facility that day, said Martinelli, who works as an aging life care manager with Mir Care Consultants in Central Texas. The three of them had a 9 a.m. meeting with the primary care doctor who would complete the paperwork for the move.
At the meeting, Martinelli explained the situation, and the doctor said he’d fill in the patient’s forms that afternoon. But later in the day, she got a call from a colleague saying that the doctor wouldn’t be able to complete the forms that day after all. That created a scramble because the woman wasn’t safe alone in her house. Martinelli ended up calling a home care agency she trusted. “I begged them to provide me with a caregiver in the next four hours,” she said.
If a combination of appointments, bureaucracy, vigilance, and worry about a vulnerable older person — often interspersed with medical emergencies — sounds familiar, it might help to know about a service its providers ruefully call the best-kept secret in eldercare.
Independent certified professionals like Martinelli used to be known as geriatric care managers. That’s what I called the people who helped my 88-year-old father make the 125-mile move from his apartment to a continuing care community near me, and later helped my disabled sister transition from her home to an assisted living facility.
I also used words like “godsend” and “indispensable.” After the moves, the care managers kept tabs on both my father and sister monthly and eased my fears that something urgent might strike the moment I left on a vacation or a work trip.
About a decade ago, these experts rebranded themselves as aging life care managers. It usually takes a couple of years to become one. Most enter the profession as nurses or social workers; some are physical or occupational therapists or gerontologists. They must attain a required combination of advanced education and supervised experience before they can take the certification exam.
The Aging Life Care Association, the nonprofit that represents these professionals, was founded in the 1980s and has grown to more than 2,000 members, but care managers still have a persistent public awareness problem.
“When we talk to someone, they say, ‘I wish I could have called you six months ago, but I didn’t know you existed,’” said Susy Elder Murphy, who owns Aging Well Eldercare, a large practice serving Washington, D.C., and its Maryland suburbs.
The caller is typically an adult child, the Aging Life Care Association has reported. Martinelli described a common scenario: “Mom is in the hospital, or the children went to visit and hadn’t realized she was so sick. They’re in a crisis.”
Enter the aging life care manager. What distinguishes her (it is usually a woman) from people with confusingly similar names — senior care advisers, patient advocates, care navigators — is her independence.
Aging life care managers work for the client and the family paying them, not for hospitals or insurance companies. Moreover, the association’s extensive code of ethics specifically prohibits “accepting or giving referral fees, fee splitting, kickbacks or other similar arrangements in exchange for client referrals.”
Contrast that with companies that promise free advice on senior living, like A Place for Mom. Care facilities pay A Place for Mom fees for steering new residents their way, as the organization discloses on its website. Advisers for companies that receive fees may be unlikely to recommend places that don’t pay, or to recommend home care, unless the company also contracts with local agencies.
“They’re really marketers, salespeople,” Julie Wagner, chief executive of the Aging Life Care Association, said about the referral companies. Some companies are more transparent than others about these financial incentives.
“If you want to buy a car and you go to the Ford dealer, they will not say, ‘I really see you in a Subaru,’” Murphy said. “You should be talking to someone who’s objective, neutral, and experienced.”
Care managers don’t come cheap. Wagner said association members’ hourly rates range from $150 to $350, with big geographic variations. In Texas, Mir’s standard rate is $185 an hour, billed in 15-minute increments. In Washington, Murphy’s practice charges $210 an hour. Sometimes families share the cost, as my sister and I did. And in some cities, social service agencies provide these specialists on a sliding scale.
Aging life care managers serve as coordinators, not hands-on caregivers, and the range of services they provide is quite broad.
They can, for example: Arrange and oversee a move to or within a senior living facility. Deal with insurers, including Medicare and Medicaid. Drive a client to the dentist. Recommend not only local residential communities and home care agencies but elder law lawyers, medical specialists, therapists, senior move managers, and hospice organizations. Visit weekly or monthly to see that everything is going smoothly. Alert family members if it isn’t.
“A part of our job is mediating between family members, acting as a sounding board,” Martinelli said.

California’s Billionaire Tax Promises Healthcare Relief. The Fine Print Is Murkier.
The pitch behind California’s billionaire tax proposal is simple: Tax the richest residents in the nation’s wealthiest state to offset steep federal cuts to healthcare, food assistance, and education.
But if approved by voters in November, it’s unclear how much money the ballot initiative would raise, how quickly the funding would become available, and how lawmakers would spend it.
The measure would steer proceeds from a first-in-the-nation wealth tax to a state healthcare fund, giving the governor and lawmakers the power to decide how to spend what California’s nonpartisan legislative analyst estimated would be “tens of billions of dollars.” Backers say it could raise up to $100 billion over five years to keep hospitals and emergency rooms open and preserve insurance coverage for millions of Californians. Yet, community health centers, doctors, and other healthcare entities that might benefit from such a cash infusion argue that the union spearheading the measure has readied a blank check for politicians.
“I’m not sure that you can say, with full security, that this will stop clinics from being closed or healthcare workers from being laid off, or people from losing their healthcare,” said Chris Hoene, executive director of the California Budget & Policy Center, a left-leaning nonprofit.
California’s billionaire tax promises healthcare relief. The fine print is murkier.
Taxing the Ultrarich
Put on the ballot by one of California’s largest healthcare unions, Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on roughly 200 Californians with a net worth of at least $1 billion, including most of their stock holdings, yachts, and artwork. It would apply to those who were residents of California on Jan. 1, 2026. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts would generally be exempt.
The revenue raised is intended to offset the roughly $30 billion a year in anticipated losses to the Golden State from congressional Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Over the next four years, state and federal funding cuts are projected to nearly double California’s uninsured population, which stands at about 2.4 million people, according to the University of California-Berkeley Labor Center.
Securing additional tax revenue is essential because state lawmakers have yet to come up with a way to pay for healthcare services that will be affected by the cuts, said Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which represents hospital workers and got the wealth tax on the ballot. It would earmark 90% of the tax revenue for healthcare, while the remaining 10% would be split between food assistance and education at lawmakers’ discretion. Regan said such broad categories would give politicians flexibility to be more responsive to the looming cuts.
“Figuring out or predicting exactly what the fallout will be, of where reductions and cuts get made, in a complicated healthcare system, it’s just too difficult to predict,” Regan said.
Among the choices the next governor and lawmakers will face are whether to provide healthcare to people cut off by the new federal Medicaid work requirements, reverse state rollbacks limiting coverage for immigrants with legal status, or raise the low physician reimbursement rates that make some providers reluctant to accept patients enrolled in Medi-Cal, the state’s version of Medicaid.
Lawmakers could also shore up subsidies on Covered California, the state’s health insurance marketplace, whose enrollees have seen their premiums skyrocket after losing millions in federal assistance after Congress last year let enhanced subsides expire.
Most of the money must be spent on health, but healthcare experts said the measure’s ambiguous language could allow lawmakers to use the new billionaire health fund to replace existing state dollars, contrary to the text of the proposition.
“A lot of times these propositions are written in a way to get attention and get support,” said Glenn Melnick, a healthcare economist at the University of Southern California. “But in fact, they can be used for other things later.”
Instead, the healthcare industry is pushing for a long-term funding plan. René Bravo, a pediatrician in San Luis Obispo County and the president of the California Medical Association, worries that a one-time infusion of tax dollars “is going to run out.”
“We need to work on a more sustainable, durable funding mechanism for the Medi-Cal system,” he said.
At the same time, doctors are asking him what will happen when the biggest Medi-Cal eligibility cuts begin to take effect next year. Even if voters approve the ballot measure, the money wouldn’t be available for at least a few months while the state collects the tax. And billionaires could spread their payments over five years.
Californians Divided
Pasadena resident Lynne Wines, a 72-year-old retired banker, knows the state needs the money. But she worries that wealthy investors will see the measure as a precedent and flee the state. Even though the ballot measure is clear that it’s a one-time tax, Wines said it’s a slippery slope.
“Taxes have a way of being needed over and over, and politicians have a way of finding those needs,” Wines said. “So, I don’t really feel secure that this is just a one-time thing.”
She noted that Google co-founder and billionaire Sergey Brin bought a home in Nevada and moved some of his businesses to the Silver State late last year. He is backing ad campaigns opposing the measure. Brin has given more than $100 million to a nonprofit promoting two competing measures, Propositions 41 and 42, designed to blunt or block it, according to contributions filed with the secretary of state’s office. This story is part of an investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project. Read the other stories here.
In January 1966, a South African ship caught fire at sea. In port in Bristol, England, after firefighters pried open the smoking container, the conflagration spread and burned for five days. A little over a month later, a Liberian steamship caught fire near Rotterdam, ignited a storage area with barrels of petrol and sank. The month after that, a Danish ship caught fire off Long Beach, California, injuring three firefighters, killing a longshoreman and causing over a million dollars in estimated damages.
The culprit in each fire was fishmeal, a dark yellow powder made by drying and pulverizing fish that, if left untreated, is known for spontaneously combusting as it decays and oxidizes.
Tied to at least 90 ship and plant fires from the 1950s through the 1970s, fishmeal’s combustibility was a serious worry for seafarers, insurers and dock workers, according to a sweep of historical news coverage by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization in Washington, D.C.
In 1967, American feed producer Cargill announced a solution: ethoxyquin.
A fire retardant previously used to keep rubber tires from drying out and applied as a preservative on fruits and alfalfa, production of the antioxidant was soon ramped up.
“Antioxidant treatment has made bulk handling an easy matter,” the director of the Canadian Department of Fisheries told an industry publication in 1966, arguing it should be required for fishmeal shipments.
The chemical was highly effective. By the 1970s, press-reported fires dropped sharply—from a typical 16 ship fires a year, according to the Liverpool Underwriters Association, to five.
By 1976, the U.S. Coast Guard imposed mandatory ethoxyquin treatment on fishmeal shipments, and three years later, the United Nations body that oversees maritime activity recommended fishmeal be treated with it “to prevent spontaneous combustion.”
But there was a problem: Ethoxyquin is a carcinogen.
“Toxic effects had been observed in laboratory animals fed high concentrations of ethoxyquin,” said a 1969 paper by U.N. food and agriculture authorities.
As its use in animal feeds and aquaculture grew, a 1987 study by British researchers found the chemical “caused severe damage” and had a potentially “carcinogenic effect” in rats. In 2015, the European Food Safety Authority said an impurity within ethoxyquin, known as p-phenetidine, was capable of causing mutations in genetic material.
There is a lack of scientific consensus on whether it is safe to eat farmed seafood raised on feed treated with ethoxyquin, but some countries have considered the risk to be high enough to justify banning or limiting the use of the chemical. In 2017, the European Commission suspended authorization for its use in animal feed across the European Union.
Today, ethoxyquin has been banned in the U.K. and by members of the European Economic Area, including Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein. But ethoxyquin, within limits, is still permitted in animal feed in Australia, Japan, South Korea and the U.S.
With more than half of the seafood eaten worldwide now coming from fish farms, and with the majority of such species fed fishmeal and fish oil, studying the chemicals added to feed is critical for understanding the possible contamination of our global food supply.
Although ethoxyquin is not banned in the U.S., it has been at the center of a half-dozen lawsuits, typically involving claims of false advertising. Some lawsuits targeted seafood companies for marketing their products as “sustainable” even though they contained ethoxyquin, while others
highlighted the potential risks that the additive poses to the environment.
In 2022, a New York resident brought a class-action lawsuit against Aldi Inc., a German supermarket chain with stores in the U.S., alleging its Atlantic salmon products were falsely labeled as “sustainable” due to “environmentally destructive” practices. The complaint cited the EU’s ban on the chemical and a study linking ethoxyquin to mortality and deformations in fish and crustaceans, noting the chemical “poses a risk for aquatic life.” The case was settled out of court.
The same year, a New York and a California resident jointly sued Gorton’s Inc., a seafood company, for labeling its frozen tilapia as “sustainably sourced” despite containing ethoxyquin. This lawsuit also cited the “risk for aquatic life” and the European Union’s ban, and was settled out of court.
In Canada, the country’s Food Inspection Agency requires feeds containing ethoxyquin to carry a label declaring that it meets the legal limits, but the agency does not specify how it tests for the chemical in feeds. Inspectors also do not check whether ethoxyquin ends up in the seafood itself, according to the agency’s latest food inspection report from 2022.
And a 2024 audit of the Canadian agency by the EU found it completed only about 40 percent of its planned inspections, citing “systematic and significant under-delivery” in terms of testing seafood products.
Cargill said in a statement that it has assessed alternative antioxidants since 2005 and no longer uses ethoxyquin in its global salmon feed business or in any market where ethoxyquin is not authorized for use in aquafeed. The company also noted that it did not develop ethoxyquin. Globally, producers and feed makers have also increasingly shifted to alternatives, including natural additives such as rosemary extract and vitamin E compounds.
“More and more destinations are not accepting ethoxyquin, starting with our local Peruvian market,” said James Frank, managing director of the Peruvian fishmeal company MSICeres, during a 2022 webinar. He added that 100 percent of Peru’s fishmeal exports to Europe, Canada, the U.S. and Australia are now ethoxyquin-free, a shift also seen among companies in the U.K. and Norway.

42a741cd61db.text: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) delivered another debate performance tailor-made for social media Tuesday night, feeding the presidential speculation he insists is entirely misplaced. Why it matters: A darling of the Democratic internet and a favorite to win the party's nomination in 2028, Ossoff emphatically ruled out a White House bid and pledged to serve a full six-year Senate term if re-elected. "He is running. He's going to be your DSA candidate," Republican challenger Rep. Mike Collins countered, seeking to paint Ossoff as a socialist with ambitions beyond Georgia. The big picture: Georgia was one of three battleground states hosting Senate debates Tuesday night, with candidates in Iowa and Maine also clashing over President Trump's foreign policy, the cost of living and their records in Washington. In Georgia, Ossoff and Collins traded vicious personal attacks throughout their second and final debate, reprising a feud that has become a viral spectacle online. "Will you commit tonight that for the remainder of this campaign — it's just three weeks, Mike — you won't allow any more neo-Nazi propaganda to be produced from your house?" Ossoff demanded , referring to Collins' son-in-law, an alleged white nationalist influencer. Collins accused Ossoff of inciting threats against his family, then attacked him over campaign support from billionaire Reid Hoffman, who had ties to Jeffrey Epstein. "Mike, you really want to bring up the Epstein files?" Ossoff shot back , pointing to Collins' initial vote against releasing the documents — a position he reversed after Trump changed course. In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins cast her independence from Trump as a political asset, arguing that her willingness to challenge the president — and work with him when necessary — has delivered for her state. Collins cited her nine votes to end the Iran war, opposition to Trump's Big Beautiful Bill and roughly $1.5 billion in federal funding secured for Maine projects. Democratic challenger Troy Jackson argued that Collins has spent years helping Trump advance policies that hurt Maine, only to express "concern" and claim credit for mitigating the damage. In his closing statement , Jackson invoked a fatal ICE shooting in Maine to accuse Collins of enabling Trump's immigration crackdown: "Sen. Collins paid for the bullets at Donald Trump's command. Now she wants credit for not pulling the trigger." In Iowa, GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democratic challenger Josh Turek squared off in a race that has Republicans on edge , as Trump's tariffs and soaring farm costs threaten their grip on a state he carried by 13 points. Hinson broke with Trump over his deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel , saying she believed there were ways to lower fuel prices without empowering Vladimir Putin and his war in Ukraine. Turek accused Hinson of helping drive Iowa toward a "second farm crisis" through her support for Trump's tariffs and votes against congressional efforts to end the Iran war. Hinson said the war should end "as quickly as possible" but rejected another congressional resolution, arguing Trump and the military could bring the conflict to a close themselves.

11cb4cc98038.text: By — Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/new-york-plans-to-ban-central-parks-horse-drawn-carriages-after-teens-death Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter New York plans to ban Central Park's horse-drawn carriages after teen's death Nation Oct 14, 2026 2:18 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — New York City lawmakers plan to ban horse-drawn carriages from Central Park, ending their more than 150-year run as an iconic, old-timey tourist attraction, following decades of opposition from animal welfare activists and the death of a teenage tourist last spring. The City Council is expected to approve a bill next week that would end the rides by 2028. Three consecutive mayors had called for an end to the carriage rides because of safety concerns, only to have lawmakers yank back the reins. A spokesperson for Julie Menin, the council speaker, confirmed the incoming vote and said the proposal had enough support to pass. Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office said he had reached a deal with the speaker on the legislation. "The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City," Mamdani said in a social media post. Teen's death reignited debate over carriage rides The latest push for a ban started in June, when 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, visiting the city from India, died after jumping from a runaway horse carriage during a ride with family members. His death, which appeared to be the first fatality in a horse carriage accident since they were introduced in Central Park, reignited the debate over whether carriages, a romantic throwback to the city's past, have a place in a modern metropolis. Mahajan's family has appeared at City Hall, in person and through videoconference calls from India, begging the city to finally end the rides. "We are shattered, our whole family shattered. The pain does not go away," his father, Deepak Mahajan, told city council members via a videocall during a hearing for the bill last summer, saying his son leapt from the carriage to try and help his mother, who was flung from her seat, after the horse bolted. "Every morning we wake up and think of nothing but the loss of our son." For decades, animal welfare activists and other critics have decried the carriage industry, arguing horses shouldn't be hauling tourists around busy streets and Central Park while having to navigate bustling traffic and gawking passersby. In the past, horses have collapsed, gotten startled and run off, hitting cars or other objects, with each accident resulting in fresh calls for a ban. READ MORE: How horses whinny has long eluded scientists. A new study reveals the answer "The tragic and preventable death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan made clear that the status quo is no longer acceptable. Horse-drawn carriages have long been part of New York City's history, but in an increasingly busy Central Park, this tradition has become a growing public safety liability," Menin said in a statement. The industry and its supporters have long cast the rides as a way for visitors to experience the New York they know from classic movies and television. Fred Astaire and Cyd Charisse danced into one of the carriages in "The Band Wagon." Robert Redford and Jane Fonda rode one in "Barefoot in the Park." Macaulay Culkin escaped bandits in a carriage in "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York." "Taking a horse and carriage ride in New York City is one of the most iconic things to do in New York City and people from all over the world know about us and travel to New York to go to a carriage ride in New York," Conor McHugh, a longtime carriage driver, told the Council earlier this year. Mayors have faced pushback in efforts to ban rides Efforts to close down the industry have been met with pushback from unions and influential supporters, often resulting in tiresome political fights that have seen mayors throw up their hands over nagging worries about putting carriage drivers out of work and what to do with the horses if they can no longer work. Transport Workers Union International President John Samuelsen said the Council's bill has "no meaningful economic relief for workers" and that Menin "used the tragic death of a tourist to contrive a public safety crisis." "This is disgraceful political opportunism, and Zohran should not simply go along with it, particularly when immigrant families' livelihoods are being destroyed. This entire situation is reprehensible," he said in a statement. The proposal as written would require the mayor's office to develop a workforce transition plan for drivers, and includes a measure that would allow the city to consider some kind of compensation for industry workers. Carriage owners could not sell their horses off for slaughter, according to the bill's language, which requires that horses be disposed of in a "humane manner." "I think we have a civic responsibility to ensure that we are not leaving anybody out to dry," Mamdani told reporters Wednesday. The mayor's predecessor, Eric Adams, called for ending the industry during the waning days of his administration, but the proposal went nowhere. The mayor before that, Bill de Blasio, had pledged to eliminate the rides on day one of his administration but abandoned the crusade after heavy opposition from unions and a media blitz involving actor Liam Neeson. Over the years, the city has placed various safety regulations around the industry, including a requirement that the horses get at least five weeks of vacation a year outside of city limits with daily access to a pasture. The horses are inspected by a veterinarian twice a year, and the maximum age they can work at is 26, according to city regulations. And they don't work when it is hotter than 89 degrees.
