âThe Youngstown area, for decades, used to vote Democrat,â the Republican senator said. âAnd then you ran for office in 2016, and flipped it red forever.â
For a decade after that, Youngstown has become the first stop on what media critics derided as âTrump voter safaris,â journeys into the working-class counties that never voted Republican until he showed up. Hustedâs claim of a permanently red state, however, isnât adding up for Democrats: As soon as I arrived this week, they insisted that MAGAâs advance was over.
This isnât because Democrats have snapped back to the image and values they ran on in the 1970s, when they had a lock on this state. No, the party insists that Republicans are in charge, making voters angry with their handling of the economy and the Middle East, so the culture-war politicking that worked for a decade wonât be as potent in November.
âPeople arenât buying that again because theyâve realized you canât deposit culture war into your bank account,â said Chris Anderson, the chairman of the Mahoning County Democrats, whoâd spent years trying to limit their losses and defections. âYou canât fill your gas tank with it.â
Campaigns have a queasy rhythm to them â hype followed by panic followed by hype. Weâve reached the time in the cycle where the party that built a post-Labor Day polling lead begins to question its own confidence.
âTheyâre undersampling Republicans,â Speaker Mike Johnson told the faithful in South Texas on Tuesday, a part of that state that seemed to be following the same rightward march as northeast Ohio â and before that, Appalachia.
Republicans around Youngstown expected the trend of underestimating their vote to hold this year, but not accelerate. They agreed that Democrats would at least be competitive. Rep. Michael Rulli, who represents the Mahoning Valley in Congress, said that the GOP got an opening when âClinton came in and lied about NAFTA,â which made local Democrats thrash around in search of a populist alternative.
âWhen Trump came around, the people just took to it, and so theyâre giving us a shot,â Rulli added. âThis area will not always stay Republican or Democrat.â
This yearâs Democrats are making hard plays for northeast Ohio, at least to trim the GOP margins. Former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost the five most Democratic counties east of Cleveland for the first time in 2024, has painted Husted as a âBig Techâ shill, captured by the next industry thatâll threaten working-class jobs. Amy Acton, the partyâs gubernatorial nominee, takes every chance to talk about her Youngstown roots; her ads often portray Vivek Ramaswamy, the billionaire GOP nominee, playing tennis as he daydreams about cutting Medicare and Social Security.
âI know what itâs like to not have the heat on, or live in a tent in the winter and experience a lot of neglect and abuse,â Acton told me on Tuesday, when I asked her to respond to the president rallying in Youngstown â specifically, about him telling voters theyâd get rebate checks and energy bill relief only if Republicans won. âAnd I can also tell you that I wouldnât be here today if it wasnât for the institutions that gave me a chance.â
A Democratic comeback in Ohio is unlikely to look like the winning maps of Barack Obamaâs campaigns, much less Bill Clintonâs. While losing to Bernie Moreno two years ago, Brown ran stronger in the suburbs of Cleveland and Cincinnati than he had in elections he actually won.
On Monday, the standard Trump rally scene of MAGA-hatted voters in line and liberals yelling at them from free speech zones showed how the coalitions had changed. The protesters skewed older; the younger they were, the more profanity they were comfortable putting on cardboard. A âprogress prideâ flag was hoisted on a pole, right under an American flag. Any Trump fan who objected got an earful about the âpedophile presidentâ they were lined up for.
Trump, at this point, was not the rebel candidate who first showed up in Youngstown 10 years ago, with rally speeches about the threat of mass Muslim immigration. He was the party leader every Republican wanted to borrow some aura from, by communing with his superfans.
Ramaswamy posed for selfies a few steps away from MAGA activist Vince Fusca. Blake Marnell, who wears a brick-patterned suit to every Trump rally, got a seat near the main stage. Both men were at the 2024 Trump rally in Butler, Pa., where a failed assassinâs bullet clipped his ear; neither needed convincing that he was saving eastern Ohio, where they didnât live, from neoliberalism.
The Covelli Centre, where Trump had rallied before, was a bit more than half-full when the president got onstage. Like Democrats used to, he described all the investments he was bringing to the region. Submarine construction was coming to Cleveland; nearby Warren was getting a new ââKimberly-Clark plant; he would figure out how to save the local heating utility company.
The applause thinned out when he talked about how heâd rebranded artificial intelligence as âSuper Intelligence.â

c30752f1cb06.text: By — Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press By — Samya Kullab, Associated Press Samya Kullab, Associated Press By — Barry Hatton, Associated Press Barry Hatton, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/sudden-starlink-limits-sap-ukraine-drone-power-as-kyiv-fears-u-s-intelligence-squeeze Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Sudden Starlink limits sap Ukraine drone power as Kyiv fears U.S. intelligence squeeze World Oct 14, 2026 12:09 PM EDT KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukrainian drones lost some of their fighting capacity after restrictions were suddenly imposed on the battlefield use of the country's U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals, officials said Wednesday as the capital endured another night of missile attacks. At the same time, Ukraine did not receive the usual advance warning from its Western partners of the devastating Russian ballistic missiles that have struck Kyiv for two consecutive nights, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, triggering fears that Ukraine is being starved of vital intelligence, especially from the U.S. READ MORE: Trump's diesel deal with Putin draws bipartisan criticism from a frustrated Congress Zelenskyy did not specify which partners he was talking about when referring to the lack of warning. U.S. President Donald Trump has said the U.S. has not stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine. The developments frustrated the Ukrainian military and deepened fears that Kyiv's relationship with Washington is unraveling. Ukrainian officials fear U.S. support for the war effort is falling away after Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and isolate Putin. READ MORE: Ukraine had no intelligence from partners about missiles headed to Kyiv, Zelenskyy says Trump said Saturday that it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end his country's war with Russia and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S. Trump's efforts to stop the fighting have resulted in no progress. Starlink is an essential tool for Ukraine Ukrainian officials are concerned that U.S. support, especially related to the sharing of military intelligence and the use of American tech titan Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications system, may be in jeopardy. Musk's SpaceX overnight imposed a speed limit on Ukraine's Starlink terminals mounted on drones, Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy, said on social media. The restriction disrupted operations, including making the slower-flying attack drones easier targets for Russian defenses. READ MORE: Zelenskyy gives Ukraine's Order of Freedom award to Musk for Starlink's role in war effort Starlink is a vital tool for the Ukrainian military, both in offensive and defensive operations. The network is used for long-range drone missions, interceptor air defense systems and front-line logistics, Beskrestnov said. "Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation," Beskrestnov said, without elaborating. Neither SpaceX nor the White House offered any immediate comment. Kyiv got no warning about initial ballistic missile attack, official says Yurii Ihnat, Ukraine's air force spokesman, said there was no warning of an initial Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday night, although Kyiv was warned about three later waves of missiles. A lawmaker on Ukraine's parliamentary Defense Committee told The Associated Press that intelligence sharing with international partners has not stopped. The lawmaker spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to give statements to the press. READ MORE: Kremlin relishes in U.S.-Russia diesel deal and Trump's criticism of Zelenskyy Five people were killed and 36 injured in a Russian attack on the Ukrainian capital that lasted from Tuesday evening into Wednesday morning, Kyiv police said. Russia keeps bombing Ukraine's power grid despite Trump's truce demand Zelenskyy voiced outrage Wednesday over Russia's continuing aerial bombardment of Ukraine's energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump's demand for a ceasefire. "We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not turn a blind eye to reality to respond — and to respond forcefully" to Russia's ongoing aerial barrages, Zelenskyy said in a social media post Wednesday. "Russia has squandered the opportunity for de-escalation and has clearly chosen to continue its insane war of annihilation," he said. Moscow's forces pounded Ukraine's power grid, as well as oil and gas facilities, for the third straight night, Zelenskyy said, after Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine had agreed not to strike energy infrastructure 4 ½ years after Moscow's forces invaded. Zelenskyy, meanwhile, has agreed to halt Ukraine's monthslong campaign targeting Russian oil refineries that caused fuel shortages for Russians. Ukraine's last reported hit on an oil refinery was Friday. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday that details of the energy ceasefire are still being decided. "The work in that direction is continuing," he told reporters. Russia hits three Kyiv power plants in attack, causing outages The Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement Wednesday that its forces attacked Ukraine's energy infrastructure in Kyiv, the wider Kyiv region and the northeastern Kharkiv region overnight, striking a total of six power plants. Russian forces hit all three of Kyiv's combined heat and power plants overnight into Wednesday, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said. At least 600,000 people were left without power, Zelenskyy said. Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region and Kharkiv overnight, Zelenskyy said. Ukraine claims it is pushing Russia back on the battlefield Ukrainia

A new study in the journal Seismica presents the first comprehensive seismic analysis of what happened during the disastrous flood in Nepal on Aug. 26. But exactly what triggered the mountainside to give way remains unclear.
A massive section of a Himalayan mountainside collapsed near the Nepal-China border, sending millions of cubic meters of rock and ice crashing downhill. The collapse unleashed a devastating flash flood that tore through valleys and communities along Nepal’s Trishuli River. At least 1,455 people were reported dead, and 5,285 remained missing as of Oct.7, according to the Associated Press.
Since this main event, at least two major flooding episodes have happened in the same broader river system, including one on Monday.
To reconstruct the August disaster, the researchers precisely timed the initial mountain collapse. Using data from seismic stations in Nepal and China, they placed the start of the main mass movement at 8:37 a.m., Nepal time.
USGS initially reported a magnitude 4.4 earthquake before realizing it was coming from the landslide itself. Then, Nepalese researchers looked at their records and also reanalyzed the signal, which did not resemble an ordinary earthquake.
“We tried to see the signals, and we didn’t find any earthquake signals,” said Lok Bijaya, chief of the National Earthquake Monitoring and Research Centre in Nepal, and one of the authors of the study.
They found a small magnitude-2.5 seismic event that occurred only about 17 minutes before the catastrophic collapse, less than 10 kilometers away. Although it could have contributed to the slide, “we are not sure the magnitude of 2.5 is enough for this kind of mass failure. It is not clear yet,” said Shiba Subedi, a geophysicist at the Nepal Academy of Science and Technology in Kathmandu, Nepal, and another author of the study.
The researchers detected more than 60 smaller seismic events in the area during the preceding two weeks, including several others in the hours immediately before the collapse.
But “seismic activity doesn’t mean it’s earthquakes,” Bijaya explained. They suggest that at least some of these seismic events may instead have been near-surface “slide-quakes” associated with gravitational movement of the mountainside. In other words, some of those signals could potentially have been the mountain destabilizing before it failed.
But it’s hard to tell how much they contributed to the main event. “Other people are now analyzing and having a closer look,” said György Hetényi, professor of geophysics at the University of Lausanne in Switzerland and another one of the authors. “Given that they’re all clustered in this area, it’s hard to believe it’s not a precursor,” he said.
The collapse itself was so enormous that seismometers around the world detected it. The authors say the seismic amplitudes were actually larger than those from the 2025 Tracy Arm landslide in Alaska.
“The size [of what collapsed] was almost 1.5 kilometers long,” said Bijaya. “It was situated at 5,200 meters, and that mass just dropped down, maybe just slid for 30 seconds, and then dropped down more than a kilometer.” The glacier and rocks sliding created a crater, which now resembles a lake.
Climate change could be part of the story, but it’s likely not the only factor. Changes in ice and glacier movement can alter stresses in the underlying rock and may have contributed to the slope’s instability, Hetényi said.

“Given the amount of rock that has fallen, I think this phenomenon would have happened anyway. Maybe next year if there’s no climate change, or maybe last year, if climate change was more important. But the fall of rock at this volume cannot be only climate change,” he said.
Reconstructing the disaster also exposed another vulnerability in the Himalaya: scientists across the region do not routinely share seismic data.
The lack of available data is a serious issue, the authors said. “It’s creating a very big uncertainty—issues for early warning systems and for locating these kinds of events,” said Bijaya.
For this paper, the team negotiated with Chinese teams and got data they needed the next day. “It was very surprising to me that the Nepalese organized some exchange with the Chinese. That’s great. Usually, it’s not so easy,” said Hetényi.
“That was the first motivation for us, for this paper,” said Bijaya.
India, China and Nepal do not have any protocols to share their data. Because much of the Himalaya is remote and difficult to access, any monitoring is valuable. According to Hetényi, this needs to change.
“I hope this major event will change the view of the politicians, and that they will commit to regional data exchange for monitoring,” he said. “It doesn’t have to be open to the whole wide world.”
Researchers say sharing data would help improve early-warning systems, but the monitoring systems themselves also need to be upgraded.
“If I had plenty of power and money, I would put in water-level measurements, water gauges,” said Hetényi. “I would also use remote sensing, so a satellite-based monitoring system, and I would also use infrasound, which is basically vibration through the air at a lower frequency than we can hear, but that propagates fast enough to give alerts,” said Hetényi.
Subedi said the scientific community must be prepared. “We can have this kind of event many, many times in the future,” he said. “So we have to invest in different kinds of warning mechanisms.”

Kathryn Vaughn returned to work at a rural West Tennessee elementary school this autumn with a lot more stress on her plate than in previous years.
The 46-year-old, like many Americans, is juggling how to provide for her family with rising costs of, as she described it, "everything".
She spends her days working three different jobs to support her family of four, including as a primary school art teacher, as US inflation continues to rise.
Inflation in September was above forecasts.
Over the past 12 months, prices rose by 3.7% - up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August, according to officials numbers released on Wednesday.
High energy prices have driven up the cost of living in America as diesel prices have hit record highs and the price of gasoline has risen too, and all of this has landed on the shoulders of everyday Americans.
Once school finishes, Vaughn heads to her second job as a facilitator at an after-school programme for at-risk youth. Her five-year-old son can join too, reducing the need and cost of after-school care for Vaughn's family.
"I have done some incredibly unhinged things to survive," she said. "I hand-modeled for a local jewelry store, I sell everything that sits longer than ten minutes at my house on Facebook swap sites, I resell clothes on ThredUp and Poshmark."
Vaughn even writes obituaries for people who have died to make extra money.
And it is still not enough to support her family.
Punal Bhavsar thought 2026 was going to be the year he saved enough money to purchase a home.
"I was thinking the interest rates would decrease and then I'd be able to purchase a house, but I don't think that's likely now," he said.
The 39-year-old said the rise in the cost of goods has made saving money difficult.
And the biggest burden for Bhavsar has become the price of gasoline.
"I drive a car that takes premium gas, and unfortunately, in California and the area that I live in, it's almost $6 (Â£4.5)," he said.
Come November, when midterm elections happen and the economic tumult is bound to be on voters' minds, Bhavsar said he may become a single-issue voter: "For me, it's just like gas prices have got to be under control."
He described the current economic outlook as bleak, and the numbers back him up.
The Gallup Economic Confidence Index summarizes Americans' assessments of current economic conditions and economic outlook and puts them on a scale of -100 to +100. In September, Americans put that number at -40.
A summer survey from the Guardian showed a staggering 95% of respondents think the US is in an affordability crisis.
This fall, across the US, people are finding ways to cope with that.
When Caitlin Green first moved to Utah seven years ago, her mom moved her into her new home and left her with some wisdom: "If you ever need a cheap, easy meal, always get ground beef."
As prices have increased, Green has struggled to follow that guidance. She remembers paying $2 a pound for ground beef; now she is paying $8, she said.
Instead, Green and her husband sometimes choose alternatives, opting for ground turkey or ground chicken.
"[Ground beef] is almost ...not a luxury like steak... but it's just to the point where it's become a luxury; we have to think about it if we're going to purchase it," she said.
Green and her husband have gone from spending some $200 a month on groceries to $400 a month.
"I understand inflation is a thing, but I just feel like in my lifetime, I've never seen inflation hit so quickly and so drastically."
For Vaughn, the Tennessee school teacher, the difficult choices keep coming.
She was gobsmacked as her children returned to school, at the $130 bill she faced for her five-year-old son's school supplies.
Vaughn made the call to have her son purchase lunch at school each day, rather than take homemade lunches, as the cost of groceries continues to rise and she calculated it would be a cheaper choice.
The family has even made the call to forgo a trip to Florida this autumn to see Vaughn's parents because the price of gasoline is too much.
"It's rough out here," she says. "The cost of everything is insane. Gas to get to work, my insurance costs have gone up, feeding two children and a husband. It's a lot."

A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".
As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings.
But, here's we do know so far.
Help from a chatbot
The engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).
Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.
Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".
The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.
Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.
The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.
Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.
But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.
Hiding in plain toilet paper
On 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper.
A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.
The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.
When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.
In a post on X, external, OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".
It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."
Who is Abdulrahman Alfozan?
Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.
He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.
Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream.
"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."
Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt."
On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.
The FBI investigation is ongoing.
If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (Â£190,000) fine.

A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporean authorities.
All 21 crew members of GFS Pride were evacuated and no injuries were reported after the attack on Tuesday, which caused damage and a fire, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said.
Another Singapore-flagged container vessel, GFS Giselle, sustained hull damage after being hit by a projectile on Wednesday but was able to reach a safe anchorage with all 22 crew, it added.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship hit naval mines and sank while passing through what they called an "unauthorised" route in the Strait of Hormuz.
The Guards released photos that appeared to show a plume of black smoke rising from a container vessel that was still afloat but down by the stern. In other photos, dozens of containers and their contents could be seen floating in the water.
The Hydrographer of Pakistan warned mariners that GFS Pride had sunk 4 nautical miles (7.4km) north-west of Ras al-Sheikh Masud in Oman's Musandam Peninsula.
Meanwhile, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said that two unnamed container ships had reported being struck by unknown projectiles while transiting the Strait of Hormuz between 16:40 and 17:00 GMT on Tuesday.
Both vessels sustained minor damage and were able to continue their passages, it added.
Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the Strait of Hormuz - which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea - and elsewhere in the Middle East since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.
At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 106 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization.
The Malta-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige, which was attacked near Oman on 4 March, is the only other vessel reported to have sunk in that time.
However, maritime risk management group Vanguard said on Wednesday that the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao was reported to be sinking after an unsuccessful rescue attempt, according to Reuters news agency.
One seafarer was killed when the Cape Dao's bridge and accommodation area were hit by an unknown projectile as it transited through the Strait of Hormuz, north-east of Khasab, Oman, on 23 September.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
Last month, crude exports through the waterway rose to around 80% of pre-war levels of 16 million barrels per day (bpd) on average, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler, despite an increase in attacks on shipping.

80695e99fe10.text: By — Hallie Golden, Associated Press Hallie Golden, Associated Press By — Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/judge-extends-order-blocking-trump-from-banning-cnn-ms-now-and-politico-reporters-from-white-house Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge extends order blocking Trump from banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from White House Politics Oct 14, 2026 11:27 AM EDT A federal judge on Tuesday extended an order blocking President Donald Trump's administration from banning reporters for three news outlets from the White House, a pivotal operational development for the organizations as the extraordinary case — pitting the president against the media that cover him — makes its way through the legal system. In a victory for media organizations at a time when tension between the White House and journalists is high, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that CNN, MS NOW and Politico are likely to succeed in their constitutional free speech and due process claims. WATCH: Press pool declines to cover Trump in protest of his ban on news outlets "Still," he added in his late-night order, "no one should interpret the Court's decision to suggest that President Trump's concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media's reporting are unfounded, or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. But Kelly agreed with the plaintiffs that the national security arguments came after the fact and were unsupported by the administration. The judge also wrote that without a preliminary injunction the outlets "are likely to suffer irreparable harm, and that the balance of the equities and the public interest tip in their favor." WATCH: Trump's attacks on free press echo rhetoric used by autocrats, Jodie Ginsberg says An email to the Justice Department, which is arguing the case on behalf of the administration, was not immediately returned. The White House also did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment. Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the three media organizations, hailed the judge's ruling. "When the President issued his 'ban on the free press,' he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment," Boutrous said in a statement. "The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this 'unconstitutional ban on the free press' for the foreseeable future." Judge says no warning given before banishment Kelly, who was nominated to the bench by Trump, previously ordered the White House to restore the reporters' "hard pass" press credentials while he weighed their claims. With that temporary order expiring Tuesday, the judge issued a preliminary injunction that preserves the status quo indefinitely while the case is pending. Kelly said that, "to put it mildly," the White House didn't give the plaintiffs any warning that they were in danger of losing their hard passes before Trump's Sept. 18 social media post about their bans. The judge also said the impact of the White House ban goes far beyond a single reporter's ability to do their job. "The ban threatens to cut off all Plaintiffs' access to the White House press area—a space open to many of their competitors—thereby restricting their ability to observe happenings there firsthand, immediately report on those activities, and try to engage with government officials," the judge wrote. Hard passes give journalists who regularly cover the White House longer term access to its campus without having to get permission ahead of time. The government asked Kelly to suspend his own decision pending an appeal, but the judge said it didn't justify that request. Kelly said the bans impacted a total of 78 reporters at the three news organizations. Earlier judicial action against White House had been only temporary Trump provided no notice before announcing the bans in a Sept. 18 social media post, which criticized their reporting as "fake news." Kelly temporarily blocked the bans on Sept. 24 at the request of the news outlets, which jointly filed a lawsuit in Washington, D.C. Attorneys for the outlets have described Trump's move as "unprecedented and blatantly unconstitutional" under the First and Fifth amendments. They argued that it's illegal for Trump to punish the journalists because he doesn't like the content of their reporting. "The ban also inflicts an injury on all news media organizations — which now risk a similar fate if they engage in fact-based, independent reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable," plaintiffs' lawyers wrote. Government lawyers argued that access to the White House is a privilege — not a right — and said the president can impose the bans to protect national security and to stem the spread of misinformation. "The White House is the official residence and workplace of the President," Justice Department attorneys wrote. "Presidents have had a relationship with the press since the beginning. They have long decided which journalists should receive privileged access, which has varied substantially from administration to administration." Associated Press reporter Rebecca Boone contributed. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Pope Leo XIV's recovery from surgery to remove a lower lobe of his lung is "progressing as expected", his doctors have said.
The 71-year-old pontiff has started to walk and has "resumed a normal diet" following the roughly 90-minute procedure, the medics said in an update shared by the Vatican.
The Pope was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.
Blood tests and an X-ray early on Wednesday showed his recovery was "proceeding normally", the doctors said, and he has also undergone respiratory physiotherapy.
The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.
"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before spending a "peaceful night" at the hospital.
The pontiff is expected to remain there for about a week as he recovers.
He had announced that he would be admitted for the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.
A Vatican source told news agency AFP that further tests were carried out to see whether the cancer had spread.
The Vatican has stressed that the Pope, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness.
The news has shaken Catholics worldwide, many of whom will have recent memories of Pope Francis's hospital visits.
Pope Leo's predecessor, who died last year, also had part of his lung removed in his youth before suffering a series of respiratory infections later in life.
What is lung adenocarcinoma?
Adenocarcinomas develop in cells that produce mucus and are one of the most common types of lung cancer.
The long-term prognosis depends on a number of things, including the stage of the cancer when identified and the person's overall health. The earlier it is spotted, the better, and treatments have improved over the last few decades.
Some adenocarcinomas are picked up early - before symptoms develop - during routine tests. At later stages, lung cancer can cause a persistent cough, breathlessness, fatigue and weight loss.

Medical implants are getting smaller and smarter. But getting them to talk to each other remains tricky.
Now, researchers have developed a way for tiny implantable devices to send electrical signals through the body’s own tissues. The approach could offer a low-power way for implants to work together, with one detecting a symptom and another delivering treatment, the team reports September 24 in Science.
Currently, getting devices to communicate through tissue comes with trade-offs. Some medical devices, such as insulin pumps linked to glucose monitors, use Bluetooth, which relies on radio signals. Receiving those signals requires power even when a device is only listening, increasing the need for battery power and making devices harder shrink. Radio signals also weaken as they travel through body tissue, limiting how far apart communicating devices can be.
The new network called SWANS, the Smart Wireless Autonomous Networking System, works differently. A wearable external hub or implant generates an electric pulse that produces a small current in the surrounding tissue. Tiny implants can detect those electrical signals while using almost no power when they are only listening. And without large batteries, those implants can be small enough to inject through a syringe.
To demonstrate how the network works, the team attached motion sensors to the front legs of rats. When the animals moved their front legs, the system’s external hub sent signals through their bodies to neurostimulator implants in the sciatic nerves, causing muscles in the back legs to contract.
The synchronized limbs weren’t really the point. The experiment was designed to show that signals could travel through the body, linking different kinds of devices, says Alex Abramson, a biomedical engineer at Georgia Tech in Atlanta. It was “a proof of concept showing that you can really connect this system to anything.”
Abramson says a network of smart implants could automatically deliver a drug or stimulate a neuron exactly when needed to treat complex conditions like Parkinson’s disease. Simple signals can be sent from one implant to another, while an external hub can coordinate more complex networks of sensors and devices, possibly using artificial intelligence.
Before the new network can be used in humans, researchers will need to show that the electrical signals do not cause unintended problems like heart rhythm disruptions. Such issues have not turned up in the experiments in rats yet, but the technology will need to be tested over longer periods of time and in larger animals, Abramson says.
Materials engineer Amir Alavi says the network’s potential could grow as other technologies improve, including wearables, AI systems and miniature, battery-free implantable sensors like those his lab is developing. “There are now several really interesting directions converging,” says Alavi, of at the University of Pittsburgh’s Swanson School of Engineering. “If those pieces eventually come together, you could have implants that are much smaller, simpler, longer-lived, and more connected than what we have today.”

Aaron Dayâs third-party campaign cost Republican Kelly Ayotte her Senate reelection bid in 2016. Now heâs trying to take his spoiler project national.
With several Senate races tight enough for an alternate candidate to make a real difference, whether theyâre Libertarian or another third party, Day is looking to spend as much as $2.5 million â or perhaps less, if his effort works as designed â to cost the GOP the Senate.
Dayâs strategy is simple: Use his Stark Freedom PAC to spend relatively small amounts on online ads made with AI that boost name ID for spoiler candidates, figuring he can do just enough to hand those races to the Democrats.
Republican leaders are highly skeptical of Dayâs efforts, but he sees a real chance at disrupting races across the country. Whatâs more remarkable is how open he is about his goal of ending the Senate Republican majority.
âYou call it a spoiler campaign, I call it holding Republicans accountable,â Day told Semafor in an interview. His website is equally explicit: âWe fund the margin. It costs the GOP the Senate.â
Day is targeting eight states where heâs deduced that boosting third-party candidates would hurt the Republican nominee: Texas, Iowa, New Hampshire, Minnesota, South Carolina, Michigan, Ohio, and Kansas. Itâs a âMoneyballâ theory of modern politics, banking on a relatively small amount of cash to mess up the margins in close contests.
Nudging a third candidateâs vote share up by a couple of percentage points higher, as he explained, takes a lot less money than the obscene amount needed to actually win a race.
âPeople are going to be shocked after the fact at how effective this is,â Day said. âMost voters donât know that the third-party option exists, and a lot of these candidates donât actually have money, and theyâre not allowed to participate in the debates.â
In addition to Ayotteâs 2016 New Hampshire campaign, Libertarian candidatesâ support boosted former Democratic Sen. Jon Tester in his 2006 and 2012 Montana races. The effect was clear in Nevadaâs 2024 Senate race, which Democrats narrowly won as nearly 5 percent of voters picked a candidate outside the two major parties.
And no one can forget Jill Steinâs Green Party spoiler effect on Hillary Clintonâs presidential chances in 2016.
Itâs hard to see how giving Democrats the Senate helps advance Dayâs causes â which include concerns over centralized digital currencies and government surveillance via cryptocurrency legislation. But Day says he wants to check President Donald Trump through âgridlockâ and that with Democrats in charge, the crypto market structure bill and other legislation he dislikes will continue to stall.
Several Republican groups, including the National Republican Senatorial Committee and Senate Leadership Fund, declined comment.
While third-party hopefuls appreciate his support, their goals are different. Ted Brown, the Libertarian candidate in Texas, said heâs running to win, not to cost Republicans Senate control.
âIâm running to defeat the corrupt two-party system,â Brown told Semafor. âBut I would say this, if the Republicans lose the Senate on November 3: The good news is, the Republicans lost control of the Senate. The bad news is, the Democrats won control of the Senate.â
Day said his model would be replicable to punish a Democratic majority in the future as well, by boosting Green Party candidates to eat into their candidatesâ margins: âI actually view this, if it works, as something that can be used to hold both major parties accountable.â
Know More
So, why do this? Day was originally planning to be a candidate himself this fall, even fighting to get ballot access in New Hampshire to take out former Sen. John Sununu, R-N.H.
But he said he didnât run, in part because he was in negotiations with Republicans and the Trump administration over a list of demands that werenât fulfilled: âI was told something definitive was going to happen, and it did not.â He declined to go into further detail; the White House did not comment.
After the schism, he threw his support behind Edmond Laplante, a Constitution Party candidate in New Hampshire. He then decided to âduplicateâ his 2016 bid against Ayotte by boosting anti-war candidates to reach the small percentage of âdisaffected voters in these swing states.â
âPeople do not want to vote for the Republican, but a lot of people still donât want to vote for the Democrat,â Day said. âTexas is in play, Kansas is in play, South Carolina is potentially in play. I mean, who would have ever thought? But itâs true, and this really could make the difference.â
Dayâs ads are unique to each race, but most have peppy AI music critiquing the GOP candidate. They knock Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., for her pro-war votes and boost Libertarian Kasie Whitener; in New Hampshire, they hit Sununu for supporting the Wall Street bailout; in Texas, they whack state attorney general Ken Paxton for being a âmouthpiece for DCâ and dub Brown the âvoice of Texas.â
Republicans are more worried about Dayâs machinations in New Hampshire and donât believe heâll be effective anywhere else.
Burgessâs view
Iâm a skeptic, and so naturally lean a bit bearish on the idea of a national spoiler campaign funded by the political equivalent of spare change. I watched a bunch of Dayâs ads, as well, and found them somewhat tedious but also relentlessly on-message in driving the name ID of these somewhat obscure candidates. (Itâs possible that AI-generated music just isnât for me.)
But Day is onto something with the spoiler effect, whether itâs induced by him or not. Itâs undeniable that disaffected Republicans who cast primary votes for, say, Sen. John Cornyn in Texas or Rep. Ralph Norman in South Carolina may struggle with voting for Paxton and Graham â but not want to support their Democratic counterparts either.

06350c517424.text: By — Ted Anthony, Associated Press Ted Anthony, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/katie-zacharias-debut-shows-the-pitfalls-and-possibilities-of-white-house-press-secretarys-role Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Katie Zacharia's debut shows the pitfalls and possibilities of White House press secretary's role Politics Oct 14, 2026 10:28 AM EDT President Donald Trump's new press secretary stepped to the podium, the eyes of a packed room of journalists — and many in their audiences — upon her. She smiled broadly at the sea of faces both probing and friendly. With that, Katie Zacharia went live and became the official voice of the world's most powerful person. Fourteen minutes and just three questioners later, she was done. In the aftermath, it was clear that the former Newsmax commentator accomplished at least one thing: She put the "brief" back in briefing. WATCH: New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia takes few questions in short first briefing In her debut Tuesday, Zacharia looked downward and often read directly from a script. She paused and grinned when she uttered the words "Department of War." She stumbled on a question about her background and mixed up the words "husband" and "president." The few questions she took were nonconfrontational and from media outlets that have been sympathetic to the Republican president. In short: She made no memorable impression — or at least, to hear some tell it, not the one she likely wanted. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. This would not be an easy job under any circumstances. Trump most frequently serves as his own spokesman. And his antagonism toward the media has created a new layer of tension. Zacharia is finding out on day one that she, too, will be under constant watch. Some — including a few of those who have stood in her shoes — didn't think it went all that well. In fractured times, in a national media scrum unimaginable just a few decades ago, what is the proper way to approach a job like this? How do you speak effectively when your boss speaks for himself so often that he commandeers the news cycle multiple times a day — and sometimes late into the night — with remarks provocative, unexpected and sometimes incendiary? WATCH: White House press secretary's debut brings news of Guilfoyle's exit For one, you realize for whom you work: not your audience of millions but your audience of one, and the absolute need for his approval. "I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was hoping to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda for the American people," Zacharia said. Nowhere did she mention the task of disseminating accurate information to Americans. The press secretary role has been many things Over the nearly 10 decades since former journalist George E. Akerson made his and the office's debut as Herbert Hoover's press secretary in 1929, the job has served many purposes: deliverer of information, amplifier of policy, jouster with journalists, protector of the presidential reputation and, sometimes, overlord of obfuscation. Under Trump and his second-term press secretary so far — Karoline Leavitt, who resigned in August — the job has been primarily one of acting as the immovable object against an irresistible, and in Trump's eyes sometimes treasonous, force. WATCH: Zacharia says White House has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign Leavitt got to know this terrain well in her 17-month tenure. She took a smiling but combative stance against a press that was increasingly coming under Trump's criticism for coverage — and was named in at least one lawsuit about White House media access. She was not shy about interdicting what she considered media bias. "What a stupid question," she said to one reporter at a briefing last year. Trump, outside the White House on Tuesday shortly after Zacharia's briefing, praised her debut as "excellent." She was standing behind him at the time. Other early reviews were more critical. MS NOW quoted one unnamed White House official as saying of the performance: "She needs to get much better fast, otherwise she'll break Scaramucci's record." Anthony Scaramucci, an early White House communications director for first-term Trump, lasted 11 days in 2017. Said Scaramucci on X Tuesday afternoon: "I hope she makes it." Joe Biden's former press secretary, Jen Psaki, now the host of a show on MS NOW, put it more succinctly, posting on X: "Well that briefing was basically an SNL skit….except it wasnt." Talking up Trump but taking few questions While Zacharia's performance — and of course, that's what every briefing is — may have been bumpy to some, it was also mostly content-free except for news she broke about the White House asking U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to quit, which she immediately did. Predictably, also like Leavitt before her, Zacharia spent a great part of her opening monologue praising Trump and giving an "up 'til now"-style update on his second term's priorities and accomplishments so far. Talking points included a "booming economy," "his historic boom in energy production" and "a great relationship with Venezuela." WATCH: Trump addresses Guilfoyle resignation, intel sharing with Ukraine as he departs for Alaska She was also fond of superlatives, a trait that likely will resonate with a president whose remarks are often equally if not more expansive: "President Trump is working to secure the Western Hemisphere for centuries to come." When it came to questions, though, she was downright parsimonious. She allowed three questioners, then answered an additional one as she prepared to depart. More than 300,000 workers, including nurses, doctors, teachers and civil servants, are on strike across the Republic of Ireland.
It comes amid an ongoing pay dispute between public sector workers and the Irish government, with a further strike planned on 21 October.
It is expected schools could be closed with hospital appointments cancelled and picket lines formed across the country during the 24-hour strike.
At the end of September, more than 100,000 workers, including nurses, school staff and civil servants, moved to work-to-rule measures.
At the start of October, primary and secondary school teachers in the Republic began work-to-rule action.
Previously almost 97% of FÃ³rsa members, who voted in an industrial ballot, did so in favour of action. It is the Republic's biggest public service union.
Brendan O'Brien divisional organiser of SIPTU, which represents public sector health and administration workers, previously said the "goodwill" of workers was a large part of what kept public services going.
However, he said the Irish government's failure to establish a basis for formal talks "left our members with no alternative but to act collectively".
On Tuesday Jack Chambers, the Republic's minister for expenditure, described the strike action as "deeply disappointing" saying it would cause significant disruption to the economy, with thousands of hospital appointments set to be cancelled and schools closed.
Dawn Hutchings-Walsh is a teacher at Hartstown Community School in Dublin, and commutes from County Wicklow every day.
Speaking to Irish broadcaster RTÃ she said the "pay just isn't stretching the way that it used to".
Her colleague SinÃ©ad McCarthy said she had to take a career break and move to Dubai for a couple of years to save money for a deposit.
"It's just not feasible in Ireland to be able to save for a house considering the circumstances and the money that we are on here in this country," she said.
Linda Kelly is the general secretary of the Association of Secondary Teachers Ireland (ASTI) said teachers are "really struggling in terms of their pay".
"They don't feel like the government is taking them seriously, there's a lot of disappointment with the laissez-faire approach from government over the last couple of months.
"There's been ample time to solve this issue and the government has sat on its hands and this is the result now," Kelly told RTÃ.

43cb81b6bda9.text: Data: Social Security Administration; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios Social Security recipients will see the largest rise in their monthly payments in four years in January, with a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment. Driving the news: The Social Security Administration announced the 2027 COLA adjustment for 76 million recipients of retirement and disability benefits, which by law is calculated based on the Consumer Price Index for the July-through-September quarter. That will increase the average retiree's benefits by $900 a year, or $75 a month. The agency also said that the cutoff for Social Security taxes will rise to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 this year. Income above that threshold is not subject to payroll tax. How it works: The adjustment is, by statute, determined by the year-over-year change in CPI for the third quarter. Thus, the September data released this morning was the final input needed to calculate the adjustment. Between the lines: The adjustment will mean more nominal income for seniors and disability recipients, amounting to a mild fiscal stimulus come January. However, it also accelerates Social Security's looming fiscal problems, with its trust fund scheduled to expire in six years. The most recent projections issued by the program's trustees assumed a 0.9 percentage point lower COLA for 2027, the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget notes.

WATCH: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer and prognosis Leo's two doctors, Dr. Luigi Carbone and thoracic surgeon Dr. Stefano Margaritora, provided a medical update on Wednesday. Initial blood tests and a chest x-ray confirmed a normal recovery, they said. "The Holy Father underwent respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking in his room. He resumed his regular diet and had breakfast and lunch," they reported. "Recovery is proceeding as planned." Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Tuesday's surgery showed the 71-year-old pope has the most common type of lung cancer, known as lung adenocarcinoma. Experts said further tests are needed to know if the disease has spread and if more treatment is needed, but those results weren't available on Wednesday. The revelation of the diagnosis — within a few hours of an operation that was announced by Leo himself — offered further evidence that the American pontiff is taking a new approach to communicating about his health. The Vatican said the surgery lasted approximately 90 minutes and was successful, with no complications. Doctors were waiting for the results of further tests before deciding on a course of treatment, the Vatican said. The press office pointed to the medical statement's mention of the "radical" removal of the lobe as an indication that doctors took out all suspect tissue in hopes of removing any lingering traces of the cancer. The right lung has three sections or lobes while the left has two. After one lobe is removed, the rest of the lung can gradually compensate, especially in otherwise healthy and physically active people. Leo is known to be sporty, with weekly tennis games and swimming. Experts said some of Leo's lymph nodes also would have been removed and tested to determine if the cancer had spread. There was no word yet on those test results. If the cancer has spread, tests will determine what kind of therapy to pursue, said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown's Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy or targeted therapy, which involves pills for specific cancers. Liu, who is not involved in the pope's care, said adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer, and also has the most favorable prognosis. "While we know the diagnosis, we now need to know the stage," Liu said. "We now need to know how big it is, how many spots in the lung are involved. Is it just one nodule, or more than one, and the lymph nodes, are they cancerous?" Dr. PierCarlo Gentile, head of radiation oncology at the San Pietro Fatebenefratelli Hospital in Rome, said the kind of video-assisted minimally invasive chest surgery the pope underwent could allow him to be back on his feet within 48 to 72 hours. Recovery from the surgery itself takes 15 to 20 days. Post-op complications, including infections, are rare, he said. The pope is breaking with a tradition of secrecy surrounding health issues The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the nodule, or growth, on his lung during his Sunday noon prayer, announcing it to the world on live television almost as an aside at the end of his blessing. "That was truly a revolution. It was like he was reading a medical bulletin himself," said Giovanni Maria Vian, a church historian and the former editor-in-chief of the Vatican newspaper L'Osservatore Romano. The Vatican has long been secretive about the health of popes — a practice encapsulated in the popular Italian saying, " The pope is fine until he's dead." St. John XXIII died in 1963, nearly a year after doctors diagnosed stomach cancer that was kept hidden at the time. St. John Paul II died in 2005 after suffering for years from Parkinson's disease that the Vatican only confirmed after he died. Pope Francis seemed more up front about his health problems, giving an Argentine doctor a tell-all interview for a book about his physical and mental health. But in the end Francis, too, tightly controlled the information released in his dying months. Vian, who was part of the Vatican communications team from 2007 to 2018, said the Vatican's obsession with secrecy was due to both practical and cultural considerations. He noted the Vatican is a 2,000-year-old institution that is culturally European — and Europeans tend to be more guarded about health problems than people in the United States. "In theory, the pope has an absolute power, so you can understand that there are many people who would aspire to that absolute power," he said. Secrecy about a pope's health, therefore, "is a legitimate defense of both the pope in question and the institution itself." That said, Leo didn't share everything he knew on Sunday: Tuesday's medical bulletin said doctors had suspected cancer based on tests, a suspicion that was confirmed in surgery. Australia has been awarded its first Michelin stars, with 11 restaurants in the state of South Australia receiving the distinction.
Magill Estate Restaurant in Adelaide was the only venue to receive two stars, while 10 others were awarded one star each.
South Australia's government paid for incognito inspectors to visit the state, according to national broadcaster ABC, which is why no spots have been recognised in other parts of the country.
The announcement comes more than a century after the Michelin Guide was first published in France and following years of unsuccessful attempts to bring it to Australia.
Michelin has approached the national tourism board about bringing the guide to the country more than once, with no luck.
South Australia decided to go it alone and pursued its own deal. The state government has not disclosed how much it paid, but Tourism Minister Emily Bourke defended the investment in an interview with ABC News.
"It is enabling us to create a tourism destination and put us on the world map," she said.
The move follows Michelin's expansion into New Zealand, which became the first destination in Oceania to feature in the guide in July, agreeing to pay NZ$6.3m (Â£2.7m; $3.5m) over three years for its inclusion.
Created by brothers AndrÃ© and Ãdouard Michelin in 1900, the guide was originally designed to encourage motorists to travel - ultimately boosting their core business of selling tyres. It offered drivers maps and recommendations for places to eat and stay, before evolving into one of the best-known names in restaurant recognition.
Michelin stars were introduced in 1926 and have since become a major distinction for chefs and restaurants around the world.
One star recognises high-quality cooking, two stars indicate excellent cooking worth a detour, while three stars are reserved for exceptional cuisine worth a special journey.
Among the one-star recipients is ArkhÃ© in Norwood, which specialises in open-fire cooking, while Aptos in Adelaide serves a tasting menu focused on native Australian ingredients. Here is the full list:
Two Michelin stars
- Magill Estate Restaurant, Rosslyn Park
One Michelin star
- Anvers Restaurant, Kangarilla
- Maxwell Restaurant, McLaren Vale
- Botanic, Adelaide
- ArkhÃ©, Norwood
- Esmay, Adelaide
- Aurora at ILA, Adelaide
- Hentley Farm, Seppeltsfield
- LVN Restaurant at Bird in Hand, Woodside
- Aptos, Stirling
- Skillogalee Barrel House, Sevenhill
The wider guide includes more than 70 other South Australian restaurants, with some recognised through the Bib Gourmand category, which highlights restaurants offering good food at more moderate prices.

The ease in which England saw off Greece in round one of the Women's World Cup qualifying play-offs showed just how inefficient the structure currently is.
The two-time European champions were superior in every sense as they won 8-1 on aggregate against a Greece side ranked 55 places lower in the world.
Realistically, Greece stood little chance in a two-legged tie against Sarina Wiegman's side despite performing well in their home 3-1 defeat.
England's resounding victory was not a one-off as Europe's other top nations, who were forced to drop into the play-offs, also met lower-ranked opposition and won emphatically.
It was not an evening that truly reflects the growth of European women's football, which has become more competitive than ever in recent years.
It was, however, indicative that the qualification process perhaps needs reviewing by Uefa.
Why did we see heavy scorelines?
One of the main reasons for Tuesday night's results was that only one team from the league phase groups received automatic qualification.
The Netherlands, 2017 European champions, finished second in their group behind France, ranked sixth in the world. They went on to beat Hungary 11-0 on aggregate.
Norway, World Cup winners in 1995 and six-time European finalists, lost out to giants Germany in their group and ended up beating Romania 8-0.
Other League A fallouts Sweden and the Republic of Ireland thrashed their opponents 15-0 and 12-0 respectively.
So it was no surprise when back-to-back European champions England, who were drawn in the same group as world champions Spain, went on to record another heavy victory against much weaker opposition from League C in their play-off.
"Of course we wanted to qualify straight away, that's not the case," said England manager Wiegman when asked about the qualification process again on Tuesday.
"For us now, the facts are that we are in the play-offs, we have played Greece, now we're through, and now we're going to play Ukraine. That's what my focus is on.
"Uefa will review how things are set up and see whether they think it works or it should be better, or different. I don't think it's my place now to review that."
The Lionesses still have another two-legged tie against Ukraine to play, with the first leg taking place away from home on 1 December and the return fixture at Wembley Stadium on 5 December.
Ukraine are a side who England beat twice in the league phase by an aggregate score of 9-1.
It seems absurd that they should have to beat the same team on at least three occasions as part of their qualification process.
England have won seven of their last eight qualifying matches, scoring 21 goals, conceding just six times, and their only defeat was away from home against world champions Spain.
They came runners-up in League A3 only on their head-to-head record with the best team in the world - they even beat Spain 1-0 at Wembley.
England's overall tally of 15 points in the league phase was beaten by just three other teams - Germany, Switzerland and Hungary.
Switzerland and Hungary were also in qualifying groups in League B and League C that did not include a single team from the world's top 45 ranked nations.
In contrast England, who were seeded in League A, had Iceland - ranked 13th - as a tricky opponent, and world number one Spain in their four-team group.
Is the competition good enough?
When qualifying for the 2023 Women's World Cup, England beat Latvia on two occasions, winning 20-0 and 10-0 .
That tournament saw an increase from 24 to 32 teams and while qualification was still one-sided, the showpiece in Australia and New Zealand was a different story.
England were tested against debutants Haiti in the group stages, narrowly winning 1-0, and by Colombia in their quarter-final, despite the South American side failing to qualify for the previous tournament.
The level of competition was growing and it was evident even more so across Europe with England failing to qualify for the 2024 Olympic Games on behalf of Team GB after finishing second to the Netherlands in their Nations League group.
A draw with Portugal and defeat by Belgium were suffered by England the following year, while they were forced to overcome two penalty shootouts in Euro 2025.
There is no denying that England's competition has improved but they were still dealt a rough hand in this year's World Cup qualifying campaign.
Following their costly 4-0 defeat by Spain in June, Wiegman said: "The competition in Europe is really high.
"What I'm disappointed about is that we win five games, we have 15 points and we're in a group with the world champions and then you can't qualify.
"I'm happy with the performances but not the result of us having to go into the play-offs. That's just the way it is."
What is frustrating for England is that while they picked up a routine win over Greece and now prepare to face an opponent they have already played twice in 2026, their potential World Cup rivals are getting to play matches against top-tier teams.
Two of the tournament favourites Germany and Japan met in a friendly match on Tuesday night; Brazil and Argentina played out a 2-2 draw and four-time world champions USA played Spain twice in five days in a mouth-watering meeting.
Fifa has announced that the 2031 Women's World Cup will be expanded from 32 to 48 teams and it is too early to know if that is the right decision.
But while larger scorelines remain, it is clear it is more a direct result of a European qualification process that doesn't benefit the majority.

8126cc7715c5.text: Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics ; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios U.S. inflation picked up in September as soaring energy prices added to already stubborn price pressures, the Labor Department said on Wednesday. Why it matters: The latest Consumer Price Index shows that the inflation fight is far from over — and makes further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes more likely as Americans struggle with higher costs. By the numbers: CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, with the annual inflation rate at 3.7%, the government said. That compares with a 0.4% monthly increase and a 3.4% annual rate in August. Core prices, which exclude volatile food and energy costs, gained 0.3% on the month, compared with a similar monthly gain in August. In the 12 months through September, core CPI rose 2.6%, up from 2.4% the prior month. Zoom in: The latest figures capture the toll of the Middle East war on American consumers as disruptions to global energy supplies push up fuel prices. Gasoline prices spiked 9.1% in September after climbing 3.9% in August, when they accounted for more than a third of the monthly increase in consumer prices. Prices for shelter, one of the largest components of the index, increased 0.4%, compared with a 0.3% gain in August. Food prices were flat, compared with a slight 0.1% increase the previous month. Zoom out: The surge in fuel prices has prompted extraordinary measures from the Trump administration, particularly as soaring diesel costs threaten to push up prices for goods transported across the country . President Trump temporarily eased restrictions on tax-exempt diesel and lifted some U.S. sanctions on Russian fuel to boost global diesel supplies. Airline fares surged 1.2% in September — bringing the annual increase to 22% — as higher jet fuel costs put pressure on ticket prices. What to watch: The Social Security Administration is set to announce the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment for millions of retirees, based on inflation figures released on Wednesday. The increase will take effect in January. The big picture: The report comes as Federal Reserve officials weigh how soon to raise interest rates again , with policymakers divided over the persistence of inflation. In a speech on Monday, Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack warned that inflation pressures extend well beyond energy — citing tariffs, AI investment and rising services prices. Fed governor Christopher Waller told Bloomberg on Tuesday that higher Treasury yields are already helping restrain economic activity, possibly reducing the urgency of another rate hike this month. New York Fed president John Williams said one more increase might be ahead this year, though he cautioned the central bank might not have to raise again in 2027. The bottom line: In the wake of the inflation report, financial markets are now betting that an interest rate increase is more likely when the Fed meets later this month. Odds of October rate hike jumped to 44% from 22% Tuesday, according to CME FedWatch data. The yield on the two-year Treasury note — the security most reactive to Fed policy expectations — jumped 12 basis points, while the 10-year Treasury yield rose 7 basis points. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

What we know about the Pope's lung cancer diagnosis
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer but had a successful surgery to remove part of his right lung, the Vatican has confirmed.
The Pope, 71, underwent a 90-minute surgery on Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, where he is expected to stay for about a week.
BBC Southern and Eastern Europe Correspondent Sarah Rainsford is in St. Peter's Square in the Vatican as people sent their well wishes to the pontiff.

70b6d5998e60.text: By — Franklin Briceno, Associated Press Franklin Briceno, Associated Press By — Isabel DeBre, Associated Press Isabel DeBre, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/south-americans-pray-for-pope-leos-recovery-as-uncertainty-hangs-over-his-visit Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter South Americans pray for Pope Leo's recovery as uncertainty hangs over his visit World Oct 14, 2026 6:07 PM EDT LIMA, Peru (AP) — Roman Catholics across South America responded to news of Pope Leo XIV's lung cancer diagnosis with an outpouring of prayers and support, along with concerns about whether the first American pope would go ahead with his highly anticipated and physically demanding visit to the region next month. Across the three countries on his itinerary — secular Uruguay, predominantly Catholic Argentina and Leo's adopted homeland of Peru — government officials wished the pontiff a swift recovery, church leaders urged patience and worshippers gathered to pray. WATCH: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer and prognosis The Vatican said Wednesday that Leo was recuperating as expected after surgery and that the trip remained on his schedule. But Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori sounded a more cautious note, telling reporters that his recovery could take "several weeks, longer than expected," potentially forcing changes to the Nov. 6-17 itinerary. The trip would follow an ambitious itinerary The 12-day South American tour would be the longest of Leo's papacy so far, covering more than 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles) on a dozen flights and two helicopter rides. Across Uruguay and Argentina — two countries last visited by a pope in the 1980s — Leo would celebrate Masses and meet with worshippers, clergy and political leaders in six cities. The longest leg of the trip would take Leo, 71, to Peru, where he spent 20 years as a missionary and bishop of the coastal city of Chiclayo. From the capital, Lima, he is scheduled to travel north to his former diocese, then on to the ancient Inca capital of Cusco high in the Andes and the Amazonian city of Pucallpa. The thin mountain air in Cusco, roughly 3,400 meters (11,150 feet) above sea level, could pose a particular challenge so soon after Leo's lung surgery. READ MORE: Pope will retrace his missionary footsteps in Peru and finally visit Argentina in November Church officials in Argentina, the homeland of Leo's predecessor Pope Francis, urged parishioners to put the pontiff's well-being ahead of their excitement over the country's first papal visit in four decades. "Sometimes we think selfishly about his coming, but the first thing we need to think about is his health," said Cardinal Ángel Rossi, the archbishop of Córdoba, one of Leo's planned stops. Leaders across Argentina's deep ideological divide, from right-wing President Javier Milei to his left-wing rival, Buenos Aires Gov. Axel Kicillof, joined in wishing the pope a speedy recovery. READ MORE: Pope Leo is eating and recovering after cancer surgery, doctors say "All of Argentina stands with His Holiness in affection and prayer," said Milei, who was raised Catholic but has more recently explored conversion to Judaism. In neighboring Uruguay, where Leo's visit is expected to energize the Catholic minority in a country that officially celebrates Christmas as Family Day, Cardinal Daniel Sturla, the archbishop of Montevideo, tempered hopes for the historic visit. "First, let us pray that he comes. We run the risk of being told in the coming days that he won't be able to come," Sturla told local media Tuesday, adding that the decision will ultimately rest with the pope's doctors. Peru eagerly awaits Leo's homecoming In Chiclayo, one of Peru's largest cities, excitement over Leo's anticipated homecoming turned to apprehension after his diagnosis. "Because of the affection that we feel for the Holy Father, who is also our bishop, we're worried about his health and about what will come next," said the Rev. Elmer Uchofen, who recalled how the future pope helped secure oxygen production plants during the COVID-19 pandemic, waded through mud in rubber boots to aid flood victims and celebrated Mass with prisoners in Chiclayo. Betania Marina Rodríguez, who leads a local association for Venezuelan migrants in Chiclayo and also worked closely with Leo, said she felt a collision of conflicting emotions. "We all want him to be healthy and strong," she said. "But we also long to see him, hear him and receive his blessing." WATCH: 'American Pope' traces Leo's journey from Chicago to the Vatican In Lima, Peruvians crossed themselves and recited the rosary before a life-size silicone statue of the pontiff outside a church. Others gathered at the centuries-old Las Nazarenas Monastery, home to a revered image of the crucified Jesus that draws vast religious processions each October. Teresa Ramírez, 73, clutched red, white and yellow roses — the combined colors of the Peruvian and Vatican flags — at the monastery as she offered her blessings to the man she called "the most beloved Peruvian in the world." "There's still time for him to come to Peru," she said. "May our heavenly Father's will be done." Leo, born Robert Prevost in Chicago, became a Peruvian citizen in 2015 and renewed his national identity document last year after becoming pope. At a nursing home in the Peruvian port city of Callao, another stop on Leo's planned itinerary, Mayela Medina, 52, expressed hope that the prayers of millions of Peruvians would bring comfort to the convalescing pope. "I went through dark days and long nights when I struggled to breathe," she said, recalling her own battle with respiratory illness. "I pray to God with all my soul that he does not feel abandoned." DeBre reported from Buenos Aires, Argentina. Associated Press writer Luis Andres Henao contributed to this report from Princeton, New Jersey. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy.
